Title: Human-specific CCG-repeat insertion in the RBFOX1 promoter implicated in autism and speech enhances EGR1-responsive activity
Authors: Lee, C.; Davenport, M. H.; Jarvis, E. D.
Abstract: Human-specific promoter innovations have been predicted to shape human-specific traits. Here, we investigated the RBFOX1 splice regulator gene, which is specifically upregulated in human and songbird speech/song brain areas. We found that the human RBFOX1 promoter associated with autism and language impairment harbors a human-specific CCG trinucleotide insertion creating a functional CCG-repeat motif. Comparative single-nucleus transcriptome analyses of primate brains indicate that the human promoter drives differential expression in cortical excitatory neurons. Reporter assays show that the human CCG-repeat motif, relative to the chimpanzee allele, increases promoter activity with the EGR1 transcription factor. Genome-wide, the CCG-repeat motif marks core promoters of 104 genes, related to postsynaptic function and autism. In PTCHD1, a clinical duplication in autism patients creates another CCG-repeat motif that similarly increases EGR1-responsive promoter activity. Our findings suggest that small CCG-repeat variants in regulatory regions can exert large effects on gene regulation and apparent associated traits.

Title: A StayGold-based calcium ion indicator
Authors: Miyazaki, I.; Tsao, K. K.; Terai, T.; Takahashi-Yamashiro, K.; Campbell, R. E.
Abstract: Genetically encoded calcium ion (Ca2+) indicators (GECIs) enable visualization of Ca2+ dynamics in living systems but often suffer from limited photostability during prolonged imaging. The recent discovery of StayGold, a green fluorescent protein (FP) with exceptional brightness and photostability, opened the possibility of addressing this longstanding challenge. Here, we sought to establish whether a monomeric variant of StayGold (mStayGold) could be converted into a single FP-based GECI. Through extensive protein engineering, we generated a functional mStayGold-based GECI, HiCaRI (Highly intensiometric Ca2+ Responsive Indicator) by fusing Calmodulin (CaM) and the ckkap binding peptide from K-GECO1 into mStayGold(J). HiCaRI exhibits a large Ca2+-dependent inverse fluorescence response ({triangleup}F/Fmin = -15) while retaining high brightness and improved photostability relative to previously reported GFP-based GECIs. Although the current variant represents a first-generation prototype with shortcomings in terms of Ca2+ affinity and photostability (relative to StayGold and mStayGold(J)), this work demonstrates the feasibility of constructing single FP-based GECIs from a highly photostable fluorescent protein.

Title: AmyloCore-ML: AI/Machine Learning Enabled Identification of Amyloid Fibril Core Regions Using Protein Language Models
Authors: Singh, J.; Jangid, R.; Srivastava, A.
Abstract: Identification of amyloid forming regions in proteins remains central to understanding of their aggregation behaviour, which are central to various neurodegenerative and systemic disorders. Many predictors have been designed to identify amyloid forming regions, however they may not necessarily identify total residues found in actual disease associated fibril structures. To address this, we formed a sequence-based based predictor-AmyloCore-ML to ascertain structural amyloid-core propensity. The predictor was developed using experimentally determined fibril structures obtained from Amyloid Atlas. Ordered residues in the experimental structures were designated as core, and unresolved sampled from the same proteins as matched controls as non-core. Core and non-core regions were encoded using various physicochemical descriptors and protein language model (PLM) embeddings (ESM-2, ANKH, ProtT5) and evaluated using protein-grouped cross-validation. PLMs consistently outperformed physicochemical descriptors, with the best models reaching AUROC values of ~0.88 and AUPRC values of ~0.85. Locked full-length protein scans further localized experimental cores, with ESM-2/ExtraTrees achieving AUROC 0.833, AUPRC 0.751, and a mean peak distance of 12.4 residues. In comparative benchmarking, our predictor showed better performance metrics than CrossBeta and AggrescanAI. The framework therefore provides residue-resolved prediction of structurally incorporated amyloid-core regions directly from sequence.

Title: MtbAIM: AI/ML-guided endpoint-specific prediction of small-molecule activity across drug-susceptible and drug-resistant Mycobacterium tuberculosis
Authors: Singh, J.; Singh, K.
Abstract: The emergence of drug resistance in Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb) presents a major challenge to drug discovery, as compounds active against drug-susceptible (DS) isolates may not retain comparable inhibitory activity against drug-resistant (DR) isolates. Here, we developed an AI/ML workflow to independently prioritize small molecules separately against DS and DR isolates of M.tb and predict MIC, MIC90, and MIC99 as distinct quantitative endpoints. Following curation of data retrieved from the ChEMBL repository, molecular-activity datasets comprised 25,645 and 3,749 compounds tested against whole cell DS and DR isolates respectively. Molecular representations were generated using RDKit descriptors and Morgan fingerprints, along with embeddings from ChemBERTa, MolCLR, and Uni-Mol, and evaluated for binary activity classification and endpoint-specific regression. The best-performing DS classifier combined RDKit/Morgan features with ExtraTrees (balanced accuracy 0.782; AUROC 0.864; AUPRC 0.870), while histogram gradient boosting using the same features performed best for DR classification (balanced accuracy 0.762; AUROC 0.836; AUPRC 0.880). Similarly, RDKit/Morgan features combined with tree-based regressors achieved the best overall performance across all six DS/DR regression endpoints, with pooled out-of-fold RMSE values ranging from 0.604 to 0.784 pMIC units. To facilitate broader application, we developed MtbAIM (https://github.com/jasdeep002/MtbAIM), a Google Colab-based prediction platform that enables users to assess and prioritize small molecules against DS and DR isolates of M.tb.

Title: Non-canonical cleavage expands prime editing in 5' direction
Authors: Chen, P.-R.; Yuan, X.-Z.; Wang, S.-G.; Xia, P.-F.
Abstract: Cleavage-dependent CRISPR-Cas gene editing relies on RNA-guided DNA cleavage that drives cellular machinery to incorporate intended edits. Beyond canonical cleavage, CRISPR nucleases can also execute non-canonical cleavage on the displaced DNA strand. Here, we report a modified design principle for prime editing that leverages the non-canonical cleavage activity, enabling editing in the 5' direction of a classic nick site. We elucidate the non-canonical-cleavage-driven reverse transcription pathway that initiates upstream of the classic nick site. We identify competition between the canonical and non-canonical routes, which can be modulated by rationally designing RNA templates carrying the intended edits. We demonstrate that cellular physiology enhances editing efficiency from individual reverse-transcription product yet exerts limited influence on pathway competitions. Our findings revise the design principle of prime editing and establish a new dimension for engineering CRISPR-Cas systems by harnessing its intrinsic, non-host-specific, non-canonical cleavage activity.

Title: InfluProto: Predicting Cross-Species Transmission of Influenza A Virus via Prototype Learning
Authors: Geng, Z.; Li, L.; Ye, R.; Wang, Y.; Song, S.
Abstract: Zoonotic influenza A viruses pose constitute a significant persistent threat to global public health, yet quantitative approaches for assessing their cross-species transmission potential remain limited. Here, we present InfluProto, a deep learning model that introduces prototype learning into host prediction for influenza A virus, framing conceptualizing host adaptation as a continuous process rather than a discrete outcome. InfluProto embeds viral sequences into a continuous representation space anchored by human, swine, and avian prototypes, using cosine distances as a quantitative measure of host adaptation. InfluProto accurately discriminated among the three host classes, achieving recall and precision exceeding 0.97, and substantially outperformed conventional classification models models--particularly on challenging zoonotic strains, including the 2009 pandemic H1N1 (pdm09) lineage. Beyond host classification, the learned representations captured biologically meaningful host-adaptive signatures,; notably, with pdm09 viruses occupying occupied an intermediate position between human and swine clusters, consistent with their evolutionary origin. Analysis of simulated reassortment further revealed that the introduction of human-origin segments into swine influenza viruses reduced their distance to the human prototype, indicating that InfluProto can detect reassortment-associated shifts in host adaptation. To facilitate broad public useaccess, we have developed an interactive web service for InfluProto. Collectively, our work establishes a continuous framework for characterizing host adaptation and evaluating zoonotic risk in influenza A viruses, with potential implications for pandemic surveillance and preparedness.

Title: Quantification of grapevine yield losses as a function downy mildew severity on foliage and cluster
Authors: Fabre, F.; Delbac, L.; Poeydebat, C.; Zaffaroni, M.
Abstract: To quantify the relationship between grapevine disease severity and crop losses at the plant scale, we conducted a three-year field experiment at two sites near Bordeaux (France), monitoring mildews and rots on both foliage and clusters. Preliminary analyses revealed that only downy mildew (DM) significantly impacted yield under our experimental conditions. We capitalized on this single-disease dominance to isolate the effect of DM severity (assessed via standardized AUDPC), on both foliage and clusters, on yield loss at the individual vine scale. At a cluster AUDPC of 5%, yield consistently declined by 24% across all years and sites. Conversely, yield loss at a 5% foliar AUDPC ranged from 9% to 60% depending on the site and year, reflecting a tenfold variation in the damage coefficient. This variability strongly correlated with a moisture risk index computed between the phenological stages of visible inflorescences and pre-ripening berries. Specifically, at 5% foliar AUDPC, the expected yield loss escalated from 9% in a dry season (10th percentile of the index) to 15% in an intermediate season (median), reaching 39% in a wet season (90th percentile). Future research should aim to validate these statistical models across broader climatic, geographic, and agronomic contexts, including the characterization of cultivar-specific responses.

Title: Identifiability of metabolic resilience from sparse longitudinal metabolomics
Authors: Aminian-Dehkordi, J.; Mofrad, M.
Abstract: Sparse and irregular longitudinal metabolomic measurements can make dynamical quantities numerically estimable without making them scientifically identifiable. We formulate effective-landscape inference as an observation-timescale inverse problem and evaluate its operating characteristics using stochastic systems with known ground truth and longitudinal stool metabolomics from the Integrative Human Microbiome Project. Across simulation ensembles, recovery of a known double-well topology declined sharply as observations became sparse, whereas the tested monostable controls did not generate spurious secondary minima. Findings establish an identifiability hierarchy: global topology requires sufficient within-subject state-space coverage, whereas local return descriptors remain vulnerable to bias from the observation process. The framework therefore shifts the emphasis from assigning stability labels to determining what a sampling design can support. It provides a basis for designing denser longitudinal experiments and for validating clinical and machine-learning studies in which sparse observations might otherwise be overinterpreted as evidence about underlying dynamics.

Title: Chromid transforms opportunistic pathogen into beneficial symbiont to raise coral's thermal tipping point
Authors: Sim, C. W. H.; Luk, H. H. C.; Pereyra, J. P. A.; Loh, A. A. R.; Lim, J. J. H.; Leong, W.; Khaw, J. C. H.; Srinivas, S.; Tiaras, I.; Kirchberger, P. C.; Lim, L. J. W.; Ng, L. C. S.; Deignan, L. K.; Tanzil, J. T. I.; Case, R. J.
Abstract: Resilient turbid coral reefs, found 1{degrees} north of the equator, experience fewer and less intense bleaching events despite being situated within the world's busiest shipping port in highly urbanised Singapore. We hypothesised that bacteria within the coral holobiont play a role in maintaining coral health by conferring traits that enhance thermal tolerance. Eleven Pseudovibrio isolates were obtained from the scleractinian coral Pachyseris speciosa, and their genomes differed by only four single nucleotide polymorphisms. A ~490 kbp chromid, pCJH, was present in 7 of the 11 isolates. A Pseudovibrio isolate without pCJH is an opportunistic pathogen of P. speciosa, accelerating bleaching disease. In contrast, the chromid reduces Pseudovibrio's fecundity, enhances its host colonisation and consequently increases P. speciosa's thermal tolerance by 1 {degrees}C. Interaction analyses in experimentally heat-stressed corals revealed a negative interaction between Pseudovibrio and Vibrio ASVs. The Pseudovibrio genomes and chromid encode several diffusible antibiotic biosynthetic gene clusters and two type six secretion systems (T6SS) for contact-dependent inhibition, with both types of inhibitory activity shown against opportunistic coral pathogens from local (i.e. isolated from the same coral host) and type-strain Vibrio spp. Together, these findings support the Coral Probiotic Hypothesis that bacteria enhance coral resilience, and identify a chromid responsible for Pseudovibrio's climatically driven Jekyll-and-Hyde lifestyle from opportunistic pathogen to beneficial symbiont.

Title: Coordinated Enhancement of Molecular and Spatial Fidelity for Biological Inference in Spatial Transcriptomics
Authors: Wang, X.; Que, N.; Liu, H.; Tao, C.; Jiang, Y.; Jiang, Y.; Zhu, P.; Xu, J.; Yan, H.; Ye, B.; Price, S.; Xi, J.; Wang, X.; Li, C.
Abstract: Understanding tissue organization requires accurate molecular quantification and faithful spatial localization. Spatial omics, particularly spatial transcriptomics (ST), face measurement trade-offs that limit simultaneous achievement of molecular and spatial fidelity across spatial resolution, detection sensitivity, molecular-tissue alignment and cell-level fidelity. Existing computational methods typically target individual aspects and optimize them in isolation, despite their interdependence. Here we present FOCUS, a multimodal generative foundation model for coordinated ST enhancement. FOCUS integrates native ST with histology images, cell masks, scRNA-seq references and spatial co-expression priors through task-specific modules, with cross-task coordination enabling joint correction of co-occurring limitations. FOCUS improved the performance of individual enhancement tasks and provided additional gains with coordinated mitigation of coupled limitations. Across immunology, tissue development and oncology, FOCUS recovered biologically consistent patterns obscured in native ST or isolated enhancement, enabling clearer inference of neutrophil-tumor interactions, spatial osteocyte differentiation and primary-metastatic HNSCC programs. Together, FOCUS establishes coordinated enhancement of molecular and spatial fidelity as a strategy for downstream biological inference from ST.

Title: Inherent limitations of zero-shot mutation prediction in protein engineering
Authors: Woolley, P. R.; Feller, A.; Ellington, A. O.; Wilke, C. O.
Abstract: Predicting mutation effects is critical for protein engineering. A commonly pursued strategy is zero-shot prediction with deep-learning models, whose performance is typically evaluated using aggregate benchmark scores that obscure multidimensional biological tradeoffs. Here, we evaluate sequence, structure, and hybrid foundation models across curated datasets to expose the practical limitations of zero-shot predictions. We demonstrate that model performance is highly variable and heavily influenced by experimental noise and competing phenotypic goals. Notably, predictions from competing models often correlate more strongly with one another than with experimental outcomes. While current models effectively filter deleterious mutations and enrich high-scoring variants for natural functions, they struggle to identify precise optimal mutations and consistently fail to predict mutations that drive new-to-nature functions. These models learn from evolutionary constraints that tend to oppose the extreme biophysical optimizations required in targeted engineering. Consequently, zero-shot scoring serves as a valuable initial filter but cannot substitute for task-specific prediction.

Title: A critical evaluation of Gene Ontology priors in biologically-informed neural networks
Authors: Verlaan, T.; Lieftinck, M.; Mwine, W.; Reinders, M.
Abstract: Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) embed prior knowledge such as the Gene Ontology (GO) into their architecture to produce interpretable representations, yet whether and how this prior improves performance or interpretation remains unclear. We introduce GONNECT, a BINN incorporating GO into an autoencoder. We evaluate GO constraints in the encoder, decoder, or both on RNA-seq tumour samples from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), comparing against published BINNs (OntoVAE, VEGA), an unconstrained baseline, randomized priors, and untrained networks. Across various performance metrics, GO structure adds little to reconstruction or latent-space organization, frequently matched by randomized or unconstrained models. Node activations agree with a gene set enrichment analysis (GSEA)-derived reference, but this agreement largely arises from the architectural constraint: it is lost when GO connections are randomized, present even before training in the encoder, and learned in the decoder. Regularized soft links outside GO (GONNECT-SL) are unstable across runs and concentrate where the ontology is sparse, compensating for the prior's constraints rather than revealing new biology. Within this setting, we find no evidence that node activations capture biological information beyond that encoded by the predefined gene sets, suggesting that their apparent interpretability largely reflects the prior imposed by the architecture.

Title: Histology-aware Inference of Cell-cell Communication in Spatial Transcriptomics
Authors: Wang, X.; Tao, C.; Jiang, Y.; Jiang, Y.; Liu, H.; Jiang, Z.; Zhu, P.; Que, N.; Xi, J.; Price, S.; Qian, B.; Xu, J.; Li, C.
Abstract: Cell-cell communication (CCC) is fundamental to tissue organization and function, yet inferring communication from spatial transcriptomics (ST) remains challenging because molecular and spatial information does not fully capture the anatomical context of signaling. Paired hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained images provide complementary insights into tissue architecture and cellular morphology, which remain underutilized as the explicit contextual constraint of CCC inference. Here we present HARMONIC, a histology-aware graph learning framework for anatomically contextualized CCC inference from ST and H&E images. HARMONIC uses conditional mutual information to model dependencies among tissue architecture, ligand-receptor-mediated signaling, gene expression and morphology, and integrates these representations through self-supervised graph learning. Across synthetic and biological datasets spanning platforms, species and tissues, HARMONIC suppresses less anatomically plausible interactions while recovering context-supported signaling across tumor-immune interfaces, necrotic transitions, anatomical compartments and microvascular structures. These findings establish tissue architecture as the explicit contextual constraint of spatial CCC inference.

Title: 'broadSeq', a benchmarking tool to contrast differential gene expression methods and identify when genomic neighbourhood matters
Authors: Das Roy, R.; Hallikas, O.; Kuure, S.; Jernvall, J.
Abstract: Several tools are available to detect differential gene expression. The predominant approach of different statistical methods is to consider changes in gene expression independent from their genomic context. Previously, DELocal was introduced that takes into consideration gene expression dynamics in the genomic neighbourhood. Whereas DELocal was shown to identify developmentally regulated genes in developing mouse tooth, its performance in other biological conditions remains undetermined. To benchmark DElocal together with other methods, we develop another tool 'broadSeq'. It provides easy to use interface for methods like DELocal , deseq2, limma, edger, EBSeq and many more. Here we report benchmarking results on different data sets that comprise wild type developing mouse organs from different embryonic time points, and also human cancer data. The examined datasets are from the heart, kidney, liver, brain, forebrain, and hindbrain. We found that most methods produce relatively comparable lists of differentially expressed genes. Nevertheless, DELocal identifies partially distinct sets of genes compared to the other methods. Evaluating the identified genes using gene and disease ontology terms show that the uniquely detected genes by DELocal are biologically relevant and also highly expressed compared to the genes identified by the other methods. Because consistently highly expressed genes show relatively subtle fold changes, the neighbourhood concept of DELocal appears to correct for the difficulty in detecting these differential expression of highly expressed genes. Finally, we provide the tools as combined bioconductor packages, allowing researchers to explore and decide the best methods for their data and questions.

Title: Cell Painting and machine learning for mechanistic profiling of hepatotoxic botanicals and their constituents
Authors: Ollitrault, G.; Mitchell, C. A.; Ferguson, S. S.; Roe, A. L.; White, B.; Titterton, K.; Ewald, J.
Abstract: BACKGROUND Botanicals are widely consumed as herbal remedies and plant-derived products, but their complex and variable chemical composition presents major challenges for safety assessment. Although hepatotoxicity has been reported for several botanicals, the constituent compounds responsible and the underlying mechanisms often remain poorly characterised. OBJECTIVES We aimed to determine whether Cell Painting could identify candidate constituent drivers of botanical bioactivity and generate hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action in primary human hepatocytes. METHODS We profiled 13 botanical extracts and 85 known constituents across multiple concentrations using Cell Painting alongside assays of metabolic activity and membrane integrity. To interpret morphological phenotypes, we trained machine-learning models using a Cell Painting reference atlas of >1,000 chemicals linked to ToxCast/Tox21 molecular and cellular bioactivity annotations. RESULTS Cell Painting detected bioactivity in 11/13 botanical extracts and 46/85 constituents, compared with 9/13 extracts and 40/85 constituents in the cell-health assays, and generally detected activity at lower concentrations. For 9/13 extracts, at least one constituent was active at a lower concentration than the corresponding botanical extract, supporting the contribution of a subset of potent constituents to mixture-level responses. Aristolochia and goldenseal were the most potent extracts across Cell Painting and cell-health assays and contained highly active constituents. Reference-atlas models generated specific mechanistic hypotheses, including cytotoxicity-, endocrine-, and genotoxicity-associated responses for several botanicals and constituents. CONCLUSION These results support Cell Painting combined with machine learning as a sensitive approach for characterising cellular responses to botanicals, prioritising candidate constituent drivers of hepatotoxicity-associated phenotypes, and generating testable hypotheses about potential mechanisms of action.

Title: A Tandem Fluorescent Rh1::eGFP mCherry Reporter Reveals Rhodopsin 1 Trafficking and Turnover In Vivo in Drosophila Photoreceptors
Authors: Gheflati, H.; Steiner, C.; Feizy, N.
Abstract: Rhodopsin 1 (Rh1), the major visual pigment of Drosophila photoreceptors, requires a vitamin A-derived chromophore for proper folding, maturation and transport to the rhabdomere. While the endocytic trafficking of mature, light-activated Rh1 to endolysosomal compartments is well characterized, the fate of immature Rh1 during defective ER maturation remains unclear. Here, we developed a Rh1::eGFP-mCherry tandem reporter to monitor Rh1 localization and compartment acidification in vivo. Exploiting the acid stability of mCherry, this reporter enables visualization of Rh1 after delivery to acidic environments and complements conventional antibody-based approaches. Under physiological conditions, pH-dependent quenching of eGFP fluorescence distinguished rhabdomeric Rh1 from Rh1 in acidic endolysosomal compartments. In vitamin A-deficient flies, immature apo-Rh1 accumulated within Calnexin-positive ER membranes, where we identified discrete acidified subdomains characterized by loss of eGFP fluorescence while mCherry fluorescence persisted. These structures remained continuous with the ER but were distinct from conventional endolysosomal compartments, revealing previously unrecognized acidified ER domains associated with immature Rh1. Together, our findings identify acidified ER subdomains as a previously unrecognized stage in Rh1 quality control and establish Rh1::eGFP-mCherry as a robust in vivo reporter for investigating rhodopsin trafficking, maturation and turnover under physiological and disease-relevant conditions.

Title: Inter-unit variability and rapid depletion of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate in stored red blood cells: implications for transfusion practice in neurocritical care
Authors: Peris, M.; Sahuquillo, J.; Ortuno, A.; Pons, V.; Rierola, M.; Poca, M. A.
Abstract: Red blood cell (RBC) transfusion aims to restore tissue oxygen delivery, yet a stored unit's capacity to unload oxygen depends on 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG), the principal allosteric modulator of hemoglobin-oxygen affinity. Randomized trials comparing fresher with older units have been consistently null, and all have used storage duration as the exposure variable. We asked whether storage age reflects the metabolic state of individual units. Twenty-four leukodepleted packed RBC units were sampled serially from day 3 to day 42 of standard cold storage. 2,3-DPG was quanti-fied by liquid chromatography-mass spectrometry (LC-MS) with isotopically labelled internal standards, pH was measured in parallel, and trajectories were modelled by linear mixed effects with unit-level random intercepts. At day 3, 2,3-DPG spanned a twenty-fold range across units of identical age (0.8-14.7 mol/g Hb; median 4.8): some were already near-depleted at the earliest sampled timepoint, while others retained near-physiological concentrations. This heterogeneity collapsed rapidly - median val-ues fell to 27% of day-3 levels by day 7 and by more than 90% by day 14 ({beta} = -0.298 mol/g Hb per day, p < 0.001) - and were below the limit of detection in most units af-ter day 17. pH declined monotonically to 6.40 {+/-} 0.04 by day 42 ({beta} = -0.0163 units per day, p < 0.001). Units of identical storage age therefore differ markedly in the metabo-lite that governs oxygen unloading, and virtually all are depleted long before the 42-day expiry, indicating that storage-age dichotomies misclassify the exposure they are intended to represent.

Title: FLEX-DBS: a flexible wireless platform for bilateral constant-current deep brain stimulation in freely moving rodents
Authors: Graham, R. D.; Creed, M. C.; Gaidica, M.
Abstract: Background: Preclinical deep brain stimulation (DBS) in rodents is central to understanding how DBS works, but most rodent DBS is delivered through a tether, which constrains behavior, home-cage experiments and uninterrupted stimulation. Most long-runtime wireless mouse stimulators achieve their runtimes by setting stimulation parameters before or around implantation and operating from supplies of about 3 V. New method: FLEX-DBS (Flexible Deep Brain Stimulation) is a head-mounted, battery-powered stimulator that delivers bilateral constant-current stimulation from improved Howland current pumps on +/-5 V rails. Amplitude, pulse width and frequency are programmable in continuous and burst modes from an iOS application over Bluetooth Low Energy, and stimulation continues autonomously after the phone disconnects. The device measures 19.5 x 22.5 x 8.72 mm, weighs 3.71 g in operation and runs on two size-13 zinc-air cells, which are exchanged by briefly detaching the device, pausing stimulation only for the exchange. Results: Into a 1 k{Omega} bench load, delivered current increased approximately linearly with the amplitude setting and was repeatable from pulse to pulse, with an asymmetric biphasic waveform whose recovery phase ran at about one fifth of the stimulating amplitude. Battery current was 1.47-1.89 mA in standby and 3.15-3.42 mA during stimulation at amplitude settings of 60-400 A, giving a projected three days of continuous stimulation per pair of cells. Firmware v0.5 left a net charge of 26-35 % of the stimulating-phase charge per pulse into 1 k{Omega}. Into 47 k{Omega}, within the in vivo load range, stimulating current was compliance-limited at 93 A. Pulse-derived estimates of the effective load presented by five implanted platinum electrodes in three mice had weekly means of 43-54 k{Omega} over eight weeks (32-80 k{Omega} across individual sessions), placing the maximum regulated current near 90 A (81-101 A at the weekly means). Analysis of the current-pump network bounds load-dependent current error at 3-8% for these loads. In vivo, we delivered cingulate FLEX-DBS at high amplitude settings intended to evoke a robust stimulation-associated behavioral phenotype in six mice. Time spent immobile in an open field rose from 46.5% at baseline to 75.7% during stimulation (a 62.7% increase in the group mean) and remained elevated after stimulation ended; without a sham control, this increase cannot be separated from within-session habituation. Comparison with existing methods: Among the published wireless rodent stimulators compared here, several offer some of these capabilities, but none combines bilateral constant current output, real-time wireless control that continues as autonomous stimulation after disconnect, and both continuous and burst modes; FLEX-DBS does so at the cost of runtime measured in days rather than weeks. Conclusions: FLEX-DBS is designed for untethered DBS experiments in which parameters must be set, changed and verified at the cage. Its measured power consumption permits a projected three days of continuous operation per cell pair; firmware v0.5 requires improved charge balancing before prolonged in vivo stimulation. The electrode load, rather than the programmable range, sets the usable stimulation amplitude in vivo. In vivo, stimulation at high amplitude settings was associated with increased immobility, consistent with effective stimulation through implanted electrodes; electrode impedance and delivered current were not measured in these mice.

Title: Surfactant-Enhanced Hybridization Capture for Direct Sequence-Specific RNA Extraction from Plasma and Whole Blood
Authors: Kim, W.; Gilligan-Steinberg, S. D.; Kline, E. C.; Beck, I.; Frenkel, L. M.; Lutz, B. R.
Abstract: Direct recovery of low-abundance RNA from complex biological samples remains a major challenge for ultrasensitive detection. Sequence-specific hybridization capture enables selective enrichment, but recovery from crude samples is compromised by RNA degradation, protein interference, RNA secondary structure, and target sequence variation. Here, we address these limitations with a sodium dodecyl sulfate (SDS)-based formulation that not only lyses virions and protects RNA, but also directly accelerates hybridization kinetics, substantially reducing the need for thermal denaturation. This enabled direct RNA capture from crude plasma or whole blood with near-quantitative recovery, outperforming a widely used silica-based kit at low input. Without centrifugation or plasma separation, we detected HIV RNA by RT-qPCR at 25 copies/mL directly from whole blood. We further developed a free energy ({Delta}G)-guided algorithm for mutation-robust probe design, achieving >85% mean recovery across HIV-1 subtypes with a single probe. This work opens low-abundance RNA biomarkers in crude biofluids to ultrasensitive detection, addressing a major barrier to early diagnosis.

Title: STARgrid: an open-source pipeline from Visium HD sequencing reads to count matrices
Authors: Hung, L.-H.; Yeung, K. Y.
Abstract: In Visium HD, transcript positions are computed from sequenced barcodes, which are matched to a list of coordinate barcodes that map to a grid of capture locations. Quantifying reads and assigning their positions have relied on Space Ranger, whose end-user licence prohibits modification and whose published source cannot be redistributed. We present STARgrid, the first open-source pipeline that takes Visium HD FASTQ files from Flex or RNA-seq based quantitation to count matrices at 2, 8 and 16 um; it is part of STAR Suite. On three human slides its output agrees closely with Space Ranger's (correlations of gene totals are at least 0.9989), and STARgrid takes 20-35% less wall time under the tested configurations. STARgrid assigns each read barcode to the coordinate barcode with the most similar sequence, as assessed by edit distance. In an examination of Space Ranger's per-read output on one further slide, Space Ranger does the same for most reads, with two differences. First, where two coordinate barcodes overlap, the shorter being the longer without its first base, Space Ranger records the shorter barcode, although the longer one matches with fewer edits; in all, Space Ranger's location is not among the closest for 0.5980% of the reads that our decoder can place. Second, Space Ranger settles each read on its own, recording one location or none, and leaves 0.2916% of these reads without a location; STARgrid keeps every matching location and chooses among them for each molecule, using all its reads. Our molecule totals are 1.9-7.6% above Space Ranger's. The larger source of this difference is probably that we resolve location for each molecule and not for each read; STAR Suite's own gene assignment and molecule counting may also contribute. The counts that STARgrid adds behave like signal. On H&E images of the same sections they fall in cells at nearly the rate of the counts that both pipelines report. Against an adjacent Xenium section of one slide, our counts are closer to Xenium than Space Ranger's for 15 of the 20 genes of a cancer gene panel that Xenium measures most abundantly (P = 0.0414). The added counts therefore appear to improve the measurement of cancer-associated expression. These results are preliminary, but the method is now open, and every comparison reported here can be repeated, extended and improved upon.

Title: Beyond Ramachandran distributions: quantifying secondary structure effects on amino acids and their pairs in the full torsional space
Authors: Carriere, G.; Robert, C. H.; Cazals, F.
Abstract: The Ramachandran diagram has long served for understanding protein secondary structure elements (SSEs), despite the multitude of factors contributing to their occurrence. Starting from recentlyintroduced circula-based multivariate torsion-angle distribution (CBMD) mixture models -- accommodating covariance structure in the full torsion-angle space of amino acids, we define continuous densities for the 20 amino acids and 400 amino-acid pairs in dimension up to 14, conditioned by SSE labels. Projecting these higher-dimensional distributions onto the classical Ramachandran diagram reveals how secondary structures in the protein universe emerge from amino-acid-dependent conformational preferences reflecting influences beyond backbone dihedrals alone. Our analysis links the traditional geometric description of local protein structure to modern statistical models of the full conformational space of amino acids and amino-acidpairs, while providing a framework for generating protein conformations consistent with any given secondary structure environment -- a feature that remains difficult to enforce explicitly in current AI-based generative models.

Title: Probabilistic Modelling of Base Editing Efficiency and Bystander Outcome Composition
Authors: Ozden, F.; Minary, P.
Abstract: Abstract. Base editors install single nucleotide substitutions without a double strand break or donor template, but editing at multiple susceptible positions can generate bystander alleles. Predicting the frequency of an intended outcome therefore requires both editing efficiency and the composition of edited products. Here we present crispAIBE, a probabilistic framework that uses separately trained transformer convolutional networks to predict Dirichlet distributions for editing efficiency and conditional allele composition. Split-conformal density-level regions are calibrated on data reserved from model selection, with composition thresholds fitted by outcome-set size. On held-out data, crispAIBE achieves Pearson correlations of 0.669 for efficiency and 0.896 for composition on measured allele sets, with empirical coverages of 0.902 and 0.906 at a nominal level of 0.90. On the published CRISPRon-BE benchmark, with test protospacers excluded from training, crispAIBE ranks first in seven of eight comparisons under the two-column Pearson statistic and first or second in seven of eight under the rank statistic. Within predicted-efficiency quintiles, the largest- and smallest-region deciles differ 1.9-fold in mean absolute error on average, compared with 1.7-fold for a boundary-distance ranking. When evaluated on U2OS, which was excluded from training, larger predictive regions were associated with larger absolute prediction errors. Local calibration with 100 U2OS protospacers yields median empirical coverage of 0.918 at the nominal 0.90 level. The crispAIBE repository is https://github.com/furkanozdenn/crispAIBE.

Title: Multivalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly
Authors: Muwonge, K.; Duran-Armenta, L. F.; Lazar, T.; Meszaros, A.; Volkov, A.; Navarro, A.; Marino-Buslje, C.; Fernandez, M. L.; Gutierrez, G. J.; Kanaan, N. M.; Loris, R.; Tompa, P.
Abstract: Liquid-liquid phase separation (LLPS) has emerged as an important intermediate in the pathological self-assembly of Tau, yet the molecular mechanisms that regulate this process remain incompletely understood. Although ubiquitin is a prominent component of pathological inclusions in tauopathies and other neurodegenerative diseases, its presence has largely been linked to targeting aberrant proteins for proteasomal or autophagic clearance. Here, we identify Tau as a ubiquitin-binding protein and demonstrate that multivalent, non-covalent ubiquitin recognition regulates multiple stages of Tau self-assembly. Biochemical, biophysical, structural, and computational analyses identified four ubiquitin-binding elements within the Tau microtubule-binding repeat region that engage the canonical hydrophobic patch of ubiquitin, providing a structural basis for multivalent recognition of mono- and poly-ubiquitin species. Functionally, mono- and poly-ubiquitin suppress Tau condensate formation while enhancing the liquid-like properties of condensates that persist. In contrast, mono-ubiquitin selectively enhances aggregation of the disease-linked Tau-P301L variant under conditions without detectable LLPS, demonstrating that ubiquitin exerts distinct effects depending on the molecular context and stage of Tau self-assembly. Together, these findings establish non-covalent ubiquitin recognition as a previously unrecognized mechanism regulating Tau phase behavior and aggregation. More broadly, they expand the role of ubiquitin beyond protein quality control, with ubiquitin architecture providing an additional layer of regulation over Tau condensate formation, dynamics, maturation, and aggregation.

Title: Scalable Decoupling Contact and Configuration Spaces in a Quantum-Enabled Protein Folding Workflow
Authors: Uttarkar, A.; Niranjan, V.
Abstract: Near-term quantum devices remain constrained by limited qubit counts, noise, and shallow circuit depth, restricting their direct application to peptide folding. This work addresses this limitation through a hybrid quantum-classical framework that separates global contact-space exploration from local configuration-space refinement. The pipeline was evaluated on the p53 transactivation peptide. The peptide was encoded using discrete torsional states and Miyazawa-Jernigan contact potentials. Global conformational search was performed using simulated annealing, followed by fragment-level CVaR-based variational quantum eigensolver refinement. Overlapping fragments were stitched and reconstructed into three-dimensional backbone coordinates for structural comparison. Three independent simulated annealing restarts produced negative-energy conformers. The workflow identified a best global conformer at E = -3.70 MJ using simulated annealing. Fragment-level CVaR-VQE refinement generated 30 candidate conformers across three overlapping fragments, the best assembled conformer reaching E = -2.58 MJ after DP stitching and post-stitch refinement. In this trial, the classical SA solution outperformed the VQE-assembled structure and was selected as the final output. The final 65-atom model was successfully reconstructed, but full-backbone alignment against 1YCR yielded an RMSD of 4.65 angstrom, improving to 2.90 angstrom after trimmed alignment. Our work demonstrates a practical quantum-enabled peptide folding workflow for short, flexible peptides, but the present structural accuracy is insufficient for claims of native fold recovery. Its main value is as an auditable framework for testing NISQ-compatible folding strategies.

Title: Nanoscale identification of organic pigments in biogenic calcite by atom probe tomography
Authors: Triccas, A.; Schwarz, T. M.; Hsu, Y.; Kim, S.-H.; Freysoldt, C.; Dumont, M.; Sardhalia, V.; Ferreira, C.; Chareyron, C.; Alberic, M.; Gault, B.
Abstract: Spatially-resolved mass spectrometry could contribute to the understanding of biological processes. Atom probe tomography (APT) is a technique which could, in principle, fill an analytical gap for nanoscale mass spectrometry. Yet, because of a limited understanding of the process of fragmentation of biomolecules, biological or biochemical interpretation of the obtained data has so far not been successful. Here, we report on analyses of synthetic and biogenic pigmented calcite minerals. The purple coloration of Sphaerechinus granularis sea urchin spines is due to the occlusion of polyhydroxylated naphthoquinone (PHNQ) molecules, mainly spinochrome A, within the calcite phase. Peaks relating to these pigments as well as to other intra-crystalline macromolecules were identified by APT analysis of the purple spine region with comparison to measurements of synthetic calcite single crystals, calcite crystals doped with PHNQ, and the uncoloured (white) region of sea urchin spines. To facilitate the molecular identification of peaks appearing solely in purple-coloured spines, which are possible fragments from PHNQ, we introduce novel APT data filtering techniques based on spatial and temporal correlations in the detection of ions of targeted mass-to-charge state ratios. This allows us to discuss the fragmentation of organic molecules under field conditions and improve the identification of peaks in the mass spectrum, while also determining nanoscale spatial distribution of fragments related to specifically targeted biomolecules in 3D and elucidate the relationship these organic pigment molecules have to the calcite lattice and inorganic elements such as magnesium. The study aims to improve identification of complex molecular structures by APT, including organic molecules, with the potential ability to provide structural information at a near-atomic scale for a range of materials.

Title: Low CAR affinity enhances T-cell synapse dynamics and activation
Authors: Nguyen, C.; Castro-Linares, G.; Gatti, L. C. D. E.; Sebestyen, Z.; Fernandes, R. A.; Tans, S. J.; Farrell, M. V.; Ganzinger, K. A.
Abstract: Low affinity chimeric antigen receptors (CARs) can clinically outperform high-affinity variants, yet the molecular mechanisms underlying affinity-dependent activity remain unclear. Here, we show that low CAR affinity enables faster CAR cluster motion, which is central to T-cell activation. We compared low-affinity CAT and high-affinity FMC63 CARs signaling at different stages of activation on supported lipid bilayers functionalized with defined CD19 densities. At low CAR expression on dense CD19 bilayers, low-affinity CAT CARs formed more mature and dynamic synapses, recruited ZAP70 more efficiently, and showed faster microcluster motion. These proximal signaling changes were accompanied by stronger calcium flux and increased NFAT nuclear translocation. Our data support a model in which weaker, lower-affinity CAR-antigen interactions promote receptor turnover, microcluster mobility, and signaling-adaptor recruitment, thereby enhancing downstream signal propagation. Our work provides a mechanistic basis for the superior functional performance reported for affinity-tuned CD19 CAR-T cells.

Title: High-throughput variant libraries and machine learning enable robust target-site selection for toehold-switch design in Detectrons
Authors: Han, J.; Shipman, S. L.
Abstract: Programmable RNA sensors enable sequence-specific detection of RNA inputs for diagnostics, genetic circuit control, and multiplexed molecular readouts. Although readily programmable, their performance varies substantially with the target site selected within a transcript, making target-site selection a major challenge. Here, we report DeSTAR (Detectron Sensor TARget-site ranker), a machine-learning-assisted target-site ranking model for programmable RNA sensors. To train this model, we generated transcript-wide, single-nucleotide-resolution tiling sensor libraries across six diverse RNA targets, enabling generalization to be tested across transcripts rather than within a single RNA. In leave-one-transcript-out evaluation, DeSTAR's top-ranked sites were enriched for high-performing sensors in held-out transcripts, driven predominantly by interpretable sequence grammar in the sensor stem rather than transcript-specific patterns. Prospectively, on an unseen SARS-CoV-2 transcript, the model's top-ranked sites yielded working sensors roughly five-fold more often than random selection. These results support DeSTAR as a generalizable strategy for target-site selection in RNA sensors across transcripts.

Title: Modular Cell-Free Extract Mixing Enables Soluble, Active Biomanufacturing of Difficult-to-Express and Aggregation-Prone Proteins
Authors: Firmansyah, L.; Delmundo, A.; Oza, J. P.
Abstract: Cell-free protein synthesis (CFPS) is a powerful platform for rapid protein prototyping and biomanufacturing, but expression of complex proteins remains limited by labor-intensive extract preparation as well as the inability of conventional Escherichia coli extracts to efficiently support disulfide bond formation and prevent protein aggregation. We previously developed a Cell-Free Autoinduction (CFAI) workflow that simplifies extract preparation, however, CFAI-derived extracts retain the folding limitations of standard E. coli systems for producing traditionally difficult proteins. Here, we address these challenges by utilizing extracts enriched with molecular chaperones or Erv1p-based oxidative folding catalysts and combining them through a modular extract mixing strategy to enable independent tuning of the cell-free folding environment. This workflow supplies folding factors through enriched extracts, avoiding recurring purchases of purified supplements and enabling a modeled reagent-cost advantage. To evaluate real-world applications and utility of lysate mixing for protein production, we demonstrate a 10-fold increase in solubility of the aggregation-prone bacterial toxin Colicin M, achieving >95% soluble protein while retaining antimicrobial activity. We further used a Design of Experiments (DoE) framework to optimize combinations of chaperone-enriched and Erv1p-based oxidative folding extracts containing either protein disulfide isomerase (PDI) or DsbC. The optimized compositions produced >95% soluble truncated human tissue plasminogen activator (vtPA), comprising the kringle 2 and protease domains, while preserving enzymatic activity. Together, these results demonstrate that CFAI-derived modular extract mixing provides a tunable, high-throughput strategy with low modeled materials costs for tailoring cell-free biochemical environments for difficult-to-express proteins, expanding CFPS utility for protein engineering and biomanufacturing.

Title: The Human Gut Cell Atlas v1.0: A Unified, Community-BuiltReference of Cellular Diversity Across the Gut
Authors: Kimler, K.; Lance, C.; Bohar, B.; Ahmed, A.; Zhou, R.; Bartolome-Casado, R.; Gudino, V.; Ramirez Flores, R. O.; Junghus, F. V.; Morbe, U. M.; Domanska, D.; Mueller, M. F.; Moy, M. R.; Sanzo-Machuca, A.; Olbei, M.; Cakir, B.; Weinert, B.; Frey, B. M.; Glinka, M.; Alegbe, T.; Pham, D.; de Sousa Casal, J.; Predeus, A. V.; Denadai-Souza, A.; Perrone, F.; Lee, H. C.; Maddipatla, S. C.; Rogers, D.; Futey, M. K.; Chatzigeorgiou, A.; Zucchi, I.; Belfiore, J.; Robson, L.; Antanaviciute, A.; Rainbow, D. B.; Karakasheva, T. A.; Baldock, R.; Houghton, D.; Shitov, V. A.; Zhu, C.; Lee, C. H.-J.; Novoa-del-T
Abstract: Single-cell RNA-sequencing (scRNA-seq) studies have transformed our understanding of cellular diversity in the human intestine, but differences in anatomical sampling, experimental processing and cell-type nomenclature limit comparison across datasets. Here, we present the Human Gut Cell Atlas (HGCA) V1, a community-curated reference of 944,390 healthy and disease-adjacent intestinal cells from 502 samples, 265 donors and 24 landmark studies, linked to detailed anatomical, clinical, and technical metadata. As this metadata is of critical importance to human biology, we developed MetaManager, an open source data management framework for standardized metadata collection and tracking. A five-level consensus taxonomy resolves 94 homeostatic cell identities and enables transferrable, high-resolution annotation of new gut datasets. By assembling cell identity, sampling metadata, and independent spatial validation, intestinal segment and radial tissue depth were revealed to systematically shape cellular composition and transcriptional state, enabling inference of the presence of sampling-dependent tissue niches, including lymphoid follicles. Reference mapping accurately and rapidly recovered cohort-level Crohn's disease and treatment signatures without de novo annotation, while mapping human intestinal organoids quantified cell-type-specific identity, regional specification, maturation, and transcriptional fidelity to native tissue. The HGCA V1 provides a standardized cellular, anatomical coordinate, and metadata system for reproducible, high-quality analysis of intestinal biology across healthy tissue, disease-associated remodelling, and experimental models, providing a continuously evolving community reference for cumulative discovery in human intestinal biology.

Title: Decision-relevant measurement for precision microbiome interventions
Authors: Aminian-Dehkordi, J.; Mofrad, M.
Abstract: Human gut microbiome studies often rely on stool, despite increasing evidence that it incompletely represents the spatially heterogeneous intestinal ecosystem. Whether this loss of spatial detail matters for downstream intervention decisions is largely unresolved. We treat compositional reconstruction and decision preservation as separate objectives. Using 16 matched recovery events from 11 participants, each containing stool and four intended regional capsule measurements, we aggregated amplicon sequence variants into 11 prespecified taxonomic and functional proxy guilds. We evaluated models that reconstruct stool from regional measurements by nested leave one participant out validation under complementary compositional geometries. We then assessed decision preservation through three spatial proxy states and measurement induced decision loss (MIDL) across normalized binary intervention thresholds. Multi region CLR ridge and Aitchison models combining regional measurements with a population reference had the lowest point estimate Aitchison errors, but evidence that either outperformed the population Aitchison center was not retained after multiplicity correction. Rankings changed under total variation and after guild amalgamation; at the coarser resolution, the primary ordering showed a small, uncertain reversal that was sensitive to zero handling. The model with the lowest compositional error did not have the lowest MIDL curve calibration error. Population centers closely reproduced the nearly uninformative MIDL curves of observed stool while retaining little individualized regional information. These findings show that reconstruction, decision preservation, and calibration to observed stool decision loss answer different questions. Evaluation of microbiome measurement strategies should therefore treat compositional geometry, biological representation, and the downstream decision task as parts of the estimand.

Title: Fast receptor-antigen dissociation kinetics promote CAR-T cell tumor infiltration, functional fitness, and antitumor efficacy in solid tumors
Authors: Mao, R.; Shi, H.; Hussein, M. S.; Karia, B.; Koomson, O.; Sadek, R.; Kota, V.; Gascoigne, N.; He, Y.
Abstract: Background: CAR-T cells have shown limited efficacy against solid tumors, where they face two major challenges: restricted tumor infiltration and sustained intensive engagement that drive them to exhaustion. Conventional CAR design has largely emphasized high-affinity interactions with slow dissociation, further limiting tumor infiltration and exacerbating exhaustion and dysfunction. We hypothesize that most current CARs are kinetically over-stabilized for solid tumors and that a fast-on/fast-off, cheek-kiss mode of engagement permits transient CAR-antigen disengagement, thereby facilitating tumor infiltration and preserving CAR-T cell fitness in tumor mass. Methods: We identified two monoclonal antibodies targeting the same epitope of epidermal growth factor receptor with comparable kon but distinct koff rates: cetuximab (Cet) and its humanized derivative H1. CAR-T cells incorporating these binders were evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Large, established human tumor xenografts were treated with low-dose CAR-T cells in NSG mice to model conditions of limited T cell availability and sustained tumor antigen exposure. Results: Cet and H1 exhibited comparable kon but markedly different koff rates, with H1 displaying fast-off kinetics with approximately 18-fold shorter binding dwell time. As CARs, H1 showed reduced antigen occupancy and less stable tumor-T cell engagement than Cet. Despite comparable in vitro cytotoxicity, H1 CAR-T cells accumulated more efficiently following tumor stimulation. At high doses, both CAR-T cell products eradicated established tumors. Under low-dose conditions, however, H1 CAR-T cells exhibited superior expansion, persistence, tumor infiltration, and antitumor efficacy, whereas Cet CAR-T cells showed limited expansion and only transient tumor control. Cet CAR-T cells progressively downregulated surface CAR expression, increased PD-1 expression, and exhibited reduced tumor infiltration and impaired functional recovery. In contrast, H1 CAR-T cells preserved surface CAR expression, exhibited greater tumor infiltration, maintained a less exhausted, more central memory-like phenotype, and retained effector function. Conclusion: Fast-on/fast-off binding kinetics enhance CAR-T tumor infiltration, expansion, persistence, and functional fitness, resulting in improved control of established solid tumors. The data provides a rationale for shifting CAR design from affinity optimization toward kinetic optimization to improve the efficacy and safety of CAR-T therapy for solid tumors.

Title: Tissue-resident memory T cells are diminished in the Kaposi sarcoma tumor microenvironment of people living with HIV
Authors: Lagodka, A.; Winkler, F.; Brazdilova, K.; Loewe, R.; Grabmeier-Pfistershammer, K.; Eidsmo, L.; Saluzzo, S.; Strobl, J.
Abstract: Kaposi sarcoma (KS) is a rare neoplasm and an AIDS-defining diagnosis in people living with HIV (PLWH). Although and chronic infection with Kaposi sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) contributes to KS progression, the local immune mechanisms that are lost during tumor progression remain incompletely understood. Here, we systematically characterized global patterns in the KS tumor microenvironment (TME) in both PLWH and HIV-negative individuals. Spatial transcriptomics revealed distinct niches comprising of tumor cells, immune cells, and surrounding skin cells. Tumor regions expressed a characteristic endothelial-fibroblastic signature attributable to KS tumor cells (CD34, LYVE1, SCN9A), TME regions expressed marker genes for T cells, B cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts. Analysis of putative cell-cell interactions demonstrated that tumor cells preferentially interact with cells of the TME, including T cells, indicating an important role as hub of cellular communication in KS. Immunofluorescence imaging confirmed increased numbers of T cells, specifically tissue-resident memory T cells (TRM), in KS samples compared to healthy skin, accompanied by a pronounced upregulation of PD-1 expression that was predominantly localized to the TME. Notably, we identified HIV-associated alterations in the KS immune microenvironment: PLWH exhibited loss of CXCR3+ and IFN-gamma producing CD8+ TRM cells in the KS TME compared to HIV-negative patients, a finding consistent with impaired antitumor immunity. Together, our findings reveal HIV-associated disruption of functional anti-tumor immunity in the KS TME of PLWH. Increased PD-1 expression within T cells of the TME highlights potential therapeutic use of immune checkpoint inhibitors in KS.

Title: Unsupervised decomposition of massively parallel TraDIS-Xpress fitness data from  Escherichia coli  identifies distinct functional and expression modules of antimicrobial resistance determinants
Authors: Yasir, M.; Turner, A. K.; Telatin, A.; Bastkowski, S.; Holden, E. R.; Charles, I. G.; Webber, M. A.
Abstract: Linking genotype to phenotype is a central goal in biology, one way to do this is using transposon insertion sequencing (TIS) where the fitness impacts of mutations across a genome are assessed in different conditions. Traditional analyses use comparison of each gene response independently in control versus test conditions, so a compendium of hundreds of test conditions returns hundreds of separate ranked gene lists. To unlock the potential information hidden within large data sets, we applied independent component (ICA) analysis to 754 Escherichia coli BW25113 TraDIS-Xpress samples. These samples included a series of antibiotic and other stress condition exposures. ICA is designed to identify hidden structure within complex data and to extract meaningfully linked components. In this analysis each annotated gene was resolved into a gene body and 198 bp 5' and 3' features so that expression effects driven by the transposon's outwards facing promoter enter the matrix separately from gene disruption effects. The decomposition returned 99 components, which we term fxModules, which were defined as containing elements with similar responses across the whole compendium rather than per any individual experiment. Of the 754 stress samples, the antibiotic arm included 110 samples derived from exposure to 14 separate agents at multiple concentrations. Many of these have been highly studied allowing us to explore the accuracy of predicted responsive fxModules. This analysis showed excellent predictive power of the approach and the fxModules responsive to individual drugs typically reproduced known mechanisms at a resolution superior to analysis of single gene sets. For example, exposure to fosfomycin identified responsive fxModules containing genes which are known to be involved in uptake of the drug, cAMP-CRP control and exposure to gentamicin identified oxidative phosphorylation split across three fxModules responding with different magnitudes and directions at different concentrations. This recapitulates recent work studying the landscape of E. coli genes sensitive to this drug with high precision without any prior knowledge of functional annotation. Similarly precise predictions were made for other drugs. Responsive modules also identified novel groups of genes and linkages beyond the boundaries of defined pathways as being responsive to various stresses demonstrating the ability to predict new genotype-phenotype links. Inclusion of the regulatory regions also resolved fxModules which were entirely contributed by promoter regions, for example for chloramphenicol genes responsible for efflux were identified by signals in intergenic control regions, and unidirectional insertions in gene bodies, a signal that a gene level matrix would not be able to predict with accuracy. These data show that ICA decomposition provides an efficient and accurate annotation independent approach to identifying sets of genes with related functional impacts in any given condition in the compendium. The functional modular association of genes also help in predicting gene functions of unknown genes based on the group function. This approach allows rapid identification of novel genotype-phenotype links and unlocks the power of multiple comparisons of transposon mutagenesis data.

Title: Pulling water from a stone: subaerial biofilm water dynamics on porous solid materials
Authors: Russo, F.; Klapper, I.
Abstract: Subaerial biofilms (SABs) are microbial communities that colonize air exposed surfaces in both natural and engineered environments, forming an interface between the atmosphere and the substrate. Often water availability is crucial for their metabolic activity and survival. While precipitation may contribute to SAB hydration, the dynamic processes of evaporation and condensation - closely linked to fluctuating temperature and humidity conditions - can be key determinants of water availability and they constitute the main focus of this study. We present a model connecting the water-related dynamics in an SAB, its surrounding ambient air and underlying stone/masonry. A central feature of the model is the increased water affinity of the SAB in comparison to the stone pore network. Based on thermodynamic principles, the model captures changes in liquid water content and availability by accounting for the evaporation and condensation at liquid-gas interfaces through gradients in water chemical potential. It accounts for the SAB's capacity to delay water loss by drawing water from substrate material pores to compensate for atmospheric evaporation. The proposed model is compared to prior experimental observations of water transport in limestone samples with and without SAB. Additional numerical simulations under variable environmental conditions demonstrate how permeability of the substrate layer may influence SAB water activity, and how the presence or absence of an SAB might affect water content within stone/masonry.

Title: Ethnic differences in gut microbiota composition and functional capacity persist over six years in the HELIUS multi-ethnic longitudinal cohort
Authors: Verhaar, B. J. H.; Boulund, U.; Herrema, H.; Nicolaou, M.; Zwinderman, A. H.; van den Born, B.-J. H.; Hamdiui, N.; Elinav, E.; Nielsen, T.; Nieuwdorp, M.
Abstract: Background: Ethnic minority groups in Western Europe carry a disproportionate cardiometabolic disease burden not fully explained by conventional risk factors, and their gut microbiomes differ markedly from those of European-origin populations. Whether these differences persist over time has not been examined prospectively. Results: We followed 1,903 participants from six ethnic groups in the HELIUS cohort over 6 years, using faecal 16S rRNA sequencing across all groups and shotgun metagenomics in a matched Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese subset (N = 238 per group). The extent of microbiota compositional change over time differed between ethnic groups: Moroccan participants showed the largest change, while the Dutch and South-Asian Surinamese participants were most stable. Diabetes mellitus and medication use at baseline were associated with greater compositional drift. However, ethnic differences in composition were largely preserved across all six groups (16S: ethnicity R2 0.044 to 0.037; all 15 pairwise contrasts significant at follow-up) and in the shotgun subset (R2 0.047 to 0.037). At the species level, 61 of 78 ethnicity-associated species remained differentially abundant at follow-up. Alistipes putredinis, the species converging most strongly, was absent at baseline in 43% of South-Asian Surinamese participants, and the convergence was consistent with acquisition of this species by this group. At strain level, within-person strain sharing declined with follow-up duration but was similar between ethnic groups. Within hosts, 90% of A. putredinis populations were retained as the same or a closely related lineage, and within the retained subset, microdiversity increased in both groups. Ethnic differences in functional profiles persisted to a similar extent as those in composition, with limited convergence in fibre-degrading enzyme families (GH5_37, GH26). The total antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) burden in the gut microbiome declined similarly in both groups over time. Dutch participants showed higher baseline ARG diversity that converged toward South-Asian Surinamese levels, while class-level differences were predominantly stable. Conclusions: Six years of follow-up in a shared urban environment narrowed ethnic differences in the gut microbiome only modestly; assuming exponential decline, the observed change corresponds to a half-life of roughly two decades.

Title: Sister species, shared and divergent responses: early transcriptomic profiling of Bursaphelenchus xylophilus exposed to Esteya spp.
Authors: Pires, D.; Varela, A. R.; Kolarik, M.; Inacio, M. L.; Mota, M.; Vicente, C. S. L.
Abstract: Bursaphelenchus xylophilus (pinewood nematode, PWN) responds transcriptionally to nematophagous fungi, but the earliest events preceding cuticle penetration are poorly characterized, and whether closely related fungal antagonists elicit comparable responses is unknown. Here, we compared PWN transcriptomic responses to Esteya floridanum V14639 (EF) and E. vermicola CCF3117 (EV) at 1 h post-inoculation (hpi), capturing the onset of host-fungus interaction. Despite their phylogenetic proximity, under our exposure conditions the two fungi elicited partly divergent host responses at 1 hpi. EF induced a broad transcriptional response enriched in peptidase activity and lysosomal pathways, accompanied by downregulation of cuticle structural components. In contrast, EV triggered a narrower response, without the proteolytic and lysosomal enrichment observed with EF. Direct comparison of the two treatments revealed no significantly enriched Gene Ontology categories, although pathway analysis identified DNA replication and repair pathways, comprising genes more highly expressed under EF. Enrichment analyses revealed a shared transcriptional signature in both interactions characterized by downregulation of xenobiotic- and central carbon-metabolism pathways, suggesting an early reduction in xenobiotic detoxification capacity rather than induction of detoxification programs. These findings suggest that phylogenetic proximity does not necessarily predict conserved early transcriptional responses, although comparisons of single isolates cannot separate species-level from isolate-level effects.

Title: Glyphosate exposure minimally alters the Corbicula fluminea microbiome while associated bacteria exhibit high tolerance and degradation potentia
Authors: Eggenberger, S. M.; Cunningham, C.; Godinez, J. P.; Diner, R. E.
Abstract: Glyphosate (GLY), the active ingredient in Roundup, is a broad-spectrum herbicide widely used in commercial agriculture and residential landscaping. Due to its extensive application and high water solubility, GLY is frequently introduced into freshwater ecosystems where it has been shown to negatively impact aquatic life and beneficial microorganisms. The freshwater clam Corbicula fluminea, a nonnative bivalve species widely distributed throughout the United States, is highly tolerant of many environmental stressors and may serve as a reservoir for microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading environmental pollutants. As efficient filter-feeders, these clams are continuously exposed to waterborne contaminants, potentially facilitating interactions between pollutants and host-associated microbial communities. In this study, we investigated how glyphosate impacts the structure and diversity of Corbicula fluminea microbiomes and characterized GLY tolerance and degradation potential in individual microbiome members. We found that microbiome taxonomic composition and abundance-based diversity metrics were minimally impacted by glyphosate, while presence/absence-based phylogenetic diversity shifted depending on treatment concentration. Furthermore, high GLY concentrations were linked to reduced Faith''s PD alpha diversity, while other alpha diversity metrics were not impacted. Additionally, we isolated and characterized glyphosate-tolerant bacterial strains from clam tissues and assessed their presence within the microbiome. Several isolates exhibited tolerance to very high GLY levels (up to 1600 mg/L), and several also utilized GLY as a sole phosphorus source and possessed the phnJ gene, suggesting potential degradation capabilities. While isolated bacteria were minority members of the microbiome, more abundant uncultured taxa were phylogenetically related to known glyphosate degraders. Collectively, these findings suggest that freshwater bivalves may harbor diverse microbial taxa capable of tolerating or degrading herbicides, which may contribute to host resilience in contaminated freshwater environments and potentially represent unexplored avenues for bioremediation research.

Title: Single-cell-resolved natural giant virus infections reveal conserved protist immunity
Authors: Fromm, A.; Alarcon-Schumacher, T.; Bellas, C.; Shaler, T. S.; Schatz, D.; Schon, M. E.; Schewe, N.; Kopejtka, K.; Sommaruga, R.; Aylward, F. O.; Fischer, M. G.; Vardi, A.
Abstract: Single-cell eukaryotes (protists) are key players in microbial ecosystems. Yet, our understanding of how they interact with viruses in nature and how antiviral defenses shape these relationships remains limited. Using a single-cell multi-omics approach, we mapped associations between giant viruses and their hosts and identified active giant-virus infections in an alpine lake protist community. In naturally infected dinoflagellates, infection was accompanied by the selective induction of viperin, an ancient antiviral enzyme conserved from bacteria to humans. We also observed virus-encoded homologs of immunity-related genes whose expression correlated with viperin expression, raising the possibility of a role in viral counter-defense. These findings reveal an ecological dimension of protist immunity and provide a framework for tracing the host-virus arms race across divergent cellular lineages.

Title: Assessment of antimicrobial potential of cell-free supernatant from Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vaginal microbiota of healthy women against uropathogens
Authors: Anand, R.; Rai, D.; Prakash, P.; Maurya, G. K.
Abstract: Among women, urinary tract infection (UTI) represents a major health concern. Approximately 50% of the adult female population experienced an episode of UTI at least once. UTI and recurrent UTIs caused by resistant bacteria are very common in clinical settings. The treatment and management of UTI is becoming more challenging because of the rise in antibiotic-resistant bacteria. Lactobacillus spp are the dominant bacterial genus in urinary and vaginal microbiota, which are also used as probiotics. In this study, Lacticaseibacillus paracasei SRG isolated from the vagina of healthy women were evaluated for its probiotic-associated properties and cell-free supernatant (CFS)-mediated antibacterial activity against eight uropathogens. The antibacterial activity of CFS was concentration- and pH-dependent, which was significantly evident at CFS/2 and CFS/4 concentrations and acidic pH values of 4 and 5. The antibacterial activity in CFS remains unaltered even after heat and proteinase K treatment, which suggests the role of heat- and protease-resistant metabolites beside the contributions from acidic conditions. L. paracasei SRG showed strong autoaggregation (85.32%) and cell-surface hydrophobicity (55.60%). In addition, it also exhibits co-aggregation with all indicator strains, suggesting substantial interaction with diverse pathogenic bacteria. These observations highlighted the L. paracasei SRG as a potential probiotic candidate developed from indigenous vaginal microbiota.

Title: A simple platform for in situ DNA-PAINT optimization enables improved multiplexed super-resolution imaging in Gram-negative bacteria
Authors: Andress, K.; Koehler, P. S.; Xu, R.; Schmidt-Heydt, A.; Diepold, A.; Spahn, C.
Abstract: DNA-PAINT enables super-resolution imaging with high multiplexing capacity, yet it is rarely used in nanoscale bacteriology. A likely reason is the lack of straightforward protocols and of systematic characterization of imager-docking strand pairs inside intact bacterial cells, whose envelope and dense cytoplasm differ markedly from both the DNA origami in vitro systems used to develop them, and eukaryotic cells. In this work, we establish a screening platform based on RNA-FISH, in which we extend the 16S rRNA-directed EUB338 probe with docking sequences of choice. This allows imager-docking pairs to be benchmarked directly inside Escherichia coli cells and characterized for parameters such as specificity, binding kinetics, and localization precision. We screened 12 different DNA-PAINT sequences and used an optimized set to perform four-target 3D Exchange-PAINT in single E. coli cells. We further applied our strategy to image three effector mRNAs in the Gram-negative pathogen Yersinia enterocolitica and quantified RNA clusters and their 3D distribution. Our work provides a framework and practical guidelines for high-quality 3D DNA-PAINT imaging in Gram-negative bacteria and should facilitate its broader adoption in nanoscale bacteriology.

Title: TFA-defluorinating microbial consortium achieved with analogue enrichment
Authors: Jensen, E. H.; Forouzandeh, A.; Trier, X.; Gotfredsen, C. H.; Enemark-Rasmussen, K.; Ahmad, S.; Nielsen, T. K.
Abstract: Trifluoroacetate (TFA) is an ultra-short chain perfluoroalkyl substance (PFAS) and a pollutant of global significance; it is persistent and ubiquitous in the environment across compartments, including food, drinking water, animals, and humans. Concentrations in the environment are rising, concerns over the toxicity of the compound are increasing, and there are currently no efficient ways to remediate TFA pollution, as conventional methods are ineffective at scale under environmental conditions. Microorganisms possessing dehalogenating enzymes targeting the structurally analogous compound monofluoroacetate (MFA) present a potential solution to degrade TFA microbiologically. Due to previously demonstrated dehalogenation of difluoroacetate (DFA) by dehalogenases, the promiscuity of such enzymes was hypothesized to be extendable to TFA as well. In this study cultures obtained from an environmental sample of PFAS contaminated wastewater sludge were incubated in M9 minimal media supplied with 33 mM acetate and either 33 mM TFA, DFA, or MFA in an iterative manner, followed by testing in a 30-day experiment. Free fluoride (F-) was measured at 5 timepoints using a fluoride ion specific electrode (ISE). One culture designated MFA1C significantly degraded MFA, DFA, and TFA (two-way ANOVA mixed model, p < 0.05). MFA1C released 11.2 {+/-} 0.7 M F- which constitutes approximately 0.01% of the potential fluoride release from the total 33 mM TFA applied and with the greatest defluorination activity in the first 9 days of incubation. Fluoride release from TFA and formation of DFA and MFA was confirmed with 19F-NMR. Genetic sequencing and protein-ligand modelling identified two candidate dehalogenase enzymes from Achromobacter denitrificans and Stenotrophomonas sp., respectively, with potential capacity to degrade TFA. The findings of this study are a crucial first step towards future potential bioremediation of TFA, and are, to the best of our knowledge, the first to identify a TFA-degrading consortium of microorganisms.

Title: Exploring recurrent urinary tract infection: paired microbiota and culture-based profiling reveals stable dysbiosis and multidrug-resistant, virulence-enriched uropathogens
Authors: Kaushik, S.; P, K.; Pal, S.; Nandi, N.; Kiran, G. S.; Kumar, S. H. K.; Selvin, J.; Veettil, V. N.; Devi, S.
Abstract: **Objectives:** Recurrent urinary tract infection (rUTI) is increasingly complicated by antimicrobial resistance (AMR), yet urinary microbiome dysbiosis and isolate-level resistance-virulence are rarely examined together across different treatment states. In this study, we characterized both within the same sample in rUTI and in healthy controls. **Methods:** In this cross-sectional cohort, mid-stream urine was collected from women with untreated, treated and prophylaxis rUTI and age-matched healthy controls at four centres in South India. Of 80 samples collected, 75 were analysed (26 controls, 20 untreated, 20 treated, 9 prophylaxis) by 16S rRNA V3-V4 sequencing. In addition, 105 culturable isolates from the same samples were identified and tested for antimicrobial susceptibility (VITEK 2) and phenotypic virulence. **Results:** rUTI groups showed approximately half the alpha diversity of controls (median Shannon 1.07-1.18 vs 2.17; Kruskal-Wallis p = 0.041). Community structure differed from controls in every rUTI subgroup (PERMANOVA R-squared = 0.091, p = 0.004; pairwise FDR = 0.008) but not among subgroups. Mean Lactobacillus relative abundance fell from 29.2% in controls to <=13.2% in rUTI groups, while Escherichia-Shigella rose from 7.2% to 25.0-43.0%.
