Control-referenced dysbiosis z-scores were elevated in all rUTI groups (community distance: FDR <= 0.003; uropathogen: Lactobacillus index: FDR < 0.001 for treated and prophylaxis groups). Among isolates, Escherichia coli predominated (35/105; 16/35, 45.7% multidrug-resistant), followed by Klebsiella spp. (32% multidrug-resistant); carbapenem susceptibility was largely retained, and multidrug-resistant E. coli co-carried more virulence traits. **Conclusions:** rUTI is associated with a stable dysbiotic state that treatment does not restore, combining Lactobacillus loss and uropathogen dominance with a multidrug-resistant culturable reservoir that co-accumulates virulence traits. Reading the community and its isolates together may support microbiome-sparing, resistance-aware management of rUTI.

Title: Context-dependent regulation of RpoS-dependent and RpoS-independent gene transcription by Crl during exponential growth in Escherichia coli
Authors: Ge, P.; Schnetz, K.; Dame, R. T.
Abstract: RpoS, an alternative sigma factor, directly regulates approximately 10% of gene transcription in E. coli. The small protein Crl functions as a partner that assists RpoS in exerting its regulatory role, particularly during the stationary phase. However, the coordinating role of Crl during the exponential phase remains unclear. In addition, whether Crl can regulate gene transcription independently of RpoS is still unknown. Therefore, in this study, we used the RpoS-dependent operon hdeAB and the RpoS-independent operon proVWX as model systems to investigate the transcriptional regulatory function of Crl using RT-qPCR and 3C-qPCR. Since the expression of both Crl and RpoS is modulated by environmental signals, we further examined the transcription of these operons under different pH and osmotic conditions. The results showed that Crl can regulate transcription independently of RpoS and exhibits environment-specific bidirectional regulation. Overall, this study improves our understanding of the regulatory mechanisms of Crl and highlights the complexity of transcriptional regulation.

Title: Red and blue light cues drive contrasting remodeling of lipophilic metabolites and photophysiology in natural benthic diatom biofilms
Authors: Desparmet, A.; Lavaud, J.; Jesus, B.; Medico, A.; Hubas, C.
Abstract: Intertidal mudflats are low hydrodynamic energy environments hosting microphytobenthic communities that experience strong spatiotemporal variability in light regimes, including changes in spectral quality and light intensity that can lead to cellular photooxidative stress. To cope with these fluctuations, autotrophs exhibit diverse and highly plastic adaptations that are often species-dependent and shaped by their ecological niches. This study investigates photophysiological responses and metabolic remodeling in a diatom assemblage originating from a natural winter microphytobenthic biofilm under contrasting red and blue light intensities. To this end, photosynthetic parameters were monitored alongside changes in lipophilic metabolites, including untargeted lipids and lipophilic pigments. While few metabolites showed temporal remodeling, rapid and contrasting changes were observed within 30 minutes in response to both spectral quality and light intensity. Red light treatments induced broader remodeling of lipophilic metabolites than blue light, whereas blue light appeared to have a greater impact on photosynthetic parameters. Moreover, red light induced xanthophyll-cycle responses comparable to those observed under blue light at equivalent incident intensity. We discuss these metabolic responses in relation to diatom photoadaptive strategies, placing these findings within the intertidal environmental framework. This work further underlines the importance of understanding rapid metabolic plasticity in coping with light fluctuations, providing new insights into the photoregulatory strategies of natural microphytobenthic communities.

Title: Role of small non-coding RNAs in DSB repair in Arabidopsis thaliana
Authors: Mochet, E.; White, C.; Verbeke, J.; Serra, H.; Da Ines, O.; Lageix, S.
Abstract: DNA double-strand breaks (DSB) are highly toxic lesions that must be repaired to avoid major losses of genetic materials or genome rearrangements. A number of highly conserved molecular pathways are involved in DSB repair, each resulting in different repair outcomes for a given DSB. Over the past decade, accumulating evidence has revealed the emergence of an unexpected new actor in DSB repair: RNA. Notably, small RNAs have been observed at DSB-flanking sequences and hypothesized to be involved in their repair. However, these DSB-induced small RNAs (diRNAs) were so far observed in studies using reporter systems, and their natural occurrence as well as their role in DNA repair remains debated. To address this question, we investigated diRNA biogenesis in Arabidopsis thaliana using CRISPR/Cas12a to induce targeted DSBs at three actively transcribed loci and one untranscribed locus. We found that 21-nt diRNAs are generated at transcribed loci, in a Dicer-like 4 (DCL4) dependent manner, but not at the untranscribed locus, indicating that active transcription is required for diRNA production. Remarkably, long-read DNA sequencing analysis shows that these diRNAs do not detectably influence DSB repair via either end-joining or microhomology-mediated end-joining. Furthermore, endogenous diRNAs have a modest effect on homologous recombination-associated repair, as impairment of the diRNA pathway in ago2 mutants resulted in only a slight reduction in RAD51 focus formation following Cas12a-induced DSBs. Together, these findings indicate that diRNAs are not essential for DSB repair itself but may function in the post-transcriptional silencing of damaged genes, likely to prevent aberrant transcription until proper repair is completed.

Title: High-performance xenograft read-sorting for DNA methylation analysis
Authors: Altendorfer, S.; Zentgraf, J.; Schmitz, J. E.; Plass, C.; Gerhauser, C.; Rahmann, S.
Abstract: Xenograft sorting tools separate sequenced DNA reads by species. We have enhanced the computational method and tool Xengsort to enable efficient epigenetic profiling of patient-derived xenograft models; it now supports cytosine-converted whole genome or reduced-representation data. Benchmarking Xengsort against several established methods (ICRG, bamcmp, XenofilteR) revealed consistently high accuracy across tools, but Xengsort outperformed the other tools in computational efficiency due to its alignment-free design.

Title: Structure-Based Drug Design of Novel Inhibitors Targeting the Thiamine Biosynthesis Pathway in Bacteria
Authors: Krishna, N.; Ulaganathan, V.
Abstract: Current generation antibiotics are limited by poor target selectivity and are often mismanaged, leading to widespread antimicrobial resistance. The bacterial thiamine biosynthesis pathway offers compelling alternative since it is highly essential for bacterial survival and yet absent in humans. Genetic perturbations within pathway lead to documented auxotrophy and virulence defects, indicating low mutational tolerance within this pathway. Thiamine phosphate synthase is a key bottleneck enzyme performing the crucial role of coupling thiazole and pyrimidine moieties to form thiamine monophosphate. To develop a suitable inhibitor against it, a structure-based drug design pipeline was implemented. High-throughput virtual screening of nearly 1.5 million molecules provided sufficient exploration of chemical space. Further, R-group substitution was utilized for lead optimization. Structure-Activity Relationship analysis upon molecular mutants reveals patterns among R-group interactions to catalytic residues across various scaffolds. Additionally, ADMET screening and validation using molecular dynamics simulations resulted in a potent orally bioavailable broad-spectrum bactericidal molecule.

Title: Structural basis for phosphorylation-induced inactivation of the rice ammonium transporter AMT1;1
Authors: Yu, F.; Huang, X.; Wang, S.; An, N.; Zhang, P.; Huang, J.; Zhang, X.
Abstract: Ammonium (NH4+) uptake and transport in plants are mediated by ammonium transporters (AMTs), which are tightly regulated by phosphorylation to prevent excess ammonium influx and toxic accumulation. However, the mechanism of phosphorylation-mediated inactivation is unique and remains unclear. Here, we report cryo-EM structures of the rice (Oryza sativa) ammonium transporter OsAMT1;1 in its wild-type and phosphomimetic variant T452D states. OsAMT1;1 forms a stable homotrimer, with conserved motifs affirming a shared transport mechanism within the AMT/MEP/Rh superfamily. Our structural analysis reveals that T452D phosphomimetic stabilizes an intracellular salt-bridge network and maintains the channel in a closed state, in which the ICL5 loop positions the hydrophobic plug residue Leu360 near the cytoplasmic exit to occlude the channel exit and abolish complementation capacity. Our findings elucidate phosphorylation-induced inactivation mechanism for the plant AMT1 subfamily, providing a structural paradigm for the post-translational regulation of nutrient uptake.

Title: Human Metalloenzymes Are Disproportionately Linked to Disease: The HEAM Structural Annotation Resource
Authors: Miller, E.; Lim, S.; Copeland, M. M.; Slusky, J. S. G.
Abstract: Catalytic metal-binding sites are established drug targets for many human diseases, yet systematic study of how metal function relates to disease is limited by the lack of a resource combining structural localization of human metal-binding sites with catalytic annotation at scale. We introduce HEAM (the Human Enzymatic Annotation of Metalloproteins), a structurally annotated dataset of 1,933 human metalloenzymes and 1,171 non-catalytic metalloproteins. HEAM incorporates annotated metals into protein structures at their corresponding binding sites and classifies each site as catalytic or non-catalytic using the machine learning classifier MAHOMES II. HEAM more than quadruples the human site-level coverage of the largest prior metalloenzyme database. Using HEAM, we show that human metalloproteins are significantly enriched in KEGG disease pathways relative to the human proteome, and that metalloenzymes specifically are significantly enriched in ClinVar pathogenic variants -- a distinction obscured in prior, catalytically unresolved metalloprotein datasets. These pathogenic variants are concentrated in metabolic disorders, indicating that metabolic dysfunction is a substantial contributor to metalloenzyme-linked disease. By pairing 3D structural annotation with catalytic classification, HEAM provides both a foundation for structure-guided drug design against metal-binding sites and a resource for determining how catalytic and non-catalytic metal function contribute to human disease.

Title: How Bacterial Growth-Phase Reshapes Synthetic Gene Circuit Function
Authors: Lu, E. J.; Del Vecchio, D.
Abstract: The development of biological engineering tools have improved the ability to embed novel functions into living organisms. Concurrently, our understanding of the interface between synthetic genetic circuits and their host has accelerated in the past decade, enabling the development of context-aware predictive models. However, long-term circuit function remains difficult to predict when designs operate in field-relevant conditions. Specifically, while synthetic genetic circuits are typically characterized during exponential growth, these must operate for extended periods of time in nutrient-limited conditions and where bacteria enter stationary growth phase. In this work, we construct a mathematical model that captures the dynamics of a genetic circuit as cells transition into stationary growth phase. To achieve this, we construct synthetic genetic circuits with fluorescent reporter output and measure plasmid DNA copy number, mRNA level, protein level, and live cell count over the course of one week in stationary growth phase. We find that transcription rates plummet shortly after entering stationary phase but settle at a basal value that depends on both the promoter and ribosome binding site. Translation rates also decline in stationary phase, but protein accumulation due to lack of cell division can increase protein levels well beyond exponential phase. Our model recapitulates these findings and is capable of predicting the output of new genetic circuits. This model can serve as a tool to determine how a genetic circuit design may change on longer time scales where cells enter stationary growth phase.

Title: A tissue time machine to forward-predict single-timepoint data applied to tuberculosis granulomas
Authors: Nanda, P.; McCaffrey, E. F.; Michael, C. T.; Delmastro, A. C.; Michael, G.; Mattila, J. T.; Flynn, J. L.; Angelo, R. M.; Kirschner, D.
Abstract: Recent advances have improved understanding of infection; however many detailed datasets are based on single timepoints post-infection and cannot generate longitudinal insights needed to predict infection outcomes. For example, pulmonary infection with Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) initiates a complex system of immune and bacterial interactions that leads to granuloma formation, yet single snapshots in time need elaboration long-term. We develop a new approach, the tissue time machine, applied to predict outcomes of non-human primate granulomas from initiation to endpoint using single timepoint tissue datasets including high-dimensional spatial features. This involves identifying granuloma digital partners, simulations most closely resembling real granulomas from a virtual library of over 50,000. By analyzing digital partners, we predict infection outcomes of 22/28 granulomas, and that Mtb-specific, IFN-{gamma}-producing T cell recruitment rates influence uncertainty for the 6/28. This method is applicable to any system that allows for mechanistic predictions over time using heterogeneous, incomplete, and high-dimensional datasets.

Title: A monoallelic immunopeptidome atlas of 10 prevalent canine DLA-88 alleles
Authors: Miyamae, J.; Murakami, K.; Hemmi, H.
Abstract: Characterization of naturally processed MHC class I (MHC-I)-bound peptides is essential for defining allele-specific peptide-binding features and understanding the functional consequences of MHC-I polymorphism. However, immunopeptidome analyses of dog leukocyte antigen (DLA) class I (DLA-I) molecules remain limited and comprehensive monoallelic ligand datasets for prevalent DLA-88 alleles are still lacking. Here, we established canine melanoma-derived cell populations expressing individual functional DLA-88 alleles and generated a monoallelic immunopeptidome atlas of prevalent DLA-88 alleles. Using liquid chromatography-tandem mass spectrometry, we identified 32,702 naturally processed peptides of 7 to15 amino acids across 10 DLA-88 alleles, substantially expanding the available DLA-88 immunopeptidome landscape. These 10 alleles exhibited canonical peptide length distributions and allele-specific binding motifs that reflected variation in binding-groove pseudo-sequences defined from human MHC-I peptide-contact residues. Ligand sharing between DLA-88 alleles was associated with binding site distance. Incorporation of the comprehensively characterized DLA-88 ligand datasets in this study increased by more than fourfold the number of published canine DLA-I alleles with ligand-characterized reference alleles predicted to have similar peptide-binding features. We also found that antigen-processing signatures were highly conserved with those reported in humans. As a proof-of-concept application, we selected 54 DLA-88-bound peptides identified in our immunopeptidome analysis as candidate peptides for canine cancer immunotherapy by evaluating the normal tissue expression profiles of their source proteins. This DLA-88 immunopeptidome atlas provides insights into allele-dependent differences in antigen presentation and represents a valuable resource for developing accurate DLA-88-binding peptide prediction tools and supporting peptide-based immunological studies in dogs.

Title: T cell engagers convert acute tumor killing into endogenous vaccination
Authors: Lecuit, M. M.; Corre, B.; Garcia, Z.; Lemaitre, F.; Vaysse, A.; Alonso, R.; Goudot, C.; Arnaud, B.; Feldmann, L. C.; Moraes Cabe, C.; Seffer, V.; Guermonprez, P.; Grandjean, C. L.; Guerin, M. V.; Bousso, P.
Abstract: T cell engagers (TCEs) redirect T cells to kill tumors by cross-linking CD3{varepsilon} to a tumor antigen, independently of T cell receptor specificity. Some patients achieve remissions that persist long after drug clearance, but whether TCEs can couple acute cytotoxicity to the generation of lasting adaptive immunity remains unknown. Here, using an immunocompetent mouse model for clinical-grade human TCEs, we show that TCE-mediated killing initiates an endogenous vaccination cascade. Intravital two-photon imaging reveals a perforin-dependent cytotoxic wave that peaks within 24 hours, then subsides despite massive T cell accumulation. Single-cell transcriptomics and adoptive transfers demonstrate that memory CD8 T cells, the principal effector reservoir in mouse and human, transit through a progenitor-like state before differentiating into cytotoxic effectors with recall competence. Crucially, tumor lysis fuels cross-priming of tumor-specific CD8 T cells by XCR1 type 1 conventional dendritic cells, a cDC1-dependent step essential for durable tumor control and protective memory upon rechallenge.

Title: Spatiotemporal profiling of T cell repertoires in Lynch syndrome reveals convergent immune responses through neoplastic progression
Authors: Edwards, P.; Swinyard, O.; Ronel, T.; Jiang, Y.; Nageswaran, G.; Sakr, C.; Yasmin, S.; Grant, H.; Smith, E.; Braeutigam, K.; Braeutigam, K.; Varughese, S.; Datt, P.; Martinez, A.; Fisher, J.; Chain, B.; Shiu, K. K.; Jansen, M.; Baker, A.-M.; Monahan, K. J.; Graham, T. A.
Abstract: Surveillance of individuals with Lynch syndrome (LS), who are carriers of heterozygous inactivating mismatch repair (MMR) gene mutations that predispose to colorectal cancer, enables the study of tumour-immune coevolution during tumour initiation. Somatic loss of MMR activity in the LS colon leads to the accrual of cancer driver mutations, and also of neoantigens likely to generate an adaptive immune response. However, the spatial and temporal immune dynamics in colon and peripheral blood are uncharacterised. Here we show that the neoplastic evolution of mismatch repair deficient (MMRd) clones leads to large-scale and sustained reorganisation of the T-cell repertoire in colon and peripheral blood. We performed dense spatiotemporal profiling of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires from 109 colonic biopsies (11 tumour samples, 98 normal bowel) from seven individuals, with eight matched blood repertoires. We additionally analysed 13 colorectal polyp repertoires from eight participants, 286 cross sectional blood repertoires from 242 participants (198 LS and 44 non-LS) and 52 longitudinal peripheral blood samples from 26 individuals with LS. We detected tumour-associated T cell clones, some of which were widely present in normal bowel tissue and also detectable in peripheral blood. Sequence similarity analysis revealed conserved TCR architectures across tissue compartments and recurrent clustering patterns between patients, that were not present in non-Lynch controls, consistent with convergent MMRd-associated antigen-driven immune selection. We identified systemic signatures associated with local tumour immune activity and revealed evidence of structured repertoire remodelling before overt malignancy. Longitudinal profiling revealed frequent turnover of low-abundance clonotypes, whereas highly abundant clonotypes persisted for several years. Collectively, our data defines the local and circulating TCR landscape associated with colonic neoplasia in LS, and provides a framework for LS blood-based immune monitoring, early interception and biomarker development.

Title: Cannabinoid receptor 1 activity promotes microbial dysbiosis by stimulating the oxygen-dependent expansion of Enterobacteriaceae
Authors: Mitchell, M. K.; Carty, M. A.; Snow, N. L.; Archambault, M. T.; Budsberg, A. E.; Carrillo, E. V.; Vignieri, E. E.; Older, E. A.; Rometo, O. L.; Van de Wal, L. E.; Floyd, K. J.; Baker, L. R.; Kunkle, C. A.; Li, J.; Ellermann, M.
Abstract: The endocannabinoid system is comprised of bioactive lipids that signal via cannabinoid receptors, which can modulate barrier and immune functions along the gastrointestinal tract. Clinical studies indicate that endocannabinoid activity is dysregulated in inflammatory bowel diseases. Here, we show that endocannabinoid activity promotes metabolic dysfunction within the colonic mucosa, resulting in microbial dysbiosis and exacerbated colitis. Stimulation of the cannabinoid receptor CB1 resulted in the expansion of Enterobacteriaceae within the gut microbiome, a common feature of inflammation-associated dysbiosis. Preceding this microbial change, CB1 activity induced transcriptional signatures of mitochondrial stress and immune activation within the colonic mucosa. This was followed by a reduction in mucosal ATP production and the induction of aerobic respiration genes in luminal Escherichia coli. Genetic inactivation of aerobic respiration in E. coli limited its proliferation, indicating that CB1 activity stimulates oxygen-dependent Enterobacteriaceae growth. In IBD susceptible mice, endocannabinoid activity promoted mucosal infection by an E. coli pathobiont, which corresponded with elevated pro-inflammatory markers. In inflammation resistant mice, acute CB1 stimulation was sufficient to accelerate the infection dynamics of an Enterobacteriaceae pathogen, resulting in exacerbated colitis. Taken together, our data support a model in which endocannabinoid signaling at the CB1 receptor disrupts respiratory metabolism in the colon, compromising the anoxic environment of the lumen that is critical for maintaining aerobically respiring pathogens at low abundance. More broadly, our findings highlight a proinflammatory effect of endocannabinoid activity that can contribute to intestinal disease development.

Title: LytM family endopeptidase LmdC is controlled by regulated auto processing and proteolytic destruction in Pseudomonas aeruginosa
Authors: Sommerfield, A.; Darwin, A. J.
Abstract: Enzymes that cleave the bacterial peptidoglycan sacculus, known collectively as autolysins, are critical for growth, division and morphogenesis, but their activities must be carefully controlled to avoid catastrophic lysis. Some autolysin control mechanisms have emerged, but we still know little about how most of them are regulated. Here, we report a novel control mechanism for the LytM/M23 family endopeptidase PA4404 in P. aeruginosa, which we have named LmdC. We have discovered that LmdC is auto catalytically cleaved into N- and C-terminal domains that are then degraded by the carboxyl-terminal processing proteases Prc and CtpA respectively. The effects of various mutations on LmdC-linked {beta}-lactam resistance suggested that full length LmdC is the functional enzyme, with its auto catalytic cleavage serving only to initiate its proteolytic destruction. The auto catalytic cleavage of LmdC was inhibited by overproducing a polymer-forming cytoskeletal protein bactofilin homolog encoded by PA0664, which we named Baf, and a protein of unknown function encoded by PA0663, which we named Api (auto processing inhibitor). We hypothesize that Baf and Api could promote a location specific role for LmdC. In this scenario, the dangerous potential for any free LmdC to cleave peptidoglycan at the wrong place would be prevented by its immediate auto processing and degradation. The widespread co-occurrence and linkage of lmdC and baf homologs, coupled with conserved features of those LmdC homologs, makes it likely that regulated LmdC auto processing is a widely conserved control mechanism.

Title: Andes virus from the MV Hondius outbreak is highly pathogenic in hamsters and airborne shed
Authors: Rissmann, M.; Wilbrink, M. F.; Herder, V.; Handrejk, K.; Filaire, F.; Ilia, G.; Jones, W. W.; Zaeck, L. M.; van Eck Schipper, D.; Vaes, V. P.; Shresta, S.; Reimerink, J.; van Dijk, L. L. A.; Power, M.; te Marvelde, M. R.; de Meulder, D.; Cassidy, H.; Wijnans, K.; Sacharoen-Rugebregt, S.; Grifoni, A.; Sette, A.; Oude Munnink, B. B.; Reusken, C. B. E. M.; Haagmans, B. L.; de Vries, R. D.; Herfst, S.; Palmarini, M.
Abstract: In May 2026, an outbreak of hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS) caused by Andes virus (ANDV) was detected aboard the cruise ship MV Hondius, sparking public health measures in multiple countries. ANDV infections in humans are mostly sporadic, most often linked to exposure to infected rodents in South America, although small clusters of human cases, like the 2026 outbreak on the MV Hondius occur as well. It is not known whether virological factors may contribute to this distinct epidemiology, and no phenotypic characterisation of the newly emerged ANDV (ANDV2026) has been carried out to date. Here, using an ANDV isolate from a presymptomatic patient from the MV Hondius, we studied pathogenesis, identified sites of viral replication, characterized innate and adaptive immune responses, and quantified shedding in golden Syrian hamsters. ANDV2026 proved to be highly pathogenic in hamsters, causing severe pulmonary disease reminiscent of HPS. ANDV2026 triggered a delayed type-I IFN response and inflammatory response in the lungs consistent with the key pathological features of HPS, and we detected viral replication in both respiratory and extra-respiratory tissues, including the brain. Infected animals mounted neutralising antibodies and T cell responses, the latter directed predominantly against the L and N proteins. Importantly, ANDV2026-infected animals shed virus through multiple routes, and we detected infectious virus in air samplers connected to cages housing ANDV2026-infected hamsters. In contrast, control hamsters infected with a rodent-derived ANDV isolate (ANDV9717869) shed little virus and air samples were consistently negative. These findings consolidate established features of ANDV pathogenesis, while revealing properties not previously described. Phenotypic characterisation of patient-derived ANDV isolates in animal models can strengthen outbreak preparedness, identify markers of disease severity, and support the development of medical countermeasures.

Title: A Third-generation Lentiviral Vector System for Flow Virometry-based Analysis of HIV-1 Env and Other Viral Envelope Proteins
Authors: Busskamp Castro, P. I.; Parreuter, J.; Brands, C.; Perkovic, A.-M.; van Bilsen, B.; Giebel, B.; Bohne, J.; Tertel, T.; Ghanam, J.; Thakur, B. K.; Karsten, C. B.
Abstract: Individual human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) particles can differ in their envelope protein (Env) despite being genetically identical. This non-genetic diversity can influence antibody recognition and has been implicated in the formation of persistent virus fractions that escape complete inhibition by broadly neutralizing antibodies. Investigating non-genetic diversity in HIV and other viruses requires approaches capable of characterizing antibody binding to individual viral particles. Flow virometry provides a promising tool for single-particle analysis, but a system combining high biosafety with specific particle labeling and versatility is lacking. Here, we developed a third-generation lentiviral vector system specifically designed for flow virometry. Fluorescent proteins were incorporated into the HIV-1 Gag polyprotein between the matrix- and capsid-encoding regions, flanked by viral protease cleavage sites, creating the packaging constructs pLentiFlow-eGFP and pLentiFlow-mCherry. Lentiviral particles (LVPs) based on pLentiFlow vectors were fluorescent and retained infectivity comparable to LVPs generated with the parental vector system despite reduced particle production. We optimized LVP detection on a CytoFLEX nano and defined a linear p24-based concentration range for reliable single-particle analysis. Using complementary controls, we demonstrated that background from the assessed sources accounted for no more than approximately 3% of events within a broad eGFP+ gate and confirmed that the detected fluorescent particles were predominantly membrane-enclosed. As a proof of concept, LVPs were pseudotyped with vesicular stomatitis virus glycoprotein, severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 spike, or HIV-1 Env. Envelope-specific antibody binding was detected using 8G5F11, CR3022 or PGT128, respectively, demonstrating that different viral surface proteins can be analyzed on a common particle backbone. Together, these results establish a third-generation lentiviral vector system for flow virometry that combines intrinsic particle labeling with high biosafety and flexible pseudotyping. The system provides a platform for investigating envelope protein-associated non-genetic diversity and its consequences for antibody recognition in HIV and other viruses.

Title: Exploring the antibiotic-producing capabilities of Canadian High Arctic bacteria
Authors: Farkas, E.; Lambeck, M.; Parish, G.; Belanger, L.; Serrador, D.; Nekouei, M.; Koteva, K.; Le Mauff, F.; Lypaczewski, P.; Shapiro, B. J.; Whyte, L.; Wright, G.; Auclair, K.; Gruenheid, S.; Nguyen, D.
Abstract: Microbial communities in harsh environments such as the Canadian high Arctic, remain a relatively unexplored source of antimicrobial natural products. In this study, we developed a pipeline for screening and evaluating bacterial isolates cultured from 23 Canadian high Arctic soil, sediment, and active-layer permafrost samples to discover antibacterial compounds. The pipeline incorporated an undergraduate studentsourcing program and produced created a collection of over 350 bacterial isolates with preliminary antibacterial activity. Following dereplication, whole genome sequencing and secondary screening by co-culture assays, five isolates were prioritized to test crude extracts for antibacterial activity. Among bioactive crude extracts from these isolates, the Pseudomonas isolate with the most potent activity against S. aureus was analyzed. Using liquid chromatography bioactivity guided fractionation, we identified a potential bioactive compound known as koreenceine A, a compound previously only isolated from a Pseudomonas from temperate soil and involved in gene expression of other their microbial community. Here we expanded the known antibiotic activity of koreenceine A and confirmed that a {triangleup}kecBCD genetic knockout of the putative biosynthetic gene cluster significantly abrogated the antibacterial activity.

Title: Microbial Dynamics Across Commercial Spaceflights of Varying Duration
Authors: Krishnavajhala, A.; Gingras, M.-C.; Santiago-Rodriguez, T.; Chen, Y.; Bandaranaike, D.; Bhamidipati, S.; Xiang, Q.; Kottapalli, K.; Momin, Z.; Santhanam, A.; Walker, K.; Wang, Q.; Griffin, S. M.; Masternak, M. M.; Ross, M. C.; Muzny, D.; Wu, J.; Urquieta, E.; Gibbs, R.; doddapaneni, H.
Abstract: Spaceflight introduces environmental stressors that can alter human microbiomes and immune responses. We analyzed 259 and 17 biospecimens for microbiome and single-cell studies from n=6 astronauts across two commercial ISS missions: Axiom 2 (10-day mission) and Axiom 3 (21-day mission). Samples included saliva, stool, urine, and body swabs from 10 anatomical sites, profiled via 16S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) gene amplicon sequencing. Gut and oral microbiomes remained stable, while skin-associated communities exhibited transient diversity shifts post-flight. Taxonomic analysis revealed individual and site-specific patterns, as well as from the spaceflight/ISS environment. Cytokine profiling from single-cell data indicated immune activation, with IL-32 and IL-16 transcripts elevated in Axiom 2 and Axiom 3. Microbiome and interleukin correlation analyses found 14 significant associations in Axiom 2 data. These findings provide an integrated view of microbiome individuality. Our study represents a descriptive comparison of two missions, informing strategies for crew health on future long-duration missions.

Title: Direct 3D isolation in gelatin methacryloyl microbeads versus conventional 2D isolation and culture: a trade-off between mesenchymal stromal cell purity and niche-associated transcriptional profiles
Authors: Hussein, N.; Miller, C.; Roger, Y.; Venturini, L.; Stadler, M.; Haertle, M.; Lavrentieva, A.; Haase, N.; Rudorf, S.; Hoffmann, A.; Egger, D.
Abstract: Bone-marrow mesenchymal stromal cell (MSC) isolation typically couples plastic-adherence selection to planar expansion. Therefore, the recovered cells may reflect culture adaptation as much as native stromal biology. Direct isolation within a three-dimensional matrix could reduce planar selection, but its effects on cellular recovery, composition and MSC transcriptional profiles remain insufficiently resolved. We therefore developed a gelatin methacryloyl (GelMA) workflow progressing from bulk hydrogels to medium-surrounded GelMA microbeads (GMBs) and compared 3D-derived cells with conventional 2D cultures. Qualitative live/dead staining with calcein acetoxymethyl ester (CAM) and propidium iodide (PI) and 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine (EdU) imaging established cellular activity in both GelMA formats. In bulk GelMA cultures from four human donors, CD73-, CD90- and CD105-associated flow-cytometric readouts did not increase from day 7 to day 21. At day 21, the combined marker readout was numerically higher in donor-matched 2D cultures than in bulk 3D cultures, which retained heterogeneous marker-defined populations. GMBs enabled cell recovery and flow-cytometric characterization and motivated an exploratory one-donor single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis. The final dataset contained 37,784 cells across four samples and 23 annotated populations. MSC-focused re-embedding resolved 13,175 cells into two 3D and four 2D clusters. A pooled comparison identified 4,840 differentially expressed genes (DEGs, false discovery rate [FDR]<0.01, |log2FC|[≥]1), indicating a broad method-associated expression shift. The 3D C1 cluster combined progenitor-, extracellular-matrix-, adhesion-, cytokine-, hypoxia/glycolysis- and predicted-interaction-associated programmes, whereas 2D clusters showed mitochondrial, cytoskeletal/mechanoadaptive and proliferative programmes. Thus, 2D culture yielded a more strongly represented and compositionally purer MSC compartment, while 3D isolation contained rare MSC clusters with niche-associated transcriptional profiles within a heterogeneous marrow environment. These findings support a testable native-associated tendency for 3D, but donor replication, matched recovery and direct native-reference mapping are required before inferring greater in-vivo similarity or functional superiority.

Title: Benchmarked sequencing methods reveal hidden mosaic variation in the human brain
Authors: Weng, J.; Cha, D. H.; Chun, J.; Santamarina-Ojeda, P.; Cheng, Y.; Howarth, R.; Xu, Y.; Huangfu, X.; Wang, P.-J.; Jung, S.; Ryu, J.; Noh, Y.; Lee, S.; Yang, X.; Ju, Y. S.; Alexandrov, L. B.; Chung, C.; Gleeson, J. G.
Abstract: Mosaic variants (MVs) record cellular lineages, but their recovery is strongly method-dependent. Here, we benchmarked four duplex sequencing methods alongside bulk and single-neuron genome sequencing in matched human brain tissue. The methods differed in genome representation, MV yield and mutational profiles, with limited caller-level concordance. However, read-level interrogation revealed substantially greater cross-method molecular support. To systematically recover this evidence, we developed Read-level Integration for Variant Evidence Recovery (RIVER), expanding the pool of cross-method-supported candidates by approximately two orders of magnitude relative to caller-level overlap. Orthogonal sequencing at ~10,000x across brain and peripheral tissues validated approximately half of the tested RIVER-rescued candidates. MVs recovered from a single brain region resolved broadly distributed and regionally restricted clones and provided lineage information among individual neurons. These findings show that RIVER substantially expands the pool of endogenous lineage markers available to investigate human development, aging, disease-associated mosaicism and clonal evolution.

Title: A telomere-to-telomere genome of Holstein cattle resolves chromosome-end architecture and the genetic basis of telomere length
Authors: Liu, F.; Wang, T.; Cao, P.; Wang, W.; Fatima,  ; Zhang, Z.; Meng, F.; Lin, P.; Wei, Z.; Liu, J.; Wu, R.; Wang, L.; Li, Y.; Zhao, G.; Bao, X.; Sun, W.; Jiang, Y.; Wang, Y.; Li, X.
Abstract: Telomeres safeguard chromosome-end integrity, yet population-scale dissection of telomere-length genetics has been largely restricted to humans. Here, we report a 3.01-Gb telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome of Holstein cattle that resolves repeat-rich chromosome ends and centromeres and enables telomere-length quantification at single-chromosome-end resolution. Holstein chromosome ends show marked telomere-length asymmetry and end-specific variation in telomere variant repeats, subtelomeric tandem repeats, GC/CpG composition, and DNA methylation. Using sequencing-depth-corrected telomere-length phenotypes from 9,591 cows, teloGWAS identifies major loci encompassing RTEL1, CTC1, and TERT, while multi-tissue eQTL, sQTL, TWAS, and co-expression analyses prioritize CTC1 and implicate DNA replication, DNA repair, and stress-response networks. Together, these findings extend population-scale telomere genetics beyond humans and establish a sequence-resolved framework for chromosome-end biology and telomere-informed livestock genomics.

Title: Pocket-Conditioned Generation and Down-Selection of Non-Oxime Reactivators
Authors: Jimenez, D.; Clay, W. K.; Barajas, C.
Abstract: Acetylcholinesterase reactivation is a structure-constrained design problem in which chemical plausibility, access to central nervous system, pocket compatibility, and reactivation geometry must be considered together. We report a computational workflow for generating and down-selecting candidate non-oxime reactivators in the paraoxon-inhibited human acetylcholinesterase pocket. For generating the candidates, the first-round utilitezed pocket-conditioned DrugFlow, but due to solubility issues, the second-round candidates were output form FlexFlow, DrugFlow-OOD, DrugFlow preference alignment, and pocket-specified BoltzMol-1. A property-guided DrugDiff output provided a protein-unconditioned baseline. Although 93.9% of the DrugDiff subset passed Lipinski criteria for druglikeness, its median synthetic accessibility (SA) score signalled that it was difficult to synthesize compared against other generative approaches. A strict predicted blood-brain barrier and solubility gate retained 31.0% of Base DrugFlow, 61.0% of FlexFlow, 27.5% of DrugFlow-OOD, 3.8% of DrugFlow-PA, and 35.1% of BoltzMol-1. The second-round top-ten lists had lower SA scores and higher quantitative estimate of drug-likeness (QED) values than the DrugDiff shortlist, while DrugDiff had fewer aggregate heuristic violations. This work compares the best performing generative drug discovery models with suggested down sleection approaches for human acetylcholinesterase reactivation.

Title: Matrix-modulated Air-liquid Interface Microenvironments Reveal Architectural Control of Lung Tumor Phenotypes
Authors: Yangin, K.; Ozturk, E.
Abstract: Lung adenocarcinoma evolves within a highly structured microenvironment shaped by air exposure, basement-membrane ligands and three-dimensional (3D) organization, yet standard in vitro models capture only fragments of this architecture. Here, we systematically disentangle how air-liquid interface (ALI), extracellular matrix (ECM) cues and dimensionality interact to regulate tumor epithelial states. Using five architectural configurations, we demonstrate that these parameters act synergistically to promote distinct morphological, transcriptional and inflammatory phenotypes not observed under conventional 2D or submerged 3D cultures. ALI broadly enhanced epithelial cohesion, progenitor activation, partial EMT programs and cytokine expression, whereas ECM embedding further induced ALI-mediated mesenchymal activation, matrix remodeling and invasive cytoskeletal organization. Notably, 3D ALI uniquely produced a hybrid alveolar-mucinous phenotype characterized by concurrent SP-C and MUC5B induction, alongside integrated epithelial, basal and mucosecretory identities. These emergent states reflect tumor-relevant plasticity and illuminate architectural controls over lineage infidelity, invasion and inflammatory activation. Together, these findings establish ALI-ECM-dimensionality intersections as critical regulators of lung tumor phenotype and provides a systematic architectural framework for designing more physiologically relevant in vitro lung cancer models.

Title: genomeRxiv: a genome-based identification web server that bridges the gap between taxonomy and strain typing
Authors: Mazloom, R.; Sharma, R.; Lorv, J. S.; Kaur, S.; Sharma, P.; Brown, C. T.; Brown, C. T.; Pierce, N. T. T.; Pritchard, L.; Heath, L. S.; Vinatzer, B.
Abstract: Precise identification depends on highly resolved classification. Therefore, whole genome-based strain typing schemes have been implemented for identification of the most important microbial human pathogens. However, there are no dedicated typing schemes for the majority of prokaryotic human, animal, and plant pathogens, or for non-pathogenic microbes, often limiting their identification to taxonomic classification tools that have the species as the smallest unit. To address this deficiency, we created the genomeRxiv web server which contains over 350,000 genomes and leverages the average nucleotide identity (ANI)-based Life Identification Number (LIN) approach, allowing users to identify prokaryotic genomes in real time from approximately genus-rank to near strain-level resolution. LINs are overlaid with circumscriptions of species and infraspecies classes, integrating taxonomy with strain typing. Metadata and distance trees are visualized to complement inferred phylogenetic relationships with epidemiological and ecological information. A command line tool is provided for users to upload k-mer sketches of unpublished genomes and associated metadata, facilitating epidemiological investigations without the need to share complete DNA sequences. In conclusion, genomeRxiv constitutes a much-needed resource for precise, rapid identification of the many prokaryotes not included in any pathogen-specific typing scheme.

Title: The eIF3a subunit drives RNA binding within the eIF3 complex
Authors: Ide, N. A.; Gentry, R. C.; Ashwood, B.; Rudbach, M. A.; Yoo, K.; Velez, P. K.; Communale, V. M.; Hartwick, E. W.; Kinz-Thompson, C. D.; Gonzalez, R. L.; Aitken, C. E.
Abstract: Eukaryotic initiation factor 3 (eIF3) is a multi-subunit protein complex that binds the 40S pre-initiation complex (PIC) and has an essential role in messenger RNA (mRNA) recruitment, a process encompassing mRNA attachment and loading, scanning, and start-codon recognition. During recruitment, eIF3 is positioned to contact both the 18S ribosomal RNA (rRNA) component of the PIC and the mRNA, but how individual eIF3 subunits contribute to these RNA interactions remains poorly understood. A major obstacle has been the lack of a compositionally defined, biochemically active reconstituted yeast eIF3 complex that enables systematic analysis of individual subunits and defined subcomplexes. Here, we reconstitute Saccharomyces cerevisiae eIF3 from individually purified recombinant subunits and show that it is compositionally stable under our assay conditions and recapitulates core biochemical activities of native eIF3, including PIC binding, stimulation of capped mRNA recruitment, and RNA binding. Using this system, we show that eIF3a provides a core RNA-binding activity within eIF3 and that interactions with other eIF3 subunits modulate this activity in the intact complex and in defined eIF3a-containing subcomplexes. These results establish a reconstituted yeast eIF3 system for dissecting subunit-level biochemical activities and support a model in which subunit context tunes eIF3a-driven RNA binding during initiation.

Title: Giant Vesicle Platform for Synthetic Endoplasmic Reticulum Networks
Authors: Vallero, C.; Pramanik, S.; Sun, T.-W.; Tarnawski, M.; Spatz, J. P.; Dimova, R.; Lipowsky, R.
Abstract: The endoplasmic reticulum (ER) is a membrane-bound organelle found in all eukaryotic cells. This organelle has a fascinating morphology, which involves a network of membrane nanotubes and three-way junctions connecting three nanotubes. Previous reconstitution studies were based on proteo-liposomes with a size of 100 to 200 nanometers, using electron microscopy as the main method to image the resulting membrane morphologies. These studies revealed the importance of membrane GTPases, that is, membrane proteins that hydrolyse GTP. Here, we introduce an alternative platform for the formation of synthetic ER networks starting from giant unilamellar vesicles with a typical size of 10 mirometers and containing a single membrane GTPase such as atlastin from fruit flies or Sey1 from yeast. This giant vesicle approach makes the networks accessible to optical microscopy, by which one can elucidate both their structure and their dynamics. We first demonstrate that the membranes' propensity to form synthetic ER networks depends strongly on the lipid composition. More precisely, we show that this propensity varies non-monotonically with the mole fraction of cholesterol and that the frequency of three-way junctions has a maximum for an optimal mole fraction between 10 and 15 mol%. This optimal value is comparable to the mole fraction of cholesterol as estimated for ER membranes in vivo. We also demonstrate the formation of synthetic ER networks when the membranes contain only the membrane GTPase Sey1 but no other membrane protein, which implies that Sey1 is able on its own to generate a high membrane curvature. Based on the reconstitution approach introduced here, the synthetic ER networks can now be further investigated using the versatile toolbox that has been developed for giant vesicles.

Title: When can site-specific glycoform compositions resolve biosynthetic rates?
Authors: Matsui, Y.; Himori, K.; Zhang, B.; Kitani, A.
Abstract: Mass spectrometry measures site-specific glycoform compositions, but when these measurements can resolve upstream biosynthetic rates remains unclear. We assess whether small changes in effective rates, each representing the processing capacity of a group of biosynthetic reactions, can be distinguished near specified baseline rates with secretion held fixed. Because proportions sum to one, m jointly normalised glycoform classes provide at most m-1 independent quantities. Distinguishing changes in k rates therefore requires at least k+1 classes, although this count alone does not ensure identifiability. In a canonical N-glycan network with eight rates, exhaustive evaluation of nine-class panels identified panels that could locally distinguish all eight rates. Among these panels, class choice changed the allowable measurement error by approximately 18-fold for the same target uncertainty in inferred rates. A separate simulation within the fixed network showed that estimating rate-change combinations with weaker composition responses reduced bias but amplified measurement noise. We applied the framework to plasma data from 40 controls and 70 patients across 14 inherited glycosylation-disorder groups. A prespecified composition score for the expected pathway disturbance ranked among the top two in 13 of 14 groups. Network responses linked observed composition shifts to biosynthetic reaction classes. Expanding site models from five to eight reaction classes improved control-composition fit but reduced the number of sites at which all modelled rates were locally distinguishable and increased noise sensitivity. Rate inference thus requires sufficient panel size, separable rate responses, adequate measurement precision and a model that fits the composition. These requirements guide measurement design and help determine whether compositions support pathway-level interpretation or individual-rate inference.

Title: An epigenetic palimpsest: the King penguin's blood methylome reveals conserved hematopoietic ageing
Authors: Hukkanen, M.; Nitta Fernandes, F. A.; Davis, L. R.; Hofer, M.; Bardon, G.; Paciello, E.; Zahn, S.; Zhu, T.; Westerlund, S.; Meyer, B. S.; Ollikainen, M.; Le Bohec, C.; Cristofari, R.
Abstract: Age-associated DNA methylation is conserved across vertebrates, but whether epigenetic ageing reflects cellular ageing programmes or age-dependent shifts in cell composition remains unresolved. Here, using 126 whole-blood methylomes from known-age King penguins (Aptenodytes patagonicus), we exploit a vertebrate system in which nucleated erythrocytes dominate peripheral blood, minimizing the influence of leukocyte heterogeneity. We identify a core set of 409 ageing-associated genes showing lifelong, clock-like methylation change. These genes are strongly enriched for regulators of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) function and niche communication. Integration of methylome, transcriptome and chromatin-accessibility data reveals that many of the strongest ageing signals derive from genes inactive in mature erythrocytes, consistent with the persistence of epigenetic states from ancestral hematopoietic progenitors. A comparison with methylation profiles from 1,501 humans identified a conserved cross-species subset of ageing genes, and a human epigenetic age model constructed solely from orthologues of penguin ageing genes predicts chronological age with high accuracy while remaining largely insensitive to blood cell composition. We propose that blood epigenetic ageing signatures contain a long-lived cellular memory of stem-cell ageing, that may represent an evolutionarily ancient layer of the vertebrate ageing process.

Title: PRC2-binding regions are hotspots of DNA methylation entropy in pre-cancer and cancer
Authors: Bukovec, D.; Misheva, M. S.; Gjorgjievska, M.; Kungulovski, G.
Abstract: DNA methylation aberrations and variability are pervasive features of cancer, yet their relationship with chromatin regulation remains incompletely understood. Across hundreds of matched tumor-normal methylomes, regions with the highest methylation entropy in both tumor and normal tissues were consistently enriched for PRC2-associated factors. In tumors, inter-sample methylation variability was increased across the full range of PRC2-associated levels, while mean methylation progressively increased from low- to high-PRC2-binding regions; this gradient was substantially weaker in matched normal tissues. PRC2-associated regions with higher DNA methylation levels were preferentially associated with poised and repressed chromatin states, reduced chromatin accessibility, and reduced gene expression. Independent normal-precancer-cancer cohorts showed that this PRC2-associated methylation state emerges early, with precancerous and malignant tissues displaying highly similar profiles that are distinct from those of healthy tissues. Single-cell colon cancer methylomes independently confirmed increased methylation entropy at PRC2 regions. Higher PRC2-region entropy was associated with scores reflecting hypoxic states, aggressive tumor features, and poorer survival outcomes. Collectively, these findings identify PRC2-binding regions as hotspots of DNA methylation variability that become dysregulated during tumorigenesis.

Title: A high-resolution protein-RNA binding atlas for structure-aware interaction prediction and post-transcriptional regulatory modeling
Authors: Karimzadeh, M.; Fish, L.; Karner, H.; Linder, J.; Emadi, A.; Hernandez-Corchado, A.; Smaili, F. Z.; Stewart, E. M.; Kelley, D. R.; Wang, B.; Najafabadi, H. S.; Leonetti, M.; Goodarzi, H.
Abstract: RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) control post-transcriptional gene expression by regulating RNA processing, localization, stability, and translation. However, our understanding of RNA regulation remains limited by the resolution, scale, and uniformity of available RBP binding maps. Here we introduce eclair CLIP (ecCLIP), a high-throughput CLIP-seq platform that combines endogenous protein tagging for uniform affinity capture with ligation-free library preparation to generate high-resolution RNA-protein binding profiles. We applied ecCLIP to 67 endogenously tagged RBPs in HEK293T cells, generating a high-quality transcriptome-scale atlas that recovered known binding preferences and captured post-transcriptional regulons linked to RNA half-life. To test the utility of the atlas, we incorporated ecCLIP into Borzuki, a Borzoi-derived sequence-to-function model trained on complementary RNA degradation, expression, CLIP, and Perturb-seq data. Inclusion of ecCLIP data improved RNA half-life prediction and assessment of 3' UTR variant effects on RNA stability, demonstrating that our atlas helps capture RNA dynamics. To directly model the cis-regulatory grammar underlying these RBP-RNA interactions, we developed Pythia, a structure-aware neural network architecture that incorporates context-free grammar-inspired fixed convolutions to explicitly encode RNA base-pairing features. Pythia predicted RBP binding from sequence and structural context and decomposed predictions into sequence- and structure-dependent components. We tested this decomposition for five RBPs using massively parallel reporter CLIP (MPRC) binding assays in cells, using synthetic RNA libraries containing mutations designed to preserve or disrupt predicted RNA structures across nominated binding sites. We used the same MPRC strategy to confirm allele-specific binding effects for variants prioritized by Pythia. Together, ecCLIP and Pythia provide a resource for structure-aware decoding of RNA-protein interaction grammar and interpretation of post-transcriptional regulatory variation.

Title: Mapping Synthetic Circuit Design Space through Massively Parallel Measurement of Single-Cell Dynamics
Authors: Olsman, N.; Shenker, J. Q.; Choudhary, D.; Paulsson, J.
Abstract: Engineering predictable and robust gene-regulatory networks requires a quantitative understanding of how their dynamics depend on genetic design and environmental conditions. To investigate these relationships, we introduce BARRACUDA, a high-throughput platform that combines combinatorial assembly and programmable perturbations with lineage-resolved time-lapse imaging and optical pooled screening. Experiments using this platform follow approximately one million cell lineages, collectively sampling tens of thousands of circuit designs. We used BARRACUDA to investigate how the robustness of circuit behavior depends on molecular components and their interactions, combining quantitative dynamic measurements with precise genetic and environmental control. Antithetic integral feedback provided a model system linking a defined molecular architecture to theoretical predictions of robust adaptation. Through a hierarchy of increasingly complex libraries, we characterized individual components and used those measurements to model and interpret the dynamics of complete feedback circuits. Circuits built from wild-type inhibitory proteins rejected disturbances but also exhibited sustained overadaptation and fast disturbance-induced oscillations unexplained by a reduced control model. These discrepancies motivated a screen of de novo binders that retained inhibitory function while reducing host-stress response. Selected de novo binders supported strong feedback regulation and robust performance in the rebuilt circuits. Across more than 20,000 recovered feedback-circuit variants, binder identity and controller expression organized regimes of strong regulation and sustained oscillation. Counterintuitively, disturbances sometimes improved compensation rather than compromising it, consistent with nonlinear changes in feedback engagement. Together, these results show how structured libraries and massively parallel measurements of single-cell dynamics can test mechanistic theories across scales of circuit complexity, reveal missing biological interactions, and map the design space of gene-regulatory networks.

Title: A mathematical model of tumor growth driven by oxygen lactate exosome feedback
Authors: Sadhu, G.; Dalal, D.; Byrne, H.
Abstract: Solid tumors develop within a heterogeneous microenvironment shaped by coupled biochemical and metabolic processes. As a tumor grows, oxygen gradients develop from the periphery towards the core, giving rise to hypoxic regions. Hypoxia induces a metabolic shift from oxidative phosphorylation to glycolysis, leading to elevated lactate production. Experimental studies further indicate that increased lactate levels enhance the secretion of tumor-derived exosomes carrying proteins, mRNA, and lipids, which in turn promote tumor cell proliferation. Together, these interactions form a feedback loop linking oxygen availability, lactate accumulation, and exosome-mediated signaling. Despite growing experimental evidence for each component, the impact of this coupled oxygen lactate exosome axis on tumor growth dynamics has not yet been systematically explored from a mathematical perspective. It remains unclear how the oxygen lactate exosome axis affects tumor growth - impact of nonlocal effects. In this paper, we develop a mechanistic mathematical model to investigate how this feedback mechanisms affects tumor growth. We first consider an in vitro setting oxygen levels are spatially homogeneous and vary periodically in time between normoxic and hypoxic states, capturing key features of cyclic hypoxia observed in vivo. Numerical simulations reveal that exosome mediated feedback has a pronounced effect on tumor volume under chronic hypoxia. In addition, we observe that the tumor volume decreases as the period of cyclic hypoxia increases. We then extend the model to an in vivo framework by incorporating oxygen diffusion and consumption, allowing spatial heterogeneity to emerge. Simulations reveal that tumor cells in normoxic regions benefit indirectly from enhanced exosome secretion driven by lactate produced in hypoxic regions. Overall, the results show how spatially mediated metabolic signaling can amplify tumor growth and aggressiveness, and illustrate how mathematical modeling can increase understanding of non local feedback mechanisms within the tumor microenvironment.

Title: Self-reactive human CD8⁺ T cells restricted by HLA-E mediate immunoregulatory and antiviral functions
Authors: Walters, L. C.; Guo, X.; Casquero, C.; Urbach, J. M.; Leddy, O.; Cakan, E.; Chan, A. O.; Balivada, P. A.; Wisner, H.; Bryson, B. D.; White, F. M.; Carrington, M.; Collins, D. R.; Birnbaum, M. E.; Walker, B. D.
Abstract: HLA-E constitutively presents self VL9 peptides on healthy cells, signaling an intact HLA class I pathway and protecting cells from natural killer cell attack. Beyond this canonical role, HLA-E-restricted CD8 T cells that recognize foreign pathogen peptides have emerged as mediators of immunity in multiple human infections, with orthologous responses conferring unprecedented protection in an HIV vaccine model. However, the poor stability of most pathogen-derived HLA-E ligands raises the possibility that additional modes of HLA-E-restricted recognition remain undiscovered. Here, we establish an alternative paradigm in which HLA-E-restricted CD8+ T cells recognize disease-associated increases in self-VL9/HLA-E rather than foreign antigen. These cells, which we term E-sensors, integrate activating and inhibitory signals to discriminate physiological from pathological levels of HLA-E expression. We demonstrate that E-sensors selectively eliminate highly activated, proliferating immune cells that express high levels of HLA-E, establishing a mechanistically resolved pathway of human CD8+ T cell immunoregulation. E-sensors also recognize pathogen-induced HLA-E upregulation and directly eliminate infected cells without prior pathogen-specific priming, demonstrating immediate immunosurveillance through recognition of increased self. Consistent with this antiviral function, we establish E-sensors as a previously unrecognized component of spontaneous HIV immune control in persons who naturally control infection. Together, our findings establish a pathway of human immunosurveillance and immunoregulation in which CD8 T cells detect pathological increases in a constitutively expressed non-classical HLA class I molecule presenting a conserved self-peptide. This disease-agnostic mechanism of immune recognition has implications across infection, cancer, autoimmune disease, and other pathologies that upregulate HLA-E. Unlike classical HLA class I molecules, the near-monomorphic nature of HLA-E further positions this pathway as an untapped effector axis, warranting investigation as a potential target for immune interventions.

Title: Disruption of cAMP Signalling and RNA Regulation Confers Cefiderocol Resistance in Acinetobacter baumannii
Authors: De Oliveira, D. M. P.; Heaton, R.; Whyte, H.; Buedenbender, L.; Indraratna, A.; Nguyen, N. T. K.; Phan, M.-D.; Alquethamy, S. F.; Hirose, Y.; Permana, B.; Wright, A.; Peleg, A. Y.; Nochomovitz, M.; Harris, P. N. A.; Ramsay, K. A.; Holmes, P.; Blaskovich, M. A. T.; Paterson, D. L.; Boyce, J. D.; Everest-Dass, A.; Schembri, M. A.; Tree, J. J.; Walker, M. J.; Forde, B. M.
Abstract: Cefiderocol is a siderophore-conjugated cephalosporin used to treat severe multidrug-resistant Gram-negative infections. Its recent prioritisation for US national preparedness underscores its clinical importance, yet resistance can emerge despite apparent in vitro susceptibility. Here, we identify two regulatory routes to cefiderocol resistance in carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii (CRAB): mutation of the cAMP-producing adenylate cyclase CavA and truncation of the glycine-rich RNA-binding domain of the post-transcriptional regulator Hfq. These variants occurred in contemporary clinical isolates, conferred resistance in a murine CRAB lung-infection model and imposed minimal fitness costs. In Escherichia coli, deletion of the CavA orthologue cyaA increased competitive fitness during sub-inhibitory cefiderocol exposure. Hfq-CLASH and integrated omics revealed Hfq-dependent regulation of Fur-associated iron homeostasis in A. baumannii. Under iron limitation, truncated-Hfq induced a defence-primed state that attenuated siderophore uptake and reduced cefiderocol activity. These findings identify bacterial regulatory state and iron availability as determinants of cefiderocol susceptibility, with implications for resistance surveillance and susceptibility testing.

Title: Excessive sample reagent incubation time increases the risk of false rifampin resistance results in Xpert(R) MTB/RIF Ultra tests performed on paucibacillary Mycobacterium tuberculosis sputum.
Authors: Chilambi, G. S.; Modi, K.; Rudra, P.; Chen, Y.; Chakravorty, S.; Alland, D.
Abstract: A high rate of false rifampicin resistance (RIF-R) was recently reported in paucibacillary sputum samples tested with the Xpert(R) MTB/RIF Ultra (Ultra) assay. However, 96% of the studied facilities started the test 8 - 12 hours after addition of sample reagent (SR), exceeding the manufacturers recommended limit of 4 hours. Assessed whether excessive long SR incubation could lead to similar false RIF-R results in paucibacillary samples in a reference laboratory setting. We evaluated the performance of the Ultra assay following incubation of TB-negative sputum spiked with 300 CFU/mL and 100,000 CFU/mL levels of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) H37Rv in SR for different durations (15 min to 24hrs.) at different temperatures (-20 to 370C) to determine the effect on RIF result calls. No false RIF-R results were observed in these samples with 105 CFU/mL Mtb at any of the conditions tested, even when they deviated largely from recommended limits. Similarly, freezing the 300 CFU/mL SR treated samples at minus 200C for 18 h also prevented the development of false RIF-R results. However, sputum spiked with 300 CFU/ml Mtb, produced false RIF-R calls at longer incubation times and higher incubation temperatures than are recommended by the manufacturer. Approximately half of the results displayed melt patterns consistent with hetero-resistance, indicating SR-induced mutagenesis in a wild-type background. This study demonstrates that extended off-label SR incubation of paucibacillary specimens beyond the recommended 4-hour limit can generate false RIF-R results. Freezing paucibacillary specimens in SR may mitigate this risk although it is not yet an approved procedure.

Title: Chimeric archaeal BHB-human pre-tRNA scaffold HARBOR system enables versatile production of functional circular RNA modalities
Authors: Cao, S.-M.; Feng, X.; Zhang, J. T.-C.; Wu, H.; Wang, X.; Ye, K.; Chen, L.-L.
Abstract: Circular RNAs (circRNAs) exhibit superior intrinsic stability and lower immunogenicity compared with linear RNAs, rendering them promising modalities for biomedical and biotechnological applications. Here, we establish the HARBOR (Human-Archaeal RNA Backbone for Overexpression of circular RNA) system, an engineered endogenous circRNA expression platform integrating a human precursor transfer RNA (pre-tRNA) scaffold with an archaeal Bulge-Helix-Bulge (BHB) motif. HARBOR repurposes the endogenous tRNA splicing machinery to generate chimeric pre-tRNA intermediates, which are rapidly degraded following processing, while producing circRNAs ranging from hundreds of nucleotides to 8 knt in cells and in vivo. Notably, it enables robust production of large-sized circRNAs with yields nearly 80-fold than the intronic complementary sequence-mediated back-splicing (3D5) system and can drive protein expression from translatable circRNAs at an efficiency close to 20-fold than the Tornado system. Such prominent properties support diverse applications of HARBOR, including producing therapeutic aptamers targeting PKR-associated neuroinflammation and pathological TDP-43 condensation, as well as protein-coding circRNAs encoding adenine base editors for genome editing and MYOD1 for fibroblast-to-myocyte trans-differentiation. Collectively, HARBOR represents a versatile, scalable, and user-friendly platform that unifies circRNA-based aptamer and protein expression applications, advancing circRNA-enabled engineering and biomedical applications.

Title: Using Polycistronic gRNAs and a tRNA Cleavage System in CRISPR-Based Genome Editing of Toxoplasma gondii
Authors: Grech, J. C.; Teng, M.; Wang, R.; Child, M. A.
Abstract: CRISPR/Cas9 is widely used for genetic manipulation in Toxoplasma gondii, but optimizing gRNA expression and multiplexed editing remains challenging. Here, we evaluated alternative promoters, gRNA scaffolds, and a tRNA-based polycistronic system to improve editing efficiency and reduce synthetic DNA costs. Four constructs targeting the SAG1 locus were used to compare the U6 and H1 promoters, as well as standard and modified gRNA scaffolds. U6-driven constructs supported robust gRNA-targeted Cas9 activity, whereas H1-driven constructs failed to produce detectable phenotypes. The alternative gRNA scaffold, modified by a number of base changes and insertions, increased knockout efficiency compared to the standard scaffold. To simplify dual gRNA-based methods, we establish a tRNA-based polycistronic system to simultaneously target two independent loci. Targeting the SAG1 and UPRT locus for proof-of-concept, all U6-driven polycistronic constructs conferred efficient SAG1 knockout and 5-fluorodeoxyuridine resistance, whereas H1-driven constructs exhibited position-dependent activity, with only the 3' gRNA being functional. These results demonstrate that U6-driven, tRNA-based polycistronic gRNA expression enables reliable multiplexed genome editing in T. gondii, with the minimal H1 promoter being insufficient for consistent multi-gRNA activity. This optimized system provides a scalable framework for dual-gRNA CRISPR strategies in this organism.

Title: A massively parallel reporter screen defines the syntax of SECReTE, a secretion-enhancing cis regulatory targeting element, in mammalian cells
Authors: Haimovich, G.; Lobinsky, G.; You, S.-T.; Schirman, D.; Grynspan, F.; Gilbert, A.; Olender, T.; Gerst, J. E.; Pilpel, Y. T.
Abstract: Messenger RNA (mRNA) localization to specific subcellular regions is crucial for proper protein translation and localization. Potential means to localize mRNAs include cis-acting or structural motifs embedded within the sequence. We previously identified a secretion-enhancing cis regulatory targeting element (SECReTE) enriched in mRNAs encoding secreted proteins from prokaryotes, eukaryotes, and viruses, found to enhance both protein synthesis and secretion by localizing mRNAs to the endoplasmic reticulum (ER) membrane. Defined as at least 10 consecutive NNY triplets (where N is any nucleotide and Y is a pyrimidine), this highly degenerate motif can be specified by approximately ~10^15 different sequence combinations. Yet, some combinations may prove more efficient than others in regulating mRNA localization and protein secretion. To better understand SECReTE syntax and to identify robust combinations, we designed and synthesized a library of ~5 x 10^4 variants and inserted them into the 3' untranslated region (3'UTR) of two reporter genes, green fluorescent protein (GFP) and immunoglobulin light chain. We expressed each variant in Chinese hamster ovary cells and assayed their activity using parallel assays to measure the effect of each variant upon mRNA partitioning between the ER and cytoplasm, and protein secretion. Our results reveal that ER-associated mRNAs are enriched with SECReTE elements of a defined syntax. Notably, RRY repeats (where R is purine) were superior to NNY repeats. Variants conferring a high mRNA ER localization score consistently enhanced protein secretion, confirming the mechanistic relationship between mRNA targeting to the ER and secretion efficiency. The correlation between variant performances across both reporters suggests a shared regulatory mechanism. Additional analysis identified a novel secretion-promoting cis element, called "split NNS" (where S is G or C). This work refines the syntactic definition of mRNA localization motifs that regulate protein secretion in both natural and heterologous expression systems.

Title: Transient transcriptomic rejuvenation during intestinal and liver regeneration in mice
Authors: Iqbal, S.; Gladyshev, V. N.
Abstract: Aging and regeneration are fundamental biological processes, but the relationship between them is poorly understood. During intestinal regeneration, adult epithelial cells reactivate developmental programs that support repair. To investigate if this plasticity alters tissue biological age, we developed and validated intestinal tissue and epithelium-specific transcriptomic aging clocks. Across various regeneration models, epithelial states were predicted by these clocks to be younger than controls. Their expression changes were also negatively associated with intestinal aging signatures. The resulting younger state was characterized by YAP-associated regeneration and reduced mature enterocyte identity. In a separate irradiation model, the predicted epithelial age first increased, then fell at the peak of regeneration and later increased again during recovery. The pace of this response differed with host age. In a chemotherapy-induced injury model, epithelium in young animals also entered this younger state earlier and then returned to its preinjury state during recovery. Old epithelium responded later, but also reversibly transitioned through a rejuvenated state. Further spatial transcriptomic analyses linked lower epithelial age with regeneration in selected injured and tumor-associated regions. In addition, liver regeneration after partial hepatectomy in old animals also led to a decreased transcriptomic age, accompanied by pathway changes negatively associated with aging signatures. Overall, these findings suggest that mammalian regeneration is associated with a transient reduction in biological age, whose timing and persistence depend on tissue, host age and the course of repair.

Title: Distinct regulation across the transcription cycle drives mitotic transcriptional silencing
Authors: Gaetani, P.; Tavares, A.; Paixao, T.; Oliveira, R. A.
Abstract: In most organisms, as cells enter mitosis, transcription is globally silenced. While individual studies have shown that each stage of the transcription cycle can be modulated during mitosis, how initiation, elongation, and termination are temporally and kinetically regulated to ensure transcriptional silencing remains unclear. Here, we combine real-time quantitative imaging of ongoing transcription in early Drosophila embryos with mathematical modelling to systematically dissect how transcriptional kinetics change as cells progress into mitosis. We found that transcription initiation undergoes a gradual repression starting in prophase, while elongation rates remain unaltered. After nuclear envelope breakdown, an abrupt mechanism causes premature termination of elongating RNA, driven at least in part by the SNF-helicase-like protein Transcription Termination factor 2 / Lodestar (TTF2/Lds). Our study provides a quantitative framework for understanding how transcription is modulated across the cell cycle, demonstrating that mitotic repression arises from multiple processes with different dynamics that collectively ensure the precise shutdown of gene expression.

Title: Cyclin E/CDK2 deficiency links cell cycle control to intestinal barrier integrity and tight junction regulation
Authors: Hatten, H.; Verwaayen, A. M.; Corcini-Berndt, M.; van der Vorst, E. P. C.; Paffen, D.; Nevzorova, Y. A.; Maas, S. L.; Penners, C.; Liedtke, C.
Abstract: Background & Aims: The intestinal epithelium renews continuously through cell cycle-dependent turnover, yet it remains unknown whether core cell cycle regulators directly control intestinal barrier function. We investigated how loss of the Cyclin E1/Cyclin E2/CDK2 complex affects intestinal homeostasis. Based on the important role of this complex in compensatory liver regeneration, we hypothesized that its combined loss would impair epithelial renewal and barrier integrity. Methods: We generated Ccne2-/- mice and triple knockout (TKO) mice with intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific deletion of Ccne1 and Cdk2 on a constitutive Ccne2-null background and characterized intestinal architecture, proliferation, and barrier function using histology, immunoblotting, qPCR, and FITC-dextran permeability assays. Mechanistic findings were validated in CRISPR/Cas9-generated Ccne2-deficient and CDK1-overexpressing MC38 colon carcinoma cells using transcriptomics and kinomics approaches. Results: Contrary to our hypothesis, TKO maintained and Ccne2-/- mice even enhanced cell cycle activity selectively in the colon, along with enhanced Cdk1 expression, had significantly lower serum FITC-dextran levels after oral administration, and increased Tjp1/ZO-1 expression, consistent with reduced intestinal permeability. Ccne2-deficient MC38 cells recapitulated the increase in ZO-1 and exhibited transcriptional enrichment of gene sets associated with tight junctions and cell cycle. CDK1 overexpression in MC38 cells increased ZO-1 protein abundance and was associated with activation of an AMPK-related kinase network. In TKO and Ccne2-/- colonic epithelium, CDK1, phosphorylated AMPK and ZO-1 showed partial colocalization at lateral epithelial cell-cell contacts. Conclusions: Loss of Cyclin E2, either alone or in combination with epithelial Cyclin E1/CDK2 deficiency, is associated with increased CDK1 expression and strengthens the colonic barrier integrity in mice. Findings from MC38 cells suggest that transcriptional reprogramming and enhanced CDK1 signaling in the context of Cyclin E2 deficiency may contribute to tight junction reinforcement and improved barrier function.

Title: Sexual reproduction impacts vertebrate organ aging
Authors: Chen, J.; Tsenter, A.; Costa, E. K.; Yu, D.; Lin, X.; Chen, K. L.; Bot, V. A.; Housh, M. J.; Heraud, L.-P.; Perry, S. V.; Khondker, R. C.; Snyder, M. P.; Webb, A. E.; Wyss-Coray, T.; Brunet, A.
Abstract: Sexual reproduction is a central component of life. Yet, an unanswered question remains: how does sexual reproduction shape physiology and health across an individual's lifetime? Unlike other external factors such as diet and exercise, the impact of sexual reproduction on organ health during aging is far less studied, particularly in vertebrates. Here, we develop the short-lived killifish as a vertebrate model to study how lifelong mating affects organ aging. We discover that mating regulates liver aging in a cell-type and sex-specific manner. In old female livers, mating dampened hepatocyte inflammation and reduced myeloid cell levels, and machine-learning models predicted that mating led to a 'younger' transcriptomic age in several liver cell types. Functionally, mating reduced hepatic accumulation of several lipid classes and was associated with enhanced female resilience against the liver toxin acetaminophen. More broadly, mating induced anti-inflammatory and metabolic rewiring transcriptomic signatures in the brain and gut, indicating that mating may affect vertebrate organ aging more globally. Using publicly available human datasets and plasma proteomics aging clocks, we observed an association between sexual experience and a 'younger' plasma proteomic age of several cell types, including hepatocytes. Our work provides evidence that lifelong mating reshapes the physiological context during aging in a vertebrate, highlighting an understudied connection between vertebrate sexual history, health, and aging.

Title: Chromatin Acetylation Overrides Substrate Stiffness-Dependent Mechanoresponse and Lineage Specification in Human Mesenchymal Stem Cells
Authors: Joshi, R.; Mukherjee, S.; Muralidharan, P.; Suryawanshi, T.; Yadav, P.; Dharnidharka, V.; Shukla, S.; Majumder, A.
Abstract: Human mesenchymal stem cells (hMSCs) exhibit a stiffness dependent cellular phenotype and lineage bias. Cells on soft substrate display reduced cell spreading, less cellular traction, smaller and fewer focal adhesions and decreased actin stress fibre organization, whereas cells on stiff substrate exhibit the converse behaviour. Further, hMSCs preferentially undergo adipogenic differentiation on soft substrate and osteogenic differentiation on stiff substrate. These stiffness dependent changes are accompanied by global chromatin condensation/decondensation on soft/stiff substrates. Despite these well documented correlations, it remains unclear whether modulating chromatin condensation alone can be sufficient to reprogram stiffness dependent cellular phenotype.
