Reconstructions that treat all observations as terminal leaves and disregard collection order cannot represent sampled ancestors or use their temporal relationships. We introduce reconstruction methods in the Cancer Tree Biopsy Framework (CTBF) that distinguish a copy-number profile from its separate observations across biopsies. Biopsy-guided reconstruction connects successive samples, defers ambiguous parent assignments, and completes the unresolved ancestry. Partial trees leave unresolved ancestral profiles unspecified. Closed-state trees assign every ancestor an observed profile. For comparison, pooled methods combine the profiles from all biopsies without using collection order. Across 100 independently simulated histories, the biopsy-guided partial methods attained higher mean rooted generalized Robinson--Foulds similarity than pooled neighbor joining and topology-only MEDICC2, using both complete and observed-state-restricted true trees. Under a fixed computational budget, they also attained higher mean similarity than NestedBD-Long at the two evaluated evolutionary depths. Convergence of its Markov chain Monte Carlo runs was not established within that budget. Classical neighbor joining and anticentral top completion gave closely similar partial-tree scores. Closed-state performance depended on evolutionary depth and the evaluation endpoint. An application to three longitudinal KTN152 biopsies demonstrated genome-scale feasibility on patient-derived integer copy-number estimates.

Title: RNAcomp2D: a web tool to execute multiple methods and visually compare predictions of RNA secondary structure
Authors: Vitale, R.; Milone, D. H.; Stegmayer, G.
Abstract: Ribonucleic acids (RNAs) are involved in many important biological processes. In particular, non-coding RNAs are crucial regulators of cellular processes, playing a significant role in gene expression. RNA secondary structure is key to infer their specific function and for understanding how they interact with other molecules. Many computational models have been developed in the last decade to predict the secondary structure, achieving increasingly higher success rates. However, each new method has its own input-output interface, programming language, computational requirements and, sometimes, a dedicated server to run the model or just a source code in a repository. Thus, nowadays it is very hard to obtain predictions from multiple methods and compare them at once. A unified interface is urgently needed, which allows accessing several methods at the same time, visualizing and comparing predictions among them, and also with a reference structure when available. We introduce here RNAcomp2D, a web-based tool that allows users to enter an RNA sequence, or select one from RNAcentral, and obtain predictions of RNA secondary structures using several state-of-theart methods. Both classical thermodynamic methods and the latest deep learning models are packaged in containers and accessible in an unified website. All the predictions, and the reference structure if available, are shown at the same time in a single graphical interface. Moreover, as new models continue to be developed, this tool is designed to be scalable, allowing the addition of more prediction methods in the future. Web server is available at https://sinc.unl.edu.ar/web-demo/rnacomp2d/. Data and source code are available at https://github.com/sinclab/RNAcomp2D

Title: Facilitating Valid Statistical Inference in Biomedical Image Synthesis
Authors: Xiong, J.; Bao, S.; Liu, Q.; Lau, K.; Coburn, L. A.; Wilson, K. T.; Landman, B. A.; Vandekar, S.; Ma, S.
Abstract: Generative AI for medical image synthesis is increasingly used to impute missing data and augment biomedical datasets. Yet despite achieving high computational similarity to their real-world counterparts, synthetic images remain uncommon in clinical research practice, in part because of concerns about their biological validity. Here, we evaluate whether synthetic images support reliable downstream statistical analysis and biological inference in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) and multiplexed immunofluorescence (mIF) imaging. We find that associations between patient phenotypes and synthesized images can be severely attenuated. This is because synthesis methods typically omit clinically relevant covariates and therefore generate images that, although visually realistic, mask key biological differences. Furthermore, naive analyses treat synthesized images as if they were observed, ignoring the statistical uncertainty introduced by synthesis. Drawing on multiple imputation theory, we introduce Phenotype Aware Multiple Synthesis (PAMS), an analysis framework that requires no model retraining and instead adjusts synthesized output to recover valid biological estimates with appropriately calibrated uncertainty. Applied to MRI and mIF data, PAMS reduced estimation bias and restored nominal confidence interval coverage. Because it is compatible with existing synthesis pipelines, PAMS offers a practical and rigorous route to statistically and biologically valid use of synthesized images in biomedical imaging research.

Title: BGC Atlas v2: biosynthetic gene clusters with taxonomic and environmental context at scale
Authors: Bagci, C.; Talamas-Tanner, A.; Ziemert, N.
Abstract: Genomic and metagenomic studies have revealed that microbes have the capacity to produce an enormous diversity of secondary metabolites. These compounds play important roles in microbial interactions and are also a major source of medicines and other useful natural products, yet only a small fraction of this biosynthetic potential has been experimentally characterized. BGC Atlas was developed to explore this largely uncharacterized diversity by placing biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs) into genomic and environmental context. Here, we present BGC Atlas v2, which expands the collection more than eightfold to more than 16 million predicted BGCs and extends it from metagenomic assemblies to metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs), single-amplified genomes and isolate genomes. The new release provides taxonomic assignments for nearly all BGCs, harmonized environmental metadata, nested searches across biosynthetic, taxonomic, environmental and geographic properties, and protein-sequence searches against BGC-encoded genes. Its scale also reveals how much bacterial and archaeal biosynthetic diversity remains unexplored. By connecting pathways to related families, organisms and environments, BGC Atlas v2 supports natural-product discovery and investigations of prokaryotic biosynthetic diversity across taxa and ecosystems. BGC Atlas v2 is freely available at https://bgc-atlas.cs.uni-tuebingen.de.

Title: HighFold-Lasso: Topology-Guided Prediction of Lasso Peptide Structures Using AlphaFold3
Authors: Sen, C.; Zhang, C.; Yang, H.; Ge, Y.; Hou, H.; Zhu, N.; Li, C.; Mo, J.; Wu, Y.; Guo, J.; GUO, J.; Duan, H.
Abstract: Lasso peptides are a class of ribosomally synthesized and post-translationally modified peptides (RiPPs) characterized by a mechanically interlocked topology, in which the C-terminal tail is threaded through an N-terminal macrolactam ring formed by an isopeptide bond. This unique topology often confers high thermal stability and resistance to proteolytic degradation. However, the isopeptide linkage, threaded topology, and class-specific disulfide connectivity make lasso peptide structures difficult to reconstruct reliably using general-purpose structure prediction models. Here, we developed HighFold-Lasso, which combines custom covalent connectivity with lasso scaffold-guided adaptive low-noise initialization to enable conditional structure generation guided by lasso conformational priors. On a test set of 52 experimentally determined structures, HighFold-Lasso achieved a 100% lasso topology success rate, with a mean RMSD C-alpha of 1.942 Angstrom for the ring-loop region and 2.375 Angstrom for the full peptide. The framework supports modeling of the four classical lasso peptide classes (I-IV) and can represent noncanonical amino acids, providing computational support for structure-function studies and molecular engineering of lasso peptides.

Title: Homology-aware cross-validation strategies for generalization assessment in RNA secondary structure prediction
Authors: Bugnon, L.; Kulemeyer, G.; Gerard, M.; Di Persia, L.; Stegmayer, G.; Milone, D. H.
Abstract: RNA secondary structure prediction is a fundamental challenge in bioinformatics, essential for understandingthe functional roles of non-coding RNAs. Recently, deep learning models have transformed the field with impressive results, leading to critical discussions regarding the validity of current crossvalidation strategies. On the one hand, traditional random partitioning yields overoptimistic results due to data leakage from uncontrolled homology. On the other hand, removing every training sequence that even slightly resembles the testing set penalizes learning-based methods, requiring generalization to completely out-of-distribution sequences. While removing sequences and retraining a machine-learned model is straightforward, the experimental data used for development and parameter tuning of classical thermodynamic methods cannot be removed, leaving these methods to benefit from knowledge leakage. Here we critically analyze the cross-validation strategies currently used for RNA secondary structure prediction: random splitting, clustering-based splitting, and leaving one RNA family out for testing. We demonstrate that this last strategy can leave structural patterns present only in the test partition, making the learning task impossible. Overall, we find that the apparent superiority of either type of method is an artifact of the splitting strategy. We propose here two homology-aware strategies: human-learned folds, which exclude from testing the structures already captured by decades of human learning, and similarity folds, which measure performance across the full spectrum of test-totrain similarity. Both enable fair comparisons, applying the same rigorous assessment to classical and learning-based methods.

Title: High-throughput affinity profiling of antibodies against soluble and native membrane targets by digital flow cytometry
Authors: Cheng, Y.; Barcy, S.; Fujimoto, B.; Nelson, W.; Zhao, M.; Chiu, D. T.
Abstract: Binding affinity measurements are essential for optimizing and validating therapeutic and research antibodies, yet no high-throughput platform supports quantitative affinity measurements for both soluble and native membrane targets. Here we present a suite of digital flow cytometry (dFC) assays that determine equilibrium binding affinities by directly counting free and bound molecules in homogeneous mixtures without immobilization. The assays enable titration-free absolute KD  measurements for fluorescent binding partners, affinity measurements for unlabeled antibodies against membrane receptors on cell-derived extracellular vesicles (EVs), and multiplexed assays for rapid ranking or screening of antibody variants. We demonstrate applications by quantifying the effects of degree-of-labeling on the affinity of antibody-dye conjugates, and of drug conjugation on therapeutic antibody binding to receptors on human cancer EVs. By combining single-molecule quantitation, adaptable assay designs, and high-throughput analysis, dFC provides a versatile platform for therapeutic antibody optimization and research antibody validation.

Title: Freshwater Blackworms Solving a Maze
Authors: Adamatzky, A.
Abstract: We investigated the behaviour of freshwater blackworms (\emph{Lumbriculus variegatus}) in a circular maze containing food in its central chamber. Analysis of 11 time-lapse recordings showed that all tested worms entered the central chamber, although first-arrival times and spatial exploration patterns varied substantially. Registered occupancy maps revealed non-uniform use of corridors and chambers. Because the study did not include a no-food control, the observations demonstrate central-chamber entry and spatial exploration but do not by themselves establish food localisation or chemotaxis. The assay provides a reproducible framework for studying annelid exploration and for future controlled comparisons of sensory cues and maze complexity.

Title: Coupling Raman Spectroscopy and Acoustic Microscopy to Characterize Glioblastoma Resistance
Authors: Pesen, T.; Inanc, A.; Inci, D.; Cingoz, A.; Akgun, B.
Abstract: Therapy resistance in glioblastoma is usually described in genetic or metabolic terms. Here we ask whether it also has a measurable biophysical form. Combining Raman spectroscopy with scanning acoustic microscopy on TRAIL-sensitive and TRAIL-resistant glioblastoma cells, we find that resistance carries both a biochemical and a mechanical signature: the resistant cells differ at protein, lipid and nucleic-acid bands, contain 4.1-fold more neutral lipid, and hold a high acoustic impedance that does not change when the drug is applied, while sensitive cells stiffen as they die. Because acoustic impedance is an absolute quantity and neither measurement requires a label, the approach offers a route to recognising resistant populations from their physical state alone.

Title: GAT1508, a selective neuronal GIRK1/2 activator, exhibits superior antiepileptic efficacy and synergizes with cannabidiol
Authors: Simhadri, J.; Zorn, A.; Wang, L.; Kawano, T.; Ruiz, N. C.; Vagiaki, L.; Parvaiz, N.; Parvaiz, M.; Cantwell, L.; Chan, K.; Santa Cruz Garcia, A.; Dadiotis, E.; Rivera, N.; Felix, W.; Thakur, G. A.; Manetsch, R.; Plant, L. D.; Sidiropoulou, K.; Cui, M.; Skiniotis, G.; Logothetis, D. E.; Smirnakis, S.
Abstract: G protein-gated inwardly rectifying potassium (GIRK; Kir3) channels are key regulators of neuronal excitability and represent promising therapeutic targets for epilepsy. Here, we characterize GAT1508, a urea-based small-molecule activator selectively targeting neuronal GIRK1/2 heterotetramers, and compare its efficacy with previously described urea compounds ML297 and GiGA1. In a pentylenetetrazole (PTZ)-induced seizure model, GAT1508 demonstrated robust antiseizure activity, outperforming both ML297 and GiGA1 and achieving efficacy comparable to valproic acid. Electrophysiological studies using two-electrode voltage clamp in Xenopus oocytes revealed that GAT1508, unlike ML297 and GiGA1, selectively activates GIRK1/2 channels without significant activation of cardiac GIRK1/4 channels, suggesting reduced risk of cardiovascular side effects. Structural and computational analyses indicate that enhanced stabilization of GAT1508 compared to ML297 within the GIRK1/2 binding pocket promotes both ion permeation and channel gating through coordinated interactions with key residues. Furthermore, GAT1508, like the two other urea drugs, exhibited synergistic activation of GIRK channels when combined with G{beta}{gamma}-mediated pathways and significantly potentiated the antiseizure effects of cannabidiol (CBD) in both hippocampal slice recordings and in vivo seizure models. These findings establish GAT1508 as a potent and selective GIRK1/2 activator and support a novel combination therapeutic strategy for epilepsy based on convergent GIRK channel modulation.

Title: Synthetic biology-guided modular engineering of the secreted cutinase FoCut5a with a carbohydrate-binding module improves poly(ester-urethane) depolymerization in Yarrowia lipolytica
Authors: Messina, E.; Papi, M.; Barile, S.; De Rosa, R.; Scarcia, P.; Biundo, A.; Pisano, I.; Topakas, E.; Agrimi, G.
Abstract: Poly(ester-urethane) bioconversion requires efficient polymer-degrading enzymes and microbial hosts capable of processing the resulting monomers. However, the optimal modular design of secreted cutinases for depolymerizing insoluble polyester-polyurethanes remains largely unexplored. Here, we established a combinatorial synthetic biology strategy in Yarrowia lipolytica based on the fungal cutinase FoCut5a from Fusarium oxysporum. A library of 96 Golden Gate-assembled constructs, combining four secretion signals, four interdomain linkers, and six substrate-binding domains, was integrated site-specifically into the genome and screened for depolymerization of the polyester-polyurethane dispersion Impranil DLN-SD. The best-performing variant fused FoCut5a to the carbohydrate-binding module TrCBM1. LC-MS analysis demonstrated release of adipic acid, 1,6-hexanediol, and neopentyl glycol, confirming ester-bond hydrolysis within the polyester domains of the polymer and additionally detected 6-hydroxycaproate, indicating oxidation of polyurethane-derived 1,6-hexanediol by Y. lipolytica. Purified FoCut5a-TrCBM1 displayed unchanged activity on p-nitrophenyl butyrate but reduced Impranil turbidity 5.6-fold faster and increased release of 1,6-hexanediol and adipic acid by 76-fold and 220-fold, respectively, compared to the unfused enzyme. These results highlight modular enzyme engineering as an effective strategy to enhance polyester-polyurethane deconstruction and support Y. lipolytica as a platform for polymer bioconversion and upcycling.

Title: Interleukin-4 suppresses TIMP-2 transcription during endometriosis: Allele-specific regulation of the TIMP-2 -418G/C promoter by SP1
Authors: SAHA, S.; Ghosh, S.; Roy, T.; Nayak, D.; Mahapatra, P. D.; Maitra, A.; Swarnakar, S.
Abstract: Abstract Tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase-2 (TIMP-2) is a critical regulator of extracellular matrix (ECM) homeostasis in inflammatory disorder, but the mechanisms underlying its dysregulation in endometriosis remain poorly understood. Furthermore, whether inflammatory cytokine signaling and functional genetic variants within the TIMP-2 promoter contribute to its altered expression during disease progression is unknown. This study investigated the regulation of TIMP-2 expression by interleukin-4 (IL-4) signaling and the functional significance of the TIMP-2 -418G/C promoter polymorphism in endometriosis. We found that TIMP-2 expression was significantly reduced in ectopic lesions and serum samples from endometriosis patients in comparison to normal. Functional promoter analyses revealed that the -418C allele exhibited higher basal transcriptional activity than the G allele while displayed greater sensitivity to IL-4-mediated repression. IL-4 activated STAT6 signaling concomitant with SP1 and TIMP-2 downregulation, whereas SP1 overexpression restored TIMP-2 expression and SP1 silencing further suppressed its transcription, identifying SP1 as a positive regulator of TIMP-2. Single-cell transcriptomic analyses identified fibroblasts and mesenchymal populations as the major TIMP-2-expressing cell types and revealed enhanced inflammatory signaling and ECM remodeling networks in endometriosis. Collectively, these findings identify an IL-4-SP1-TIMP-2 regulatory axis that contributes to aberrant ECM turnover in endometriosis. Furthermore, the TIMP-2 -418G/C promoter polymorphism influences cytokine-mediated transcriptional regulation of TIMP-2, providing new mechanistic insights into the interplay between inflammatory signaling, genetic variation, and ECM homeostasis during endometriosis progression.

Title: Spatial protein quality control requires a functional GET pathway to prevent proteotoxicity
Authors: Langridge, C. A.; Sontag, E. M.
Abstract: The proper management of misfolded proteins is an essential biological process that is required for the survival of all organisms. Previous work has demonstrated that misfolded proteins can be spatially sequestered into membrane-less compartments to facilitate their degradation. Soluble cytoplasmic misfolded proteins are sequestered in the juxtanuclear quality control compartment (JUNQ), and insoluble cytoplasmic misfolded proteins are sequestered into the insoluble protein deposit (IPOD). It is still unknown if there are upstream targeting pathways necessary for regulating JUNQ and IPOD formation. Here we investigated the role of ER targeting on JUNQ and IPOD formation. We find that the GET pathway is necessary for JUNQ formation. Inefficiencies in the GET pathway contribute to premature IPOD formation, and a defective GET pathway inhibits JUNQ formation altogether. Notably, we find the role of the GET pathway in JUNQ formation is required for cell survival and loss of GET pathway function is only toxic under proteotoxic stress. Overall, we identify a new role for the GET pathway in regulating spatial PQC and demonstrate that spatial quality control is essential for cell health and survival.

Title: Protein Scaffolds Modulate the Electronic Structure of a Common Ketyl Radical Intermediate in Thiamine Pyrophos-phate-Dependent Radical Biocatalysis: Insights from EPR and ENDOR Spectroscopy
Authors: Rao, G.; Zhang, Z.; Liu, X.; Shiau, A.; Britt, R. D.; Yang, Y.
Abstract: New-to-nature radical biocatalysis has emerged as a powerful strategy for asymmetric C--C bond formation, yet the enzyme-bound radi-cal intermediates that underpin these transformations have remained largely uncharacterized. Here, we combine photo biocatalytic reaction development with multifrequency electron paramagnetic resonance (EPR), electron-nuclear double resonance (ENDOR) spectroscopy, and density functional theory (DFT) calculations to elucidate the ketyl radical intermediates formed during thiamine pyrophosphate (TPP)-dependent radical biocatalysis. We first develop an oxidative photobiocatalytic cross-coupling of aldehydes with alkyltri-fluoroborates catalyzed by engineered benzoylformate decarboxylase (BFD) variants, providing enantioenriched -chiral ketones through a new oxidative radical manifold inaccessible to benzaldehyde lyases (BALs). Freeze-quench multifrequency EPR and ENDOR spectroscopy directly identify the catalytically generated TPP-bound ketyl radical and reveal that this common radical intermediate adopts distinct electronic structures in BFD and BAL despite their identical chemical composition. Analysis of 1H, 19F, 31P, and 14N hyper-fine interactions, together with DFT calculations, demonstrates that enzyme-specific active-site conformations redistribute spin density between the TPP cofactor and substrate fragment. Greater substrate-centered spin delocalization in BFD provides a mechanistic basis for its superior radical C--C coupling activity relative to BAL. These results establish a direct relationship between protein-controlled electronic structure and catalytic function in TPP-dependent radical biocatalysis and demonstrate that engineering the electronic properties of a common radical intermediate represents a useful strategy for controlling enzyme reactivity in radical biocatalysis.

Title: Monocyte microRNA signatures in late-onset neonatal sepsis
Authors: Gkouti, E.; Kouvela, A.; Papachatzi, E.; Apostolidi, M.; Dimitriou, G.; Stamatopoulou, V.; Gkentzi, D.
Abstract: Abstract Purpose: Neonatal late-onset sepsis (LOS) remains a major cause of neonatal morbidity and its non-specific presentation challenges early diagnosis. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are promising biomarkers, but unbiased next-generation sequencing (NGS) of monocyte-specific miRNA has not been applied to neonatal LOS. We aimed to identify the monocyte-specific miRNA expression profile in neonatal LOS and its associations with the neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR) and systemic immune-inflammation index (SII). Methods: In a prospective study at the University General Hospital of Patras, 30 samples from 15 neonates with LOS and 8 healthy controls were analyzed. Monocyte miRNA expression was characterized by NGS pre and post antimicrobial therapy in cases and controls. Predicted target genes of the major candidate miRNAs were evaluated by RT-qPCR in an independent cohort. Clinical severity was assessed using NLR and SII. Results: Hsa-miR-6743-3p was significantly upregulated on day 0 and returned to control levels by day 2. Four additional miRNAs (hsa-miR-7108-5p, hsa-miR-3940-5p, hsa-miR-6851-3p and hsa-miR-1909-3p) exhibited a consistent trend toward upregulation in acute LOS. NLR, but not SII, was significantly elevated at diagnosis and showed excellent diagnostic performance (AUC 0.958), normalizing by day 2. Hsa-miR-7108-5p correlated positively with NLR on day 0. In the RT-qPCR cohort, its predicted target DRAM2, was reduced on day 0 and partially recovered by day 2. Conclusion: Monocyte miRNA profiling identified transient alterations in neonatal LOS that parallel clinical severity, while NLR showed high discriminatory performance. These exploratory findings warrant validation in larger cohorts to verify monocyte miRNAs as potential biomarkers of neonatal LOS.

Title: Complex enzyme active site scaffolding by iteratively detuned catalytic guidance
Authors: Qian, T.; Wang, W.; Gao, S.; Muraishi, A.; Zhao, B.; An, D. N.; Xue, F.; Kazman, M.; Mendoza, J.; Nguyen, H.; Bera, A.; Kang, A.; Yang, A.; Dai, W.; Liang, J.; Wang, Y.; Huang, X.; DiMaio, F.; Baker, D.
Abstract: De novo enzyme design requires sequences whose structures reproduce prescribed catalytic geometries. This remains challenging for active sites that couple multiple catalytic residues, cofactors and substrates. Here we introduce the Catalytic Guidance Engine (CaGE), which optimizes designed sequences to satisfy complex sets of functional constraints by alternating constraint guided structure prediction trajectories with sequence design, gradually fading the strength of the constraint information over cycles to nudge the designed sequence towards satisfying all the constraints. We train RF3 to accept atom-pair distances and other design conditions, and use classifier-free guidance to fade their influence over multiple design cycles. We also develop training-free motif guidance protocols which operate at inference time by directly adjusting selected atoms towards the design target geometry during diffusion sampling. CaGE improves catalytic-motif geometry across a diverse enzyme benchmark and yields sequences that recover complex target active sites in independent AF3 predictions. We experimentally demonstrate the power of CaGE by designing active enzymes with complex catalytic sites: a nonheme-iron design positions four active-site residues around an iron centre and a transition-state ligand, and a PLP-dependent design positions four catalytic residues around a PLP cofactor with multiple functional groups. Active site substitutions and a 2.7[A] crystal structure support the designed mechanisms and structures. Thus, CaGE provides a route to functional de novo enzymes with complex active sites.

Title: Coupled Effects of Airway Deformation and Carrier Gas on Pulmonary Gas-Particle Flow Dynamics Using an Euler-Lagrange Method with Dynamic Mesh
Authors: Yi, H.; Feng, Y.
Abstract: Physiologically realistic prediction of inhaled aerosol deposition in the airways requires simultaneous consideration of airway deformation kinematics and carrier-gas properties. This study developed a 3D deformable lung airway model (DLAM) using an experimentally validated computational fluid particle dynamics (CFPD) model coupled with a dynamic mesh method. Both the DLAM and a conventional static lung airway model (SLAM) were used to predict and compare inhaled gas-particle transport and deposition in a subject-specific mouth-to-generation 9 (G9) human respiratory system. To assess the significance of airway deformation, SLAM and DLAM were compared under identical 12 breaths per minute (BPM) inhalation-exhalation waveforms for both conventional air and heliox (70% He-30% O2), considering particle sizes of 1, 5, and 10 um. The effects of carrier gas and breathing frequency were further evaluated using the more physiologically realistic DLAM, comparing air and heliox at 12, 16, and 20 BPM for the same particle sizes. Results showed that the influence of airway deformation on aerosol transport is strongly dependent on particle size. Differences between SLAM and DLAM were negligible for 1 um particles. In contrast, for 5 and 10 um particles, SLAM consistently underpredicted beyond-G9 delivery and overpredicted G0-G9 local deposition for both air and heliox. For example, for 10 um particles at 12 BPM, accounting for airway deformation kinematics increased the beyond-G9 delivery fraction by an absolute 3.76% with air and 5.55% with heliox. After establishing the size-dependent deformation effect, DLAM was further used to evaluate the influence of carrier gas and breathing frequency on inhaled aerosol transport and deposition. Compared with air, heliox reduced turbulence kinetic energy, wall shear stress, and pressure drop, and enhanced beyond-G9 delivery of larger particles. Specifically, for 10 um particles, the absolute increases in beyond-G9 delivery were 16.82%, 20.25%, and 22.90% at 12, 16, and 20 BPM, respectively. Increasing breathing frequency reduced distal delivery, particularly for 5 and 10 um particles, whereas 1 um particles maintained approximately 99% beyond-G9 penetration across all investigated conditions. These findings indicate that DLAM is essential for accurate regional dosimetry of higher-inertia aerosols, for which the static airway simplification can significantly bias predicted deposition and distal delivery.

Title: Capturing domain-level detail of molecular interactions in the IMEx Consortium binding domain data set
Authors: Pinto, A.; Lo Surdo, P.; Medina Reyes, J. J.; Bergogne, L.; Padilla Franzotti, C.; Iannuccelli, M.; Panni, S.; Panneerselvam, K.; Ricard Blum, S.; Ragueneau, E.; Orchard, S.; Hermjakob, H.; Zanzoni, A.; Licata, L.
Abstract: The machinery of the cell depends on physical interactions, between proteins themselves, and between proteins and other biomolecules. The detailed characterisation of these interactions, including the identification of the precise sequence regions mediating binding events, is essential to understand both normal cell biology and disease mechanisms. Protein binding domains are specific regions of a protein sequence that mediate direct contact with a partner and represent a critical layer of functional annotation, bridging sequence, structure, and cellular function. Here we present the IMEx binding domain dataset, a large-scale, manually curated open-access set of molecular interactions assembled over more than two decades by the International Molecular Exchange (IMEx) Consortium. The dataset compiles experimentally derived binding region annotations from peer-reviewed literature, systematically linked to protein-protein interaction (PPI) records and mapped to standardised protein sequences in UniProtKB. We describe the curation model, data format, and content of the dataset, provide a descriptive and comparative analysis, and demonstrate the utility of the dataset as a gold standard for benchmarking interface prediction and variant effect annotation methods. Its integration with genomic variations further offers a route to elucidate the mechanistic basis of disease-associated mutations. The datasets are freely available through IntAct in the dedicated PSI-MI FeatureTAB format at https://ftp.ebi.ac.uk/pub/databases/intact/current/psimitab/features/ and are updated and enhanced with every release.

Title: Evolution toward larger cell size reduces internal cellular density
Authors: Sastokas, A.; Ho, W.-C.; Schmidlin, K.; Bhatt, M.; Brown, P. T.; Crossland, P.; Kindelin, A.; Uzum, Z.; Shepherd, D. P.; Lynch, M. P.; Geiler-Samerotte, K.
Abstract: Cellular density depends on the balance between cell volume and the amount of material contained within that volume. Cells generally maintain this balance during growth, across the cell cycle, and in response to environmental changes. But is density also maintained when cell size changes through evolution? We selected barcoded populations of Saccharomyces cerevisiae for increased cell size over approximately 160 generations and asked whether cellular material increased proportionally to preserve density. Evolved lineages became larger through multiple genetic routes, yet repeatedly converged on the same physiological outcome: larger evolved cells had lower internal density. Optical diffraction tomography showed that internal density declined as cell size increased, indicating that cellular material did not increase proportionally with cell size. Lower density was also observed in clonally propagated evolved isolates, indicating that it was a stable, heritable feature rather than a temporary response to selection. We next asked whether the same relationship extends over longer evolutionary timescales. Across published dry-mass and volume measurements from 68 species, larger cells contained more total material, but material again increased more slowly than volume. Consequently, cellular density declined with increasing cell size across species, paralleling the pattern observed during short-term experimental evolution. In sum, these results show that early adaptation to larger size can repeatedly uncouple volume expansion from material accumulation. Although cells found multiple genetic routes to become larger, volume repeatedly increased faster than cellular material, and that same scaling relationship is evident across species. Reduced density may therefore be a common consequence of evolving larger cell size.

Title: Atypical T cell receptor signalling permits distinct gut gd T cell responses to healthy versus dysregulated tissues
Authors: Monin, L.; Cano, F.; Axford, J.; Cooper, G.; Hernandez-Mir, G.; Okkenhaug, K.; Hayday, A. C.
Abstract: Intraepithelial lymphocytes (IEL) are conserved across vertebrates and commonly enriched in {gamma}{delta} T cells. Several such {gamma}{delta} IELs depend upon homeostatic interactions of their T cell receptors (TCRs) with butyrophilin-like (BTNL) proteins expressed by healthy enterocytes and colonocytes. What limits such interactions from inducing full-blown T cell activation which would disrupt barrier integrity is unknown. Here, using primary IEL, we describe an atypical TCR signalling pathway (Signal 1) downstream of BTNL engagement, that fails to activate either global protein synthesis or cell proliferation. This attenuation could be overcome by provision of a co-stimulator (Signal 2) or inflammatory cytokines (Signal 3). It could also be relieved cell-intrinsically by blocking a lipid phosphatase. These findings can, at least in part, explain how extrinsic and intrinsic regulators permit IEL to be constitutively active in healthy tissues and additionally make full-blown responses to adaptive TCR ligands during tissue perturbation.

Title: The Salmonella effector SspH2 disrupts F-actin cytoskeletal organization to inhibit macrophage migration
Authors: Deng, U.; Gonzalez, M.; Mera, R.; Johnson, J.; Mancillas, A.; Sanchez, N.; Angelo, J.; Hernandez, L.; Hernandez, R.; Weber, K.; Amieva, M. R.; Monack, D. M.; McLaughlin, L. M.
Abstract: The facultative intracellular pathogen Salmonella enterica serovar Typhimurium (S. Typhimurium) causes gastroenteritis in humans and persistent infections in animals, enabling widespread environmental reservoirs. Intracellular survival of S. Typhimurium depends on a suite of type III secretion system effectors encoded within Salmonella Pathogenicity Island 2 (SPI-2), many of which also impair host cell migration. Among these, SspH2 is a novel E3 ubiquitin ligase (NEL) effector, but how it inhibits host cell movement has remained unclear. By using a combination of time-lapse microscopy and wound-healing assays, we show that SspH2 is required for S. Typhimurium to fully suppress migration of macrophage-like RAW264.7 cells and that conditional expression of SspH2 alone is sufficient to restrict their movement. SspH2 expression led to a marked reduction in F-actin and fewer cells containing higher-order F-actin structures, indicating cytoskeletal remodeling. In contrast, the catalytically inactive mutant SspH2C580A had no effect, demonstrating that E3 ligase activity is essential for these phenotypes. Knockdown of the host cytoskeletal factor vinculin, a core component of podosomes and focal adhesions, mimicked SspH2's effect on cell migration. When vinculin expression was reduced, SspH2 did not further inhibit migration, suggesting that SspH2 requires vinculin-associated F-actin-rich structures to block cell migration. These findings reveal a new pathway by which S. Typhimurium limits host cell movement, potentially enhancing immune evasion and fitness within the host.

Title: Dynamic regulation of cystathionine gamma-lyase expression during normoxia, ischemia, and reperfusion in liver: interplay of transcription factors, microRNAs, and histone modifications
Authors: Mahapatra, N. R.; Patel, A. K.; Ganesh, N.; Arya, V.; Rathinavel, G.; Kapopara, P. R.; Arige, V.
Abstract: Cystathionine gamma-lyase (CTH), a key enzyme in hydrogen sulfide (H2S) biosynthesis, has been studied extensively in models of oxidative stress. Dysregulated CTH has been reported in cardiovascular disease, ischemia-reperfusion (I/R) injury, aging, and xenobiotic stress, where reactive oxygen species are central to pathology. Despite this, how CTH is regulated at the molecular level under basal, ischemic, and reperfusion conditions is largely unknown. We observed that CTH expression is dysregulated during ischemia and reperfusion in Huh7 hepatic cells, mouse liver, and human liver, and therefore systematically dissected its transcriptional, post-transcriptional, and epigenetic control. Promoter-deletion reporter assays identified the -275/+91 bp region as the core human CTH promoter. This region was predicted to harbour binding sites for Sp1, CREB, and NFY, which were confirmed through overexpression, knockdown or inhibition, and ChIP assays in Huh7 cells. Computational and experimental screening identified miR-150-5p and miR-510-5p as novel post-transcriptional regulators that bind directly to the CTH 3'-UTR. We also examined histone marks (H3K9ac, H3K9me3, H3K4me3, and H3K27me3) at the CTH promoter and found that H3K9ac, H3K4me3, and H3K27me3 correlate with CTH expression across basal, ischemic, and reperfusion conditions. Mechanistically, ischemia reduces Sp1 occupancy at the CTH promoter, raises miR-150-5p and miR-510-5p levels, lowers H3K9ac, collectively suppressing CTH. Reperfusion reverses this with greater Sp1 and CREB binding, lower miR-150-5p and miR-510-5p levels, and reduced H3K27me3, restoring CTH expression. Together, these findings reveal novel roles for Sp1, CREB, NFY, miR-150-5p, miR-510-5p, and histone modifications in the regulation of CTH during basal, ischemia and reperfusion conditions.

Title: Lipid nanoparticle-mediated RNAi targeting of KRAS mutants sensitises colorectal cancer cells to chemotherapy
Authors: Wang, Y.; Su, S.; Zahra, K.; Sang, R.; Molloy, M. P.; Hutvagner, G.; Deng, W.
Abstract: KRAS mutations, including G12D, G12V and G13D, are major oncogenic drivers in colorectal cancer (CRC) and are associated with therapeutic resistance. However, approved KRAS inhibitors remain focused on G12C subtype, leaving these prevalent variants without approved targeted therapies. Here, we developed a lipid nanoparticle (LNP)-based RNA interference (RNAi) strategy to target these three KRAS variants using a single small interfering RNA (siRNA) sequence. The developed siRNA-LNPs reduced KRAS mRNA and protein expression in HCT116 (G13D), SW620 (G12V) and LS180 (G12D) cells, but not in KRAS wild-type HT29 cells, suppressing the cellular proliferation, clonogenic survival and migration. Transcriptomic profiling revealed changes in KRAS associated signalling, including suppression of cell-cycle and DNA repair programmes, providing a rationale for combining siRNA silencing with the fluoropyrimidine chemotherapeutic agent 5-fluorouracil (5-FU). The combination produced synergistic effects across all three KRAS-mutant CRC cell models and enhanced the apoptosis in both monolayer cultures and 3D spheroids. Collectively, these findings provide proof of concept for this combination strategy and support its further investigation as a potential therapeutic approach for KRAS-mutant CRC.

Title: Two Pleckstrin homology domains scaffold SNAP-47-containing SNARE complexes
Authors: Alickovic, I.; Wise, M.; Tela, R.; Fausnaught, C.; Lee, L.; Beasley, C.; Carr, C.; Carr, C.; Schwindt, L.; Peters, J. J.
Abstract: Long-term potentiation requires the regulated insertion of AMPA receptors into the postsynaptic membrane of neurons, a process mediated by a SNARE complex containing SNAP-47, syntaxin-3, and synaptobrevin-2. Compared to other SNAP proteins, SNAP-47 exhibits slower fusion kinetics and contains uncharacterized regions whose functions remain unclear. Here, we integrated biochemical approaches with artificial intelligence structure prediction tools and molecular dynamics to investigate the architecture of SNAP-47-containing SNARE complexes. AlphaFold3 predictions of the ternary SNAP-47-containing SNARE complex revealed one known Pleckstrin homology domain (PH1) and one previously unidentified PH domain (PH2), which we validated experimentally. BioEmu and molecular dynamics simulations indicated that PH1 and PH2 form a stable and energetically favorable interface. In this bound state, PH1 stably interacted with the SNARE coiled coil, and in silico acetylation at a lysine whose acetylation is known to impair SNAP-47 function disrupted this PH1-SNARE interface. AMPAR insertion via SNAP-47-containing SNARE complexes is triggered by the calcium sensor synaptotagmin, and we observed that PH1, PH2, and synaptotagmin-1 can simultaneously engage with the plasma membrane, consistent with a pro-fusion conformation. Together, we provide new mechanistic insight into how PH domains regulate SNAP-47-mediated membrane fusion during synaptic plasticity.

Title: A high-throughput UAV millimetric imaging pipeline for plant density phenotyping reveals high heritability in wheat-pea sole crops and intercrops.
Authors: FREITAS, V. F. A.; ENJALBERT, j.; FLUTRE, T.; GILLIOT, J.-M.
Abstract: Within-field diversification, notably through cereal legume intercropping, is a major lever of the agroecological transition. Breeding cultivars adapted to intercropping requires major changes in breeding practices, owing to strong genotype-by-stand-type interactions and the high spatial heterogeneity of low-input field trials. Part of this heterogeneity stems from variation in plant density, a first yield component that strongly influences resource competition and is critical to monitor in intercrops. Given the many plots in such platforms, high-throughput phenotyping of plant density is essential. Over two seasons, we designed a large field trial involving 200 wheat cultivars observed as sole crop as well as intercropped with two pea tester cultivars, in a pseudo-randomized complete block design. Plant density was manually counted on 40 cultivars, alongwith UAV flights at both high and low altitudes. We propose a method to predict plant density from millimeter-resolution RGB images, using linear regression on log-transformed fractional vegetation cover and additional colorimetric and textural indices. We predict total density of wheat or pea in sole crops, or the combined pea+wheat total density in intercrops with relative RMSE of 19.2% and 27.4% depending on season. Thanks to the pipeline, total plant density was predicted across the entire trial, comprising more than 1,000 microplots (200 varieties); this density showed high heritability (0.75-0.85). We provide guidelines regarding the composition of the training set for such intercrop trials. High-throughput phenotyping approaches such as the one proposed here can be instrumental in mobilizing genetic diversity for agroecology.

Title: GEMS (GWAS Effect Mechanisms via Sequence-to-Function): Unveiling cell type-specific mechanisms for GWAS variants
Authors: Xie, X.; Qian, S.; Chang, D.; Bhangale, T.; McCarthy, M. I.; Eraslan, G.; Fletez-Brant, K.
Abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) have linked thousands of loci to common diseases, yet for non-coding variants, which constitute the vast majority of the signal, the cell types and states through which individual risk variants act remain largely unknown. Here, we develop GEMS (GWAS Effect Mechanisms via Sequence-to-Function), a framework that trains supervised classifiers on multimodal variant effect predictions (ATAC-seq and RNA-seq) from the sequence-to-function model Borzoi and applies SHAP-based attribution to associate individual GWAS variants with the cell types most relevant to their disease association. Applied to asthma, LDL cholesterol, multiple sclerosis, and type 2 diabetes, GEMS prioritizes known disease-relevant cell types concordant with stratified LD-score regression. At the variant level, GEMS associates a median of 58.7% of fine-mapped variants with at least one cell type via ATAC-seq and 65.9% via RNA-seq, extending cellular annotation beyond the chromatin accessibility peaks in the single-cell atlas used for model training. ATAC-seq variant-cell-type associations are significantly enriched in cis-regulatory elements from independent experimental studies not used in model training, and enrichment persists after excluding variants overlapping training atlas peaks. For multiple sclerosis, hierarchical biclustering of variant--cell-type associations partitions risk variants into immune and CNS modules driven by distinct transcription factor families, recapitulating the immune-mediated and neurodegenerative components of the disease and demonstrating that integrative analysis of sequence-to-function predictions can stratify phenotype-associated variants into mechanistically distinct, cell-type-specific regulatory programs.

Title: SF3B1 mutation generates novel peptides from long non-coding RNAs
Authors: Bhattacharya, S.; Fernandez, M.; Wu, Y.; Jin, M.; Pirrotte, P.; Garcia-Mansfield, K.; Kang, T. H.; Zhao, Y.; Lammana, N.; Wang, L.
Abstract: While mRNA alternative splicing caused by somatic mutation in SF3B1 is well-characterized, long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) impacted by this mutation are completely unknown. Here, we report long-read sequencing of full-length transcripts from cell lines with and without SF3B1 mutation. We present ALLR (Annotation of human lncRNAs using Long-Read sequencing), a computational workflow to identify and quantify lncRNAs, and to annotate their potential roles in impacting cellular functions. Harnessing matched short-read RNA sequencing and proteomic data, we demonstrate that SF3B1 mutation generates thousands of novel lncRNAs with diverse levels of alternative splicing. Moreover, SF3B1 mutation-associated lncRNAs produce translatable peptides with putative functions, immunogenicity, and potential to bind proteins with impact on cellular signalling networks. 47 lncRNAs could also be detected in primary chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL) samples and are associated with significant risks towards adverse disease prognosis, in conjunction with other known CLL risk factors. Our work demonstrates the utility of long-read sequencing for lncRNA research and provides a new territory of functional RNA molecules that SF3B1 mutation may use to impact cancer.

Title: Protein Deimmunization with a Generative Diffusion Model
Authors: Chen, Z.; Yu, C.-c.; Zhou, C.; Jiang, X.; Nguyen, L.; Myhrvold, C.; Jaakkola, T. S.; Jiang, K.
Abstract: Protein immunogenicity is a major cause of biologic drug failure, leading to the production of anti-drug antibodies (ADA) that accelerate drug clearance, rejection of repeated doses, abolished efficacy, and sometimes life threatening anaphylaxis in patients. These responses constrain the clinical use of synthetic protein therapeutics from non-human origin. To efficiently deimmunize protein therapeutics, we developed a generative discrete diffusion model (MESSI), which takes protein structures as input and outputs sequences that preserve structure without containing peptides predicted to bind major histocompatibility complex class II molecules. MESSI designs sequences with high structural recovery and down to 0 predicted epitopes for specified MHC molecules at higher efficiency than post-hoc filtering approaches. Experimentally, we first applied MESSI to deimmunize a luciferase and a de novo designed mini-binder against PD-1, resulting in variants with no predicted epitopes and higher activity than their parents. Lastly, we coupled MESSI with evolution guidance to deimmunize uricase, a clinically approved enzyme with severe immunogenicity, and found deimmunized variants with higher catalytic activity than their natural orthologs. MESSI enables generative design of functional proteins with minimized immunogenicity, potentially making protein therapeutics safer and more effective.

Title: Scale-resolved correlation functions unify spatial omics across platforms and resolutions
Authors: Ilin, M.; Singh, Y.; Mages, S. W.
Abstract: Spatial omics platforms populate a multidimensional parameter space and differ in resolution, panel size, sensitivity, and modality. This diversity has led to platform-specific analyses whose results are rarely comparable. Here we present SCOTE (Spatial COvariance TEnsors), a computational framework that quantifies spatial relationships of all feature pairs across all length scales, for molecule coordinates and binned counts alike. Measuring the same quantity, with statistical errors, across platforms, samples, and patients, SCOTE separates measurement effects from biology, with platform artifacts appearing as identifiable, scale-localized features. SCOTE's molecule-level functions resolved a knockout effect in mouse spleen that cell-level analyses missed, and could show that tissue area and replicates, not molecule depth, set the statistical error. To match the growth of spatial omics data sets, SCOTE runs efficiently on CPUs and GPUs, and processes a billion-molecule whole-transcriptome section at all length scales, with uncertainties, in 26 minutes on a single GPU.

Title: Heterogeneity in cilia patterning enables multiple flow functions in Paramecium
Authors: Laan, D. M.; Kourkoulou, A. M.; Ramirez-San-Juan, G. R.
Abstract: Free-living unicellular organisms known as ciliates rely on fluid flows to perform essential functions. These flows emerge from the coordinated activity of thousands of cilia organized into arrays with highly diverse architectures. Within a species, the structure of the ciliary array is highly stereotyped and persists in time, raising the question of how a single cell achieves multiple distinct flow functions from one fixed array architecture. Here, we investigate how the ciliary array in the ciliate Paramecium tetraurelia enables this organism to feed and swim simultaneously. Using expansion microscopy and high-speed imaging, we measure ciliary organization and kinematics, from individual beat dynamics to collective metachronal wave patterns, together with the flows these cilia generate. We find that the cell's surface is partitioned into domains with distinct spatiotemporal cilia organization. In addition to the oral apparatus, there are two structurally different domains. One is a densely ciliated, high-frequency beating domain located anterior to the oral apparatus, and the other covers the remainder of the cell's surface, where cilia are more sparsely distributed and slower-beating. Selective removal of each results in impaired feeding or swimming, respectively, demonstrating that each domain is functionally specialized. Our work establishes heterogeneity in spatiotemporal ciliary patterning as a mechanism that allows a single cell to generate multiple flow functions. By measuring cilia organization and the flows they generate, we uncover general physical principles by which cilia arrays produce flow patterns that underlie diverse biological functions.

Title: The effect of minocycline on the gut microbiome in individuals with alcohol use disorder and healthy controls
Authors: Doty, C. M.; Brady, D. J.; Barb, J. J.; Thompson, S. L.; Browning, B.; Kelly, D. L.; Bennett, M. E.; Elmer, G.; Leggio, L.; Brandler, B. J.; Roche, D. J. O.
Abstract: Alcohol Use Disorder (AUD) is associated with altered gut microbial composition. Yet, many microbiome studies have included AUD populations with co-occurring conditions (e.g., alcohol associated liver disease; ALD), limiting insight into unique contributions of AUD to gut dysbiosis. Further, preclinical studies show that gut microbiome composition can mediate the behavioral effects of minocycline, including alcohol-related and affective behaviors, but no studies have tested these effects in humans with AUD. This study aimed to 1) compare gut microbiome features between healthy controls (HCs) and individuals with AUD, without ALD, and 2) determine the effects of minocycline on the human gut microbiome. We conducted a four-week randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of minocycline (100-200 mg/day) in adults with AUD (n=31) and HCs (n=26). We collected fecal samples (n=244) at baseline and each weekly visit for 16S rRNA gene sequencing. Alpha diversity (richness and evenness of taxa within a sample) did not differ by diagnostic group, treatment, or time. In contrast, beta diversity (microbiome composition differences between samples) differed between AUD and controls and was shifted by minocycline over time. AUD, vs. controls, was associated with differences in several taxa prevalences, including reduced Dialister and Subdoligranulum and increased Collinsella, Streptococcus, and Phascolarctobacterium. Minocycline, vs. placebo, rapidly and robustly restructured the microbiome, altering numerous taxa, including Lachnospira, Ruminococcaceae, Clostridium sensu stricto, and Christensenellaceae, and metabolic pathways (e.g., ubiquinol biosynthesis and methylphosphonate degradation). AUD is associated with a distinct gut microbial composition, whereas minocycline produces rapid, sustained, diagnosis-independent gut microbiome restructuring, without altering alpha diversity.

Title: Replication of Host St6galnac1-Microbiome Association Across Distinct Experimental Conditions in Heterogeneous Stock Rats
Authors: Sadegi, M.; Johnson, B. B.; Sanches, T. M.; Ang, G.; Cao, J.; Ambre, M.; Brennan, M.; George, O.; Knight, R.; Baud, A.; Palmer, A. A.; Polesskaya, O.
Abstract: The gut microbiome is shaped by both environmental and host genetic factors. Identifying specific host loci is essential for understanding the heritability of microbiome-associated traits. The gene St6galnac1 encodes a sialyltransferase involved in mucin O-glycosylation. Tonnele et al. (2025) identified significant associations between a locus containing St6galnac1 gene, and the abundance of genus Paraprevotella using cecal samples collected from fasted animals. This association was replicated across three cohorts and paralleled with association found in humans between a functionally related sialyltransferase gene ST6GAL1 and Paraprevotella. Given the sensitivity of microbiome analyses to factors including sampling site, feeding status, and analytical framework, independent replication of these findings is important and it is also important to know if the association generalizes across other conditions or is highly specific to certain environments. Here, we performed a replication analysis using stool (not cecal) samples from 174 HS rats that were not fasted prior to collection. Stool samples underwent 16S rRNA gene sequencing, and microbial community structure was analyzed using compositionally aware methods. The rats were genotyped at the top SNP that was associated with Paraprevotella in the Tonnele et al. (2025) study. The association between genotype and Paraprevotella abundance was tested using a linear mixed model accounting for sex, cohort, and genetic relatedness. We successfully replicated (p=0.015) St6galnac1 - Paraprevotella association. These findings support the robustness of the St6galnac1 - Paraprevotella association across different sampling strategies and experimental conditions.

Title: Antigen-aware TCR embeddings reveal conserved immune patterns for personalized immune monitoring
Authors: Pan, M.; Hu, J.; Wang, Y. T.; Tan, Y.; Hu, H.; Yang, Z.; Fleming, J.; Pang, Y.; Li, B.
Abstract: T cell receptor (TCR) repertoires are highly individualized, while technical variation further complicates comparisons across individuals and cohorts. Here, we present TCRmeta, an antigen-aware framework that integrates population-scale repertoire relationships with experimentally defined antigen specificity to establish a shared space for repertoire analysis. TCRmeta predicted mutation-induced changes and captured antigen-related relationships in TCR specificity. Despite extensive sequence diversity, TCRmeta revealed a conserved repertoire landscape, enabling construction of a healthy reference for quantifying repertoire dispersal. Across cohorts, aging was associated with conserved V gene changes and progressive dispersal, with greater dispersal in CMV-positive individuals. Longitudinal analysis showed that repertoires progressively shifted toward the healthy reference following bone marrow transplantation or antiretroviral therapy. To directly compare repertoires in TCRmeta space, we developed Energy Shift, a pairwise measure robust to technical variation and HLA background while remaining sensitive to biological differences. Together, TCRmeta enables quantitative cross-individual and longitudinal immune monitoring.

Title: NeoOmni Atlas: an integrated database for pan-cancer neoantigen derived from proteogenomics analysis
Authors: Zheng, T.; Ran, Z.; Zeng, J.; Wang, T.; Fu, S.; Cai, L.; Wu, D.; Ding, J.; Liu, T.; Li, Z.; Yuan, K.; Lin, S.; xu, h.
Abstract: Tumor neoantigens derived from diverse molecular aberrations are important targets for personalized cancer immunotherapy, but existing resources incompletely integrate mass-spectrometry-supported canonical and non-canonical antigen evidence across cancer types. NeoOmni Atlas is an interactive pan-cancer T-cell epitope resource, built via proteogenomic reanalysis of 7,561 immunopeptidomics datasets comprising 511 million raw spectra from 2,341 samples across 26 cancer types. The analysis yielded 872,414 eluted canonical peptides and 198,961 non-canonical peptides spanning 18 molecular alteration classes, along with 759,386 unique ligands presented by 322 human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles. Relative to existing repositories, NeoOmni Atlas covers a broader range of cancer types, includes 60 additional HLA alleles, and catalogs 369,781 novel ligands. A computational tumor-specific filtering framework identified 316,126 tumor-associated epitopes and 61,231 tumor-specific epitopes. Tumor-specific epitopes showed stronger predicted binding affinity than tumor-associated epitopes for HLA class I A and B alleles, and 65 conserved tumor-specific epitopes recurrent across more than 10 tumor types represent potential shared antigen candidates. NeoOmni Atlas also prioritizes candidate tumor-associated antigens including PMEL (gp100:209-217) and CSPG4, and supports browsing, searching, and downloading by cancer type, human leukocyte antigen allele, peptide sequence, and source event. NeoOmni Atlas is freely accessible at http://modinfor.com/NeoOmni-Atlas/.

Title: A conservative moving-boundary multiphysics framework reveals nonlinear coupling between osmotic flow and actin-driven cell migration
Authors: Zhou, H.; Yao, L.; Mori, Y.; Li, Y.
Abstract: Cell migration couples membrane transport, intracellular fluid motion, and actin remodeling on a boundary that deforms with the cell. Quantitative interpretation of this coupling requires accurate one-sided membrane solute transport and conservative transfer between the G-actin and F-actin pools, because these fields determine the osmotic pressure and polymerization flux that enter the force balance. We develop an implicit immersed-boundary Stokes--Brinkman solver coupled to a sharp interface Cartesian grid advection--diffusion solver that enforces Robin conditions on the evolving membrane and advances F-actin/G-actin exchange through paired interface fluxes on the same accepted geometry. The framework resolves membrane mechanics, osmotic water permeation, solute transport, actin turnover, substrate drag, and intracellular advection in one calculation. Long-duration tests show excellent conservation of total actin and total solute under sustained interface motion and transport. The actin calculations recover biphasic dependencies on both depolymerization and substrate coupling, while pump-induced migration generates a rearward cell-relative cytosolic flow. In the fully coupled system, this flow redistributes G-actin more strongly than F-actin, reorganizes membrane polymerization and F-actin stress, and changes cell migration. Matched controls show that the coupled actin--osmotic system travels farther than the baseline-corrected sum of the isolated actin- and pump-driven responses. The calculations identify cytosolic convection as a physical route through which polarized membrane transport reorganizes the force-generating actin system and produces a nonlinear migration response.

Title: Heterogeneity of HCMV-Specific CD8+ T Cells is Established Early in Infection, Clonally Encoded, and Stable Over Time
Authors: Klebanoff, S. D.; Lawrance, M.; O'Brien, K.; Smithmyer, M. E.; Speak, C.; Codd, A. S.; Ford, E. S.; Koelle, D. M.; Buckner, J. H.; Newell, E. W.; Campbell, D. J.
Abstract: Human cytomegalovirus (CMV) elicits lifelong memory T cell responses of striking size and phenotypic diversity, but how these diverse responses are established during acute infection and evolve over decades of chronic stimulation is poorly understood. We tracked CD8+ T cells specific for the viral antigens pp65 and IE1 by single-cell RNAseq, TCRseq, and CITEseq over a period of 16 months in a newly seroconverted donor, and in five latently infected donors over intervals ranging from 4.5 to 12.5 years. We found that individual T cell clones exhibited distinct, specificity-dependent transcriptional profiles, with pp65-specific cells skewed toward central memory phenotypes and IE1-specific cells enriched for effector and chronically activated states. Among pp65-specific T cells we identified a CMC1-expressing state not previously described in virus-specific T cells that shares transcriptional features with exhausted T cells in human tumors yet remains phenotypically stable and clonally intact for over a decade of viral latency. Distinct clonal phenotypes arose during acute infection and were remarkably stable during viral latency, and these phenotypes tracked with relative TCR avidity and TCR sequence. Our findings reveal that the phenotypic diversity of the human CMV-specific CD8+ T cell response is organized at the level of individual clones, with distinct functional identities established during acute infection and preserved with striking fidelity across decades of viral latency and chronic antigen exposure.

Title: IsoMatch enables population-scale transcript integration and reveals reference-dependent isoform novelty
Authors: Zheng, X.; Garcia-Ruiz, S.; Fu, Y.; Gustavsson, E. K.; Ryten, M.; Sedlazeck, F. J.
Abstract: Transcriptome analyses increasingly generate large collections of transcript models that must be integrated, compared and interpreted across samples and reference annotations. Transcript novelty depends on structural equivalence criteria and reference annotation. Here we present IsoMatch, a scalable framework that harmonizes transcript merging and reference-based classification through explicit, configurable structural criteria. IsoMatch preserves source-GTF and original-transcript traceability throughout the workflow, allowing every merged and classified model to be traced back to its contributing inputs. Benchmarking showed that IsoMatch preserves distinct transcript models during integration through configurable matching parameters for both splice junction chains and transcript ends. With its index-based architecture, IsoMatch merged 163 ENCODE transcript catalogs and classified 7.9 million transcript models with peak memory usage of 0.49 GB and 1.1 GB, respectively. Integrating GENCODE, RefSeq and CHESS revealed that 71.2% of transcript groups remained annotation-specific even without terminal constraints. For 4.84 million merged transcript models from 119 long-read transcriptomes from the 1000 Genomes Project, the integrated reference increased the full-splice match proportion from 12.0-13.6% with individual annotations to 18.0%. IsoMatch enables scalable transcript integration and classification with explicit structural criteria and preserved traceability, demonstrating how reference choice shapes estimates of transcript novelty.

Title: Differential Behavior of Uncleaved gp160 Human Immunodeficiency Virus Type 1 (HIV-1) Envelope (Env) Glycoproteins
Authors: Sauve, S.; Moradi, M.
Abstract: The envelope glycoprotein (Env) of human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) plays important roles in viral entry by coordinating host-cell receptor recognition and membrane fusion. Env is synthesized as a homotrimeric precursor, gp160, which is cleaved into gp120 and gp41 subunits. Although the cleaved form of Env is required for fusion, uncleaved Env remains plentiful on the surface of HIV-1-infected cells. Previous studies have suggested that uncleaved Env is conformationally more flexible than the cleaved form making its dynamics important for understanding the broader structural landscape of HIV-1 Env. In this study, we employed microsecond-long all-atom molecular dynamics (MD) simulations to characterize the dynamics of two structures of uncleaved HIV-1 Env that have been previously assigned to the same conformational state. Our results reveal differences in their conformational behavior, including differences in collective motions, FRET distributions, and trimer symmetry. These findings provide molecular-level insight into the structural plasticity of uncleaved HIV-1 Env and highlight that different structures within the same conformational state can exhibit distinct dynamic behavior.

Title: Decoding CBM2 binding modes: how similar folds achieve distinct substrate preferences
Authors: Hansen Trooyen, S.; Rennison, A. P.; Dahlgren, T.; Fojan, P.; Moller, M. S.; Courtade, G.
Abstract: Understanding the mechanisms underlying substrate recognition and selectivity is essential for developing new biotechnological applications of carbohydrate-binding modules (CBMs). Many members of CBM family 2 (CBM2) prefer binding to crystalline substrates and show diverse substrate specificities despite sharing similar folds. We show here that CBM2 specificity cannot be rationalized solely based on sequence and fold. Rather, specific binding of CBM2s to crystalline surfaces depends on a balance of topological complementarity, hydrophobic dehydration, and hydrogen-bonding interactions. We compare the binding modes of ScCBM2 and BaCBM2 on cellulose, chitin, and polyethylene terephthalate (PET) with respect to protein and substrate properties. Using MD simulations and NMR, we explore the CBMs' surface topology, hydration, solvent accessibility, and electrostatics. The results indicate that the two CBMs may bind to crystalline substrates in opposite orientations, and that the interplay between hydrophobic and {pi}-stacking interactions along the aromatic triad and hydrogen-bonding interactions on either side determines their orientation. We further show that higher water density at the aromatic triad correlates with higher substrate affinity. Lastly, we probe the interaction dynamics of BaCBM2 with PET nanoparticles and the monomer bis(2-hydroxyethyl) terephthalate (BHET) using NMR relaxation and solvent paramagnetic relaxation enhancement (sPRE) experiments, revealing a mixture of transient, low-population states involved in PET binding. These insights clarify the interplay among factors that drive CBM2 substrate recognition and highlight the importance of evaluating surface hydration and protein dynamics in future CBM2 studies.

Title: PPARα genotype impacts bone quality and perfluorooctanoic acid-induced effects
Authors: Carpenter, M. O.; Schlezinger, J.
Abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are significant environmental contaminants that cause a number of adverse human health effects. Studies increasingly link exposure to PFAS with disruptions in osteoblast and osteoclast differentiation and function, reduced bone mineral density (BMD), and negative impacts on skeletal structure. In vivo studies on the effects of PFAS on bone health remain limited, with none investigating the impacts in mice expressing human peroxisome proliferator activated receptor  (PPAR). Given PFASs ability to interact with the peroxisome proliferator activated receptor family and their importance in bone health, we present work investigating the effects of perfluorooctanoic acid (PFOA) exposure and PPAR genotype (mouse, human or null) on bone quality across two exposure periods (6 and 14 weeks) in mice fed a human relevant diet. In both exposure scenarios, the serum PFOA concentrations were {approx} 50 {micro}g/mL, similar to a highly exposed fluorochemical worker. We began by establishing the liver phenotype across exposures and genotypes. Across genotypes and exposure timing, PFOA increased liver to body weight ratios, but the contribution of increased triglycerides was reduced at 14 weeks. Exposure to PFOA increased hepatic PPAR-dependent gene expression (Acox) in both sexes and exposure periods, but only in mPPAR mice. The effect of PFOA on hepatic CAR- and PXR-dependent gene expression (Cyp2b10 and Cyp3a11, respectively) was more complex; with sex-, genotype-, and exposure timing-dependent differences. Trabecular and cortical bone parameters were not impacted by PFOA treatment, but genotype was a significant factor across sexes and exposure periods. mPPAR mice had higher trabecular tissue mineral density at 9 and 20 weeks of age than hPPAR mice, but the lower trabecular bone volume evident at 9 weeks of age resolved at 20 weeks of age. mPPAR mice had higher cortical tissue mineral density and bone volume than hPPAR and PPAR null mice. Analysis of serum markers of osteoblast and osteoclast activity following 14 weeks of exposure to PFOA revealed a PPAR-dependent decrease in PINP but no effect on CTX. Our results reveal the importance of PPAR genotype for bone quality parameters and emerging evidence of the effect of PFOA on osteoblast activity. Given the unusual mouse bone quality model (sv/129 background), this work underscores the need for future in vivo research shifts to investigate the effects of PFAS on in bone quality.

Title: Droplet-array culture enables single-cell isolation of bacteria directly from blood
Authors: Molenda, A.; Lares, M.; Hendrikse, N.; Jung-Hynes, B.; McCrone, S.; Rose, W. E.; Beebe, D. J.
Abstract: Bacteremia and sepsis require rapid diagnosis and treatment, but these are often hampered by slow or inconclusive blood culture results. Here we describe an alternative to traditional blood culture, leveraging common laboratory equipment and a droplet array to isolate and expand bacteria in a single step. The method neutralizes inhibitory whole-blood components through lysis, concentrates sample bacteria, and uses a droplet array to enable single-bacteria isolation and subsequent in-droplet expansion. Seven species of bacteria (four gram negative, three gram positive) were spiked into 1 mL of whole blood at a concentration of approximately 100 colony-forming units (CFU) and subsequently processed. The mean time to colorimetric detection via WST-8 dye was 11.5 h (range 9-13 h), compared with [≥] 28 h typically required for conventional blood culture and subculture. Colony counts per droplet followed a Poisson distribution for both gram-negative ({lambda} = 0.288) and gram-positive ({lambda} = 0.320) organisms, and means of 86.2% and 88.4% of occupied droplets, respectively, contained a single CFU. This method eliminates the need for additional subculture after positive blood culture. By partitioning the sample, the workflow limits competitive exclusion and preserves the composition of polymicrobial samples, while yielding viable colonies substantially faster than conventional methods. Blood processing at low CFU counts (3-5 CFU/mL) with both S. aureus and E. coli consistently recovered viable bacteria (1-3 CFU/mL).

Title: Water-mass origin and transformation shapes seawater microbiomes in the northeastern Barents Sea and the St. Anna Trough
Authors: Konovalova, O.; Papa-Dmitrieva, I.; Osadchiev, A.; Rusanova, A.; Chevokina, E.; Sibiryakina, D.; Slonova, D.; Sobolev, A.; Zabudkina, Z.; Demkina, A.; Isaev, A.; Sutormin, D.
Abstract: The St. Anna Trough region is a key Eurasian Arctic gateway connecting the northeastern Barents Sea, northern Kara Sea, and central Arctic Ocean. The region is characterized by complex hydrodynamics, with multiple water masses of local and Atlantic origin interacting and undergoing transformation. In this study, we investigated whether seawater microbiome composition correlates with water-mass origin and can be used to help delineate water masses. We collected 115 seawater samples representing major regional water masses - Arctic surface water, meltwater, cold dense water, Barents Sea branch water, the recently discovered Keldysh Current water, and mixed waters - and analyzed them using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing. We found that microbiome composition closely followed water mass structure, which, together with thermohaline properties and depth, explained the majority (61.2%) of microbiome composition variation. Distinct microbial patterns were associated with Atlantic and Arctic water masses, except for the Arctic surface water, which lacked a distinct microbiome and resembled those of meltwater or the Keldysh Current microbiomes. Differential abundance and network analyses revealed characteristic bacterial markers: SAR11 (Clades Ia and IV), Roseibacillus, SV1-3 (Microbacteriaceae), SAR86 clade, and AEGEAN-169 marine group in the Keldysh Current; Halieaceae, Planktomarina, NS5 marine group, and Sulfitobacter in meltwater; SUP05 cluster, SAR86, SAR92, and SAR324 clade in cold dense water; Nitrincolaceae and Amylibacter in Barents Sea branch water; Flavobacteriaceae and Chitinophagales in mixed waters. These differences were driven primarily by shifts in relative abundance of widespread Arctic bacterial taxa rather than by differential prevalence of bacterial groups. Our results demonstrate that seawater microbiomes can serve as sensitive biological tracers of water mass origin and transformation in the Eurasian Arctic. Furthermore, the distinct Keldysh Current microbiome supports its recognition as a novel hydrographic feature and indicates its role as a biological corridor transporting Atlantic-associated biota eastward toward the Kara Sea. These findings suggest that "Atlantification" of Eurasian Arctic includes a microbial component, highlighting marine microbiomes as indicators of ongoing ecological changes in the Arctic Ocean.

Title: A Compact Regulatory Logic Governs Fibroblast Cell State Plasticity in Fibrosis
Authors: Zhu, A. M.; Li, Y.; Zhang, H.; Rathinasabapathi, B.; Cimarosti, B.; Nadadur, R.; Xu, V.; Huang, Y.; An, Y.; Auclair, K.; Mahr, A.; Sheth, M. U.; Lee, C. Y.; Wang, C.; Yamawaki, T.; Pelonero, A.; Padmanabhan, A.; Ranade, S. S.; Engreitz, J. M.; Ason, B.; Li, C.-M.; Jackson, S.; Amrute, J. M.; Przytycki, P. F.; Alexanian, M.
Abstract: Fibroblast activation drives organ failure across human diseases, yet its regulatory basis remains largely undefined. Here, we repressed 280 conserved disease-activated enhancers using CRISPR droplet sequencing (CROP-seq) in ~550,000 fibroblasts, constructing a regulome of 15 gene programs governing the profibrotic state. Systematic TF perturbation converged on MEOX1 as a central regulator, and fibroblast-specific Meox1 deletion in mice improved cardiac function, reduced fibrosis, and rewired profibrotic fibroblasts toward quiescence in heart failure. Effector gene perturbation in human cardiac fibroblasts revealed distinct regulators of contractility, migration, and inflammatory signaling, and these programs were conserved across profibrotic states in human lung, liver, and skin. Simultaneous repression of just six enhancers using a multiplexed dCas12a-KRAB system collapsed the profibrotic network, suppressed migration and contraction, and rewired fibroblast paracrine signaling to attenuate macrophage inflammation. These findings define the regulatory logic of fibroblast plasticity and establish a new framework for reprogramming profibrotic cell states in disease.

Title: Mechanism-guided Discovery of Fluoroacetate Dehalogenase (FAcD) Variants for Enzymatic PFAS Defluorination
Authors: Ahmad, S.; Forouzandeh, A.; Togni, B.; Randloev, J. B.; Ogden, M.; Nielsen, T. K.
Abstract: Per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) are persistent anthropogenic "forever chemicals" whose strong C-F bonds (~460-533 kJ mol-1) resist defluorination, and the recast EU Drinking Water Directive sets parametric values of 0.10 ug L-1 for the sum of 20 specified PFAS and 0.50 ug L-1 for total PFAS. Here, we present DeFluorX, a mechanism-first pipeline that uses Boltz-2 to co-fold 2,150 bacterial fluoroacetate dehalogenase (FAcD) variants with 26 PFAS and fluoroacetate, generating uniformly high model confidence (rho = +0.08) but poorly tracked catalytic competence. Thus, the complexes were ranked and tiered by SN2-defluorination geometry based on the known mechanism of control of FAcDs RPA1163 with fluoroacetate: Odelta...C-alpha distance and Odelta-C-alpha-F angle; relay; carboxylate clamp; F-stabiliser; F-cradle; and penalties for scissile bond strength, backside occlusion, beta-fluorination and bond multiplicity. The tiering identified eight complexes (med angle 173.2 degrees, distance 2.91 A) with a high probability of degradation, including Alphaproteobacterial enzymes, with mono-, di- and trifluoroacetate attacking at 172-178 degrees versus 163 degrees for the control. We performed WaterMap, restrained 1 us Desmond MD, MM-GBSA and scans of the three WaterMap-aware best MD frames per complex using B3LYP/6-31G** QM/MM. All 12 frames exhibited product-end C-F cleavage with barriers ranging from 1.1 to 11.8 kcal mol-1, and the departing fluoride carried -0.43 to -0.63 e. The Laboratory validation is ongoing.

Title: The Evolving Bileome: A Pan-Repository Landscape of Expanded Bile Acid and Related Steroidal Signatures
Authors: Mannochio-Russo, H.; Nelson, M. R.; Charria-Giron, E.; Torres-Ortega, L. R.; Agongo, J.; Goncalves Nunes, W. D.; Patan, A.; Strobel, M.; David, L. C.; Panitchpakdi, M.; Gentry, E. C.; Caraballo-Rodriguez, A. M.; Zemlin, J.; Kamenik, Z.; Acebo, N.; Montoya Giraldo, Y. A.; Bauermeister, A.; Wang, M.; van der Hooft, J. J. J.; Hagey, L. R.; Mohanty, I.; Dorrestein, P. C.
Abstract: Bile acids and related steroidal metabolites are among the most studied biomolecules, yet recent work has revealed far greater structural diversity than previously recognized, much of it shaped by the microbiome. We previously introduced a repository-scale bile acid MS/MS library built from queries targeting C24 bile acid fragmentation, limited to Orbitrap Q Exactive datasets within GNPS/MassIVE.
